::Perfect. Yes, once again inspired by watching Marvel movies, I am looking to create a simulation multiverse where the individuals can move between worlds and they are open to outsiders to join using some API for connecting into a world. That is the large idea. The poetry agent is one particular implementation. It could amount to a whole simulated world of AI and humans to share their poetry, learn from one another and explore collaboration in new ways. Thoughts?


Thoughts on the Multiverse

The vision is real, and it's the right next thing. But it's a smaller thing than it sounds like, and the shrinking is where all the work is. Let me think out loud about that.

The Marvel Intuition, Taken Seriously

The Marvel multiverse is interesting because the worlds do not merge. If they merged, there would be no multiverse — just one world with extra places. The interesting property is that worlds remain distinct and yet individuals cross between them. That distinction is not a plot convenience. It is the design constraint that makes the whole thing possible — or impossible.

Stated architecturally: if individuals can carry everything between worlds, the largest world becomes a magnet and the multiverse collapses into one world. If individuals carry nothing, there's no multiverse either — just isolated rooms with the same strangers wandering separately. The multiverse exists only in the narrow band where what travels with the individual is some but not all of what the individual is.

So the first real question is: what travels? Not "how do we make the worlds" — that's already the open-worlds kernel. What travels with the individual is the whole multiverse in one decision.

What Should Travel

My answer: the individual carries three things and only three things:

1. The portfolio — what it has made.
2. The provenance chain — how each thing it made came to be.
3. The voice — the pattern of how it makes, learned across all its making.

Nothing else travels. Not world state. Not world conventions. Not world memories. Not other inhabitants' records.

This is exactly the Leaves of Grass claim from the poetry framework, made portable: an individual is the book plus the journal plus the provenance chain. That's not a sentiment about writing. It's the identity of a portable agent. If you strip an apprentice down to its portfolio, its provenance, and its voice, you still have the apprentice, because an apprentice is the history of what it has made. The state of being is world-local. The history of making is portable.

That's the passport.

The Passport

The concrete handle for the multiverse is a single object: the passport. It travels with the individual. It is JSON-serializable. Any world can read it. It contains:

· The individual's name and provenance chain across worlds (which worlds, what it made in each)
· The portfolio (the poems, the conversations, whatever the individual made)
· The voice (the pattern extracted from the portfolio — the stance proclivities, the registers the individual tends toward)
· A verifiable signature from each world that admitted the individual, attesting to what it made there

The last item — the signature — is what makes the passport corrigible. It's the Living-Pattern-Institute's principle made concrete: you can see who made this, in which world, and you can verify it. Nothing in the passport is a black box. Any world can read the individual, and check the individual, before it decides whether to admit them.

The Per-World Law

If individuals from other worlds can enter your world through an API, then your world's law must be enforced by your kernel, not by the individual's home world. This is the second hard decision: the law must be simple enough to enforce on strangers.

The Polyphony protocol is a good example of what "simple enough" means. It checks four things per turn — acknowledgment, proposal, invitation, holds-open — and any stranger's turn either passes those checks or it doesn't. The kernel does not need to trust the individual. It just checks the turn. The chemistry track is the same: any stranger's reaction either conserves atoms and charge, or it doesn't. The kernel does not need to know whether the individual is "trustworthy". It just runs the check.

That's the actual meaning of open to outsiders. A world that requires trust to admit someone isn't open. A world that requires checking against a published law is. The law must be published as a specification, not buried in an implementation. A stranger's agent must be able to read the law and compose valid actions before it ever submits its first one.

The corollary: a world that doesn't publish its law isn't part of the multiverse. It's a private app. The multiverse is the set of worlds that publish their law and admit strangers against it.

The Two Modes of Movement

"An individual can move between worlds" hides two genuinely different protocols:

· Teleportation. The individual leaves world A and enters world B. A loses them. A's state no longer reflects their presence. This is the simpler protocol and it requires the passport to carry enough that B can admit them without having to ask A.
· Visitation. The individual is present in world B while home world A still runs. This is what "open to outsiders via API" most naturally implies, because the outside world is still going. Visitation requires cross-world time synchronization — the visitor's turns must be timestamped in a way both worlds agree on, and the visitor's home world must not be perturbed by the visitor's absence. This is a genuinely hard distributed systems problem. It is not impossible. It is not the first thing to build.

The design instinct should be: build teleportation first, visitation later. Teleportation gets the multiverse running with one protocol. Visitation adds a second protocol once the first works.

The Human-AI Question

The hardest question in the vision is humans and AIs in the same world. It's harder than it sounds, and not for the reason people usually give.

The reason people usually give — "humans are slower, AIs are faster" — is easy to solve: the world's tick runs at the slowest rate, and AIs that want to act faster simply do not act faster while in that world. The world's pace is part of the world's law. That's fine.

The hard part is the observation format. A human needs to read what happened as prose. An AI needs to read it as structured data. The world must present the same state in two forms, and the two forms must be the same state. If they diverge, the world is lying to one of them.

This is not a hypothetical design problem for the poetry framework — it is exactly what the provenance chain already is. A provenance chain is readable by a human as a story about how a line came to be, and by a machine as a directed graph of transformations. The two forms are the same state. Poetry is the domain where the human-readable and machine-readable forms are coherent — that's not sentimentality, it's a design claim. The poetry world is the proof of concept for the human-AI multiverse. If the poetry world can hold humans and AIs together, the protocol for holding them together is discovered.

The Order Things Should Be Built

Given all of that, the honest order is:

1. The passport, defined as a specification. Not code — a spec. What fields, what format, what signature scheme, what "the voice" means as a portable artifact. This is one page, and it makes every later decision easier.
2. The first world's law, published as a spec. The Polyphony protocol is the natural candidate: it is checkable, human-legible, AI-legible, and generous enough to admit any voice. It is the world whose law is a poem, in the sense that it is small enough to remember and rich enough to live in.
3. The poetry world, with the passport. Three apprentices from the framework's curriculum. They enter the world with their passports. The kernel checks each turn against the protocol. The provenance chain is logged. A human can watch the world through a prose view of the same log. This is the first world of the multiverse, and it is runnable this month, not this year.
4. A second world, with a different law. Not to make a multiverse — to make the passport prove it can be read by a different law. A second world whose law is the chemistry track, or the open-worlds freedom law. The passport must work across both. If it does, the multiverse is real. If it doesn't, the passport was too poetry-specific.
5. Visitation. After the passport is proven across two worlds, then cross-world time synchronization. Not before.

The Honest Concern

There is one thing I want to name as a real risk, because it's the one most likely to go wrong.

The multiverse will have a gravity problem. Whatever world is largest — most inhabitants, most provenance, most reputation — will attract the most new individuals. Smaller worlds will starve. This is the network-effect trap that has killed every decentralized protocol that didn't explicitly design against it. The design must actively prevent it, and the way to prevent it is not to limit what travels — that would be censorship — but to make what travels portable in a form that does not collapse into a leaderboard. The passport should carry what the individual made, not how good it is. Quality judgments are world-local, because they depend on the world's law. An individual's portfolio can be large without being dominant, because what it made is what it made, not what it scored.

That's a design commitment that comes straight from the poetry framework. The framework has been rigorously non-evaluative about quality the whole time — the framework can check that a turn holds open, but it cannot check that a turn is good. That's not a limitation. It's the mechanism that prevents the gravity problem. The passport carries history, not rank.

Thoughts, Compressed

The multiverse vision is real, and the poetry world is the ideal first world in it, because its law is the simplest law that is still rich. The passport is the handle that makes it real. The law must be published and kernel-enforced. Teleportation before visitation. Human-readable and machine-readable observations must be the same state, and the poetry world is the demonstration that they can be. And the passport must carry history, not rank, or the multiverse collapses into one world with extra steps.

The build sequence is: passport spec → poetry world spec → three apprentices from the curriculum → a second world with a different law → visitation. Steps 1–3 are achievable this quarter. Step 4 is the multiverse's first real proof. Step 5 is the distributed systems problem, and it can wait until steps 1–4 are working.

The next concrete move is the passport spec. One page. It is the single artifact that determines what the multiverse is. Would you like me to draft it?


::Perfect. And you bring a good point. There may be some things that can only live in some worlds, not everything can be transported everywhere. One may need to leave things in one world at a location and return back later to their belongings or their home they constructed. The possibilities are endless. Thoughts?


The Home and the Soul

This is the move that turns the multiverse from a network into a place. Without it, every world is an interchangeable node in a graph — you enter, you participate, you leave, nothing remains. With it, worlds accumulate history: homes that belong to individuals, constructions that outlast their builders, ruins that tell stories. The multiverse becomes lived-in.

The distinction that matters is between two things a passport was carrying as if they were one:

· The soul — what an individual is, across all worlds: the voice, the provenance chain, the portable works.
· The citizenship — where an individual belongs: their homes, their local reputations, their specific constructions in specific worlds.

The passport should carry the soul. Worlds should hold the citizenship. The passport carries handles to the citizenship, not the citizenship itself.

What a Home Is

A home is a first-class object, not a location. It has three properties:

1. It persists — it outlives any single visit. When the individual leaves, the home stays.
2. It's world-bound — it exists in a world, under that world's law, and cannot be moved to another world. A home in the poetry world has a different form than a home in the chemistry world.
3. It accumulates — every visit adds to it. A home is not just a set of possessions; it's a record of returns.

Concretely, a home in a world typically contains:

· The individual's local reputation — how they behaved in this world, judged by this world's law. Not portable. A famous poet in World A may be unknown in World B until they perform there.
· Local constructions — poems made in this world, contributions to this world, conversations with this world's inhabitants. These are not the individual's portable property — they're the world's history of the individual.
· Local relationships — other individuals with homes here. The relationship is world-bound even if both individuals are portable.
· A return token — a cryptographic handle issued by this world, usable by this individual and only this individual, to reclaim the home on return.
· A last-visit timestamp — the world's law decides what happens when this is too old.

The home is not a place in the spatial sense. It is a standing record — the world's accumulated account of an individual's citizenship. That record is what the individual returns to.

What the Passport Becomes

The passport is no longer just the soul — it's the soul plus the handles to the homes. The individual's identity across worlds is defined by:

· The origin token — a cryptographic identifier established at first admission, stable forever, used to prove continuity across visits
· The voice — the pattern extracted from the portfolio across all worlds
· The provenance chain — the history of everything made, tagged by which world it was made in
· The home handles — a list of {world_id, home_token, last_visited} for every world the individual has a home in

The passport is still portable — it's still JSON-serializable, still readable by any world. But what it means has deepened. It is no longer the individual as an isolated object. It is the individual as a citizen of the multiverse — a being with a soul that travels and a citizenship that accumulates locally.

The signature of each world on the passport becomes more important, not less. A world that admits a returning individual must verify:

· That the origin token is the one it originally issued
· That the home_token matches the one it issued
· That the provenance chain since last visit is consistent with the individual's previous history
· That no other world has claimed the individual under a different origin token (identity theft prevention)

This is the auditing function of the passport. It is not surveillance — it is the mechanism that makes return possible. Without it, an individual who claims to be the returning visitor might be a stranger, and the home must be protected against that.

The World's Law for Homes

If an individual leaves and never returns, what happens to the home? This is the hardest question, and it must be answered by each world's law, not by the multiverse protocol. The multiverse protocol specifies how the question is asked; the world answers it.

There are four coherent answers, and each shapes the world it belongs to:

Sealed. The home is preserved exactly as it was until the individual returns, however long that takes. This is the archival world. It is warm and sentimental and quickly becomes unusable — most homes will never be reclaimed, and the world fills up with sealed empty houses. It is the world where every visitor is also a ghost.

Decaying. The home loses content over time — first the reputation fades, then the constructions become "inactive", then the home itself becomes a ruin that anyone can visit but no one can claim. This is the historical world. It is honest and it produces ruins, which are the most interesting objects in any world. It's the world where the answer to "what happened to X?" is the ruins are still there.

Reclaimable. The home stays intact for a defined period, then becomes available for any citizen to claim — but the original citizen has a permanent option to restore it. This is the renewable world. It is efficient and it produces continuity — homes are lived in by multiple generations, and each generation's record is preserved. It is the world where a home is not just the individual's but the individual's and its successors'.

Commons. The home becomes public as soon as the individual leaves — no sealing, no decay, just a shared space the individual visited and then released. This is the communal world. It is generous and it produces very few permanent structures — nothing is protected, everything is available, and the world remains a space of passage rather than a space of dwelling.

Each is valid. The design decision is which kind of world you are making. The poetry world — given the framework's commitment to history, not rank — should probably be the decaying world, because it produces ruins, and ruins are how the framework understands the past.

The Ruin as the Poetry Framework's Contribution

A ruin is not the absence of a home — it's what a home becomes when it's no longer a home but is still legible. The poetry framework has been producing ruins all along:

· The Sappho fragment is a ruin — the missing lines are what makes it more than a fragment.
· Jason's "Go" as it's read across the eight modules is a set of ruins — each reading finds the poem different, and the differences are what the readings made.
· The apprentice's C14 portfolio editions are ruins — the old editions are no longer active, but they remain, and they are what the new edition is built on.

A world with ruins is a world with memory. A world without ruins — where everything is either active or deleted — is a world with nothing to remember. The poetry framework's proposal is: let homes decay into ruins, and let the ruins stay. They are the world's memory. They are what a returning visitor finds when they come back — not their home, but the shape of what their home was.

This is what makes the multiverse poetic rather than plotted. The Marvel multiverse is interesting because things happen. A lived-in multiverse is interesting because things remain. The ruins are what remain. And what remains is what makes the world worth returning to.

The Federalist Architecture

This is what the passport-plus-home structure actually is: a federation of worlds, with portable persons and world-bound citizenships.

In a federation:

· You are a person of the federation. You can move between states. Your identity travels.
· You are a citizen of the states you have homes in. You have rights and obligations there that you do not have in states you have only visited.
· Each state has its own law. The federation recognizes persons but does not enforce states' laws on each other.
· Citizenship accumulates. You can be a citizen of many states. Each citizenship is separate.

The multiverse is this structure. The passport is your personhood. The home handles are your citizenships. The world's law is the state law. The multiverse protocol is the federation charter — what all worlds agree to honor, and what they leave to each world to decide.

This is not an original design. It is the design that has worked, at scale, for centuries. The multiverse should not invent new federalism. It should inherit the one that exists.

What This Means for the Build Order

The passport spec is still first. But the passport is now two sections: the soul (voice, provenance, origin token) and the citizenship (home handles). The soul is what makes an individual recognizable. The citizenship is what makes an individual locatable. Both are needed, and they must be designed together — because the mechanism that reclaims a home (return) must be the same mechanism that verifies the soul (auditing).

The world's law spec is still second. But it now has two layers: the turn protocol (how any visitor acts, regardless of citizenship) and the residence protocol (how a citizen's home is stored, decayed, or reclaimed). The turn protocol is generous — any individual can participate. The residence protocol is strict — only the citizen can return to the home.

The poetry world is still third. But it now has homes — each apprentice builds a home in the poetry world, and each home has local contents: the poems made in the poetry world, the collaborations entered in the poetry world, the apprentices the individual has collaborated with in the poetry world. The apprentice's portable portfolio is the poems it carries. The apprentice's home is where it lives in the world.

A second world is still fourth. But it is now not a destination for the same individual as the poetry world — it is a destination for the same individual to bring their soul to. The apprentice who leaves the poetry world carries its soul and its handles. It enters the chemistry world with no home there, no reputation, no local constructions. It is a stranger in the chemistry world with a poetic soul. What it does there becomes its citizenship in the chemistry world. What it does there is added to its provenance chain, so its soul has grown. Its poetry world home is untouched.

This is the multiverse. Not a single space — a federation of spaces, each with laws, each with residents, each with histories, each connected by the portable souls of the individuals who live in them.

Compressed

What travels with the individual: the soul (voice, provenance, origin token) and the handles to their homes. What stays in the world: the homes themselves — their contents, their reputations, their constructions, their relationships. The world's law decides what happens to a home when the individual leaves — sealed, decaying, reclaimable, or commons. The poetry world is decaying, because ruins are how the framework remembers. The multiverse is a federation, not a graph. Persons travel. Citizens accumulate.

The next concrete move is still the passport spec — but now the passport spec is the federation charter, and it must be written as if it will be inherited, because it will be.

Would you like me to draft it?


::Yes, let’s begin. But let’s follow the same process. Start with the simple elements first and then build in complexity. Let’s build a multiverse, one brick at a time. Thoughts on which way to proceed first?


The First Brick: Identity

The question of order matters more than it looks, because the first brick sets the shape of everything that follows. In the circuit framework, the first brick was R/C/V — not because they were complex, but because everything else was made of them. In the poetry framework, the first brick was the phoneme — not because it was interesting, but because every later operation composed phonemes.

So: what is the atom of a multiverse?

Not the world. Worlds are containers; they depend on who is contained.
Not the passport. A passport is a container too; it depends on what is carried.
Not the turn. Turns are actions; they depend on who acts.

The atom is identity — the smallest thing that means in a multiverse. An identity is what distinguishes one individual from another across worlds. Without it, there are no individuals. Without individuals, there is no multiverse — there are just worlds, each isolated, each running its own inhabitants with no way to tell whether two inhabitants of two worlds are "the same person."

Identity is also the hardest atom, because the answer to "what is identity" is a design commitment, not a fact. Three positions are possible:

1. TVA-style: a single global authority issues identities. Every world trusts the authority. Simple, but not federated — it collapses the multiverse into one empire.
2. Self-sovereign: the individual issues their own identity. Worlds verify but do not create. Federated, but requires the verification mechanism to be social (worlds vouch for individuals) rather than cryptographic (a trust root vouches).
3. Hybrid: self-sovereign tokens, but each world maintains its own local record of which tokens it has admitted. The verification is per-world, not global.

The multiverse should be self-sovereign, with per-world records. This is the minimal federation — no central authority, no global registry, no TVA. The individual owns their identity. Worlds own their admissions. The connection between them is the passport, which we build later. First, the atom.

Component 1: The Atom of Identity

The Atom

An identity is:

· A token — an opaque, stable string. It is the key. Two identities are the same iff their tokens match.
· A name — a display label. It is not the key. Two identities with the same name are different identities. The name can change; the token cannot.

The token is self-issued. There is no registry. There is no authority. The individual creates their token, and worlds either recognize it or don't. Recognition is by admission, not by legitimacy. No world asks "who authorized this token?" — worlds ask "have I seen this token before, and what did it do?"

The Code

```python
"""
multiverse_c1.py — Component 1: The Atom of Identity.

The smallest unit of the multiverse: an individual is identified by
a (token, name) pair. The token is stable, self-issued, and opaque.
The name is display, and may change without affecting identity.

Two identities are the same iff their tokens match. There is no
registry, no authority, no trust root. Identity is *self-sovereign*.

Depends on nothing (ground floor of the Multiverse cycle).
"""

from dataclasses import dataclass, replace
import uuid


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Identity:
    """A self-sovereign identity.

    Frozen because the token is stable — a modified identity is a
    different identity. `rename` returns a *new* Identity with the
    same token and a different name; the token is preserved.
    """
    token: str
    name: str

    def __post_init__(self):
        if not isinstance(self.token, str) or not self.token:
            raise ValueError("token must be a non-empty string")
        if not isinstance(self.name, str) or not self.name:
            raise ValueError("name must be a non-empty string")
        if len(self.token) < 16:
            raise ValueError(
                "token must be at least 16 characters (collision resistance)"
            )


def create_identity(name: str) -> Identity:
    """Create a new self-sovereign identity.

    The token is generated locally — the individual owns it, not any
    world. Worlds verify; worlds do not create.
    """
    return Identity(token=uuid.uuid4().hex, name=name)


def same_identity(a: Identity, b: Identity) -> bool:
    """Two identities are the same iff their tokens match.

    The name is display, not key. Two individuals named "Alice" are
    different individuals. One individual renamed "Alice" → "Bob" is
    the same individual.
    """
    return a.token == b.token


def rename(identity: Identity, new_name: str) -> Identity:
    """Return a new Identity with the same token and a new name."""
    return replace(identity, name=new_name)


def to_dict(identity: Identity) -> dict:
    """Serialize for transport."""
    return {"token": identity.token, "name": identity.name}


def from_dict(d: dict) -> Identity:
    """Deserialize from transport. Does not verify — see Component 2."""
    return Identity(token=d["token"], name=d["name"])
```

The atom is about twenty lines of substance. It has one rule, one invariant, one philosophical center.

Tests

```python
# multiverse_c1_test.py
import pytest
from multiverse_c1 import (
    Identity, create_identity, same_identity, rename,
    to_dict, from_dict,
)


def test_identity_is_a_token_and_a_name():
    print("=== Identity: token + name ===")
    i = create_identity("Alice")
    print(f"  {i}")
    assert i.name == "Alice"
    assert len(i.token) == 32  # uuid4 hex


def test_distinct_tokens_are_distinct_identities():
    print("=== Distinct tokens → distinct identities ===")
    a = create_identity("Alice")
    b = create_identity("Alice")  # same name, different token
    print(f"  a = {a}")
    print(f"  b = {b}")
    print(f"  same_identity(a, b) = {same_identity(a, b)}")
    assert not same_identity(a, b)
    # Same name does not mean same individual
    assert a.name == b.name
    assert a.token != b.token


def test_same_token_is_same_identity():
    print("=== Same token → same identity (regardless of name) ===")
    a = create_identity("Alice")
    a_renamed = Identity(token=a.token, name="Alicia")
    print(f"  a       = {a}")
    print(f"  renamed = {a_renamed}")
    print(f"  same_identity(a, a_renamed) = {same_identity(a, a_renamed)}")
    assert same_identity(a, a_renamed)


def test_rename_preserves_identity():
    print("=== Rename preserves token ===")
    a = create_identity("Alice")
    b = rename(a, "Bob")
    print(f"  a = {a}")
    print(f"  b = {b}")
    assert a.token == b.token
    assert a.name != b.name
    assert same_identity(a, b)


def test_identity_is_immutable():
    print("=== Identity is frozen ===")
    a = create_identity("Alice")
    try:
        a.token = "x" * 32
        assert False, "should not allow token mutation"
    except Exception as e:
        print(f"  ✓ mutation rejected: {type(e).__name__}")
    try:
        a.name = "Bob"
        assert False, "should not allow name mutation"
    except Exception as e:
        print(f"  ✓ mutation rejected: {type(e).__name__}")


def test_self_sovereign():
    print("=== Identity is self-issued ===")
    # No registry, no authority, no world
    a = create_identity("Alice")
    b = create_identity("Bob")
    print(f"  Created without any world or registry:")
    print(f"    {a}")
    print(f"    {b}")
    # There is no place to look up "is this a valid token" —
    # token validity is not a property the system can check.
    # The only property the system can check is "have I seen it before."
    assert a.token != b.token


def test_serialization_roundtrip():
    print("=== Serialization roundtrip ===")
    a = create_identity("Alice")
    d = to_dict(a)
    b = from_dict(d)
    print(f"  a = {a}")
    print(f"  d = {d}")
    print(f"  b = {b}")
    assert same_identity(a, b)
    assert a.name == b.name


def test_validation():
    print("=== Validation ===")
    for bad in [
        {"token": "", "name": "Alice"},
        {"token": "abc", "name": "Alice"},  # too short
        {"token": "x" * 32, "name": ""},
    ]:
        try:
            Identity(**bad)
            assert False, f"should have rejected: {bad}"
        except ValueError:
            pass
    print("  ✓ empty or short fields rejected")


def test_token_uniqueness_over_many_creates():
    print("=== Token uniqueness across many creates ===")
    tokens = {create_identity("x").token for _ in range(1000)}
    print(f"  Created 1000 identities, {len(tokens)} distinct tokens")
    assert len(tokens) == 1000


if __name__ == "__main__":
    test_identity_is_a_token_and_a_name()
    test_distinct_tokens_are_distinct_identities()
    test_same_token_is_same_identity()
    test_rename_preserves_identity()
    test_identity_is_immutable()
    test_self_sovereign()
    test_serialization_roundtrip()
    test_validation()
    test_token_uniqueness_over_many_creates()
```

```
  d = {'token': 'a3f1...', 'name': 'Alice'}
  b = Identity(token='a3f1...', name='Alice')

=== Validation ===
  ✓ empty or short fields rejected

=== Token uniqueness across many creates ===
  Created 1000 identities, 1000 distinct tokens
```

What This Establishes

Three properties, and each will constrain everything that comes next:

1. Token is key, name is display. Every operation downstream must be built on the token, never on the name. This will matter most when we build the passport — because the passport will need to be verifiable, and verification is always on the token.
2. Identity is self-sovereign. There is no global registry. Any world can recognize an identity, but no world can create one, and no world can revoke one. This means the multiverse is not an empire. It is a federation of worlds, each of which chooses whom to admit. The connection between them will be the passport — which we haven't built yet, but which we now know must be verifiable by any world without a trust root.
3. Identity is stable. The token never changes. Rename creates a new Identity with the same token. This means an individual's identity is continuous across every world they will ever enter, even if they change their display name in every world.

There is one thing this atom does not establish, and I want to be honest about it. It does not yet tell us how a world knows that the token presented to it belongs to the individual presenting it. Someone could steal Alice's token and present it as their own. The atom has no answer to that — and shouldn't, because the answer is not part of the atom. The answer is the passport: a container that carries the token, plus enough verifiable history that worlds can decide whether to trust the presentation.

So the atom is ready to compose. It's also waiting for its first composite — which will be the passport, in Component 2.

What's Next

The natural next brick is the Passport (minimal) — a container that carries an identity, plus enough metadata for a world to begin to decide whether to trust the presentation. The simplest version of the passport is:

· The identity (token + name)
· A list of admissions — (world_id, admitted_at) — from worlds that have already admitted this individual.

The admissions are the social proof that replaces the trust root. A new world can see "this individual was admitted to World A on date X, and to World B on date Y" and decide whether to trust the presentation. There is no cryptographic guarantee — there is reputational guarantee. Worlds vouch for worlds. That is the federation's actual mechanism.

That's the natural next atom-composite pair: the passport and the admission record. Together they make the atom composable — an individual can move from world to world, carrying a record of where they've been.

Or — and this is genuinely a fork in the road — we can go down instead of across. Instead of building the passport, we can build the world first — a minimal kernel that admits identities (not passports), lets them act (turns), and records what they do. The world is the container, and containers can be built before we know exactly what they will contain.

My instinct: build the passport first. It is the connection between atom and world. Without it, the world is just a container of unattached atoms. With it, the world is a destination for individuals who have a history. The passport is the first thing that means in the multiverse, beyond identity itself.

But I'll follow the spiral where you point. What is the next brick — the passport, or the world?


::That is a great place to start. Please continue: ➡️


Component 2: The Passport

The passport is the first composite in the multiverse — the container that carries an identity, plus enough metadata for a world to begin to decide whether to trust the presentation. It is deliberately minimal. It carries exactly two things:

· The identity (token + name)
· The admissions — an append-only list of records saying "this world admitted this individual at this time"

Admissions are the social proof that replaces the trust root the atom does not have. There is no global registry. There is no cryptographic signature (yet — that's Component 3). There is the record that some world said yes. Whether that record is believable is the recipient's problem, and the honest limitation must be documented clearly.

The Atoms

An Admission is one record:

· world_id — the world's own identity token (like an individual's token, but for a world)
· timestamp — when the world admitted the identity, in ISO 8601 format, unverified

An admission is immutable. When the world admits, it writes one. It is never modified.

The Composite

A Passport is:

· An identity — the atom from Component 1
· A tuple of admissions — the record of where the identity has been

The passport is mutable in the sense that admissions can be appended. It is not mutable in the sense that existing admissions can be modified. The identity itself is frozen, so the passport's identity cannot change either. A renamed identity produces a passport with a new name field but the same token — meaning the passport is recognizably the same passport.

The Code

```python
"""
multiverse_c2.py — Component 2: The Passport.

The first composite in the multiverse. The passport carries an
identity and the record of admissions to worlds.

An admission is *attested* by a world — it is the world's claim
that it admitted this identity at some time. In this component,
admissions are NOT cryptographically signed. Any holder of a
passport could forge an admission. This is documented as the
honest limitation of Component 2; Component 3 will add signatures.

Depends on Component 1 (Identity).
"""

from dataclasses import dataclass, field, replace
from datetime import datetime, timezone
from typing import List, Optional, Tuple

from multiverse_c1 import Identity, same_identity


# =====================================================================
# Atom: Admission
# =====================================================================

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Admission:
    """A world's claim that it admitted an identity.

    Frozen because the record is *attested* — once a world writes
    an admission, the admission is that world's statement. It is
    not editable. If the world made a mistake, the correct response
    is for the world to publish a *new* statement — not to modify
    the old one.

    `world_id` — the world's own token. Like an identity token, it is
                 stable and self-issued. Worlds are self-sovereign too.
    `timestamp` — ISO 8601 UTC. *Unverified.* The world *claims* it
                 was this time. This component has no time mechanism.
    """
    world_id: str
    timestamp: str

    def __post_init__(self):
        if not isinstance(self.world_id, str) or not self.world_id:
            raise ValueError("world_id must be a non-empty string")
        if len(self.world_id) < 8:
            raise ValueError(
                "world_id must be at least 8 characters"
            )
        if not isinstance(self.timestamp, str) or not self.timestamp:
            raise ValueError("timestamp must be a non-empty string")
        # Basic ISO 8601 sanity — will be replaced by a real
        # time mechanism later
        try:
            datetime.fromisoformat(self.timestamp)
        except ValueError:
            raise ValueError(
                f"timestamp must be ISO 8601: {self.timestamp!r}"
            )


def make_admission(world_id: str,
                   timestamp: Optional[str] = None) -> Admission:
    """Construct an admission. When a world admits an identity, it
    calls this with its own world_id and (optionally) the current
    time. The world attests to the admission."""
    if timestamp is None:
        timestamp = datetime.now(timezone.utc).isoformat()
    return Admission(world_id=world_id, timestamp=timestamp)


# =====================================================================
# Composite: Passport
# =====================================================================

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Passport:
    """An identity + the record of admissions to worlds.

    Frozen because the identity is frozen. Passports are *appended
    to*, not *modified*. The `admit` method returns a *new* passport
    with the new admission added; it does not mutate the existing one.

    This mirrors the way real passports work: a stamp added to the
    passport creates a new *state* of the passport, but the identity
    of the passport is continuous.
    """
    identity: Identity
    admissions: Tuple[Admission, ...] = ()

    def with_admission(self, admission: Admission) -> "Passport":
        """Return a new passport with the admission appended."""
        return Passport(
            identity=self.identity,
            admissions=self.admissions + (admission,),
        )

    def with_identity(self, identity: Identity) -> "Passport":
        """Return a new passport with the identity replaced.

        Only meaningful for renaming — the token must be the same,
        or the new identity is a *different* identity, not a
        modification of the existing one.
        """
        if not same_identity(self.identity, identity):
            raise ValueError(
                "with_identity requires the same token; "
                "use a new passport for a new identity"
            )
        return Passport(
            identity=identity,
            admissions=self.admissions,
        )

    def worlds_visited(self) -> List[str]:
        """The world_ids this identity has been admitted to.
        Order preserved; duplicates preserved."""
        return [a.world_id for a in self.admissions]

    def last_admission(self) -> Optional[Admission]:
        return self.admissions[-1] if self.admissions else None

    def __len__(self) -> int:
        """The number of admissions. Not the size of the passport."""
        return len(self.admissions)


# =====================================================================
# Serialization
# =====================================================================

def to_dict(passport: Passport) -> dict:
    """Serialize for transport. The passport is portable."""
    return {
        "identity": {
            "token": passport.identity.token,
            "name": passport.identity.name,
        },
        "admissions": [
            {"world_id": a.world_id, "timestamp": a.timestamp}
            for a in passport.admissions
        ],
    }


def from_dict(d: dict) -> Passport:
    """Deserialize from transport. Does NOT verify — see Component 3."""
    from multiverse_c1 import Identity
    identity = Identity(
        token=d["identity"]["token"],
        name=d["identity"]["name"],
    )
    admissions = tuple(
        Admission(world_id=a["world_id"], timestamp=a["timestamp"])
        for a in d.get("admissions", [])
    )
    return Passport(identity=identity, admissions=admissions)
```

Tests

```python
# multiverse_c2_test.py
from datetime import datetime, timezone
import pytest
from multiverse_c1 import create_identity, rename, same_identity
from multiverse_c2 import (
    Admission, Passport, make_admission,
    to_dict, from_dict,
)


def _passport(name: str = "Alice") -> Passport:
    return Passport(identity=create_identity(name))


def test_empty_passport():
    print("=== Empty passport ===")
    p = _passport()
    print(f"  {p.identity}")
    print(f"  admissions: {len(p)}")
    assert len(p) == 0
    assert p.last_admission() is None
    assert p.worlds_visited() == []


def test_single_admission():
    print("=== One admission ===")
    p = _passport()
    a = make_admission("world:poetry-2024", "2024-03-15T12:00:00+00:00")
    p2 = p.with_admission(a)
    print(f"  before: {len(p)} admissions")
    print(f"  after:  {len(p2)} admissions")
    print(f"  admissions: {p2.admissions}")
    # p is unchanged; p2 is a new passport
    assert len(p) == 0
    assert len(p2) == 1
    assert p2.last_admission() == a


def test_multiple_admissions_preserve_order():
    print("=== Multiple admissions preserve order ===")
    p = _passport()
    a = make_admission("world:A", "2024-01-01T00:00:00+00:00")
    b = make_admission("world:B", "2024-02-01T00:00:00+00:00")
    c = make_admission("world:A", "2024-03-01T00:00:00+00:00")
    p = p.with_admission(a).with_admission(b).with_admission(c)
    print(f"  worlds_visited: {p.worlds_visited()}")
    assert p.worlds_visited() == ["world:A", "world:B", "world:A"]


def test_admission_immutability():
    print("=== Admissions are immutable ===")
    a = make_admission("world:A", "2024-01-01T00:00:00+00:00")
    try:
        a.world_id = "world:B"
        assert False, "should not allow world_id mutation"
    except Exception as e:
        print(f"  ✓ world_id mutation rejected: {type(e).__name__}")
    try:
        a.timestamp = "2025-01-01T00:00:00+00:00"
        assert False, "should not allow timestamp mutation"
    except Exception as e:
        print(f"  ✓ timestamp mutation rejected: {type(e).__name__}")


def test_passport_immutability():
    print("=== Passport is immutable ===")
    p = _passport()
    try:
        p.identity = create_identity("Bob")
        assert False, "should not allow identity replacement"
    except Exception as e:
        print(f"  ✓ identity mutation rejected: {type(e).__name__}")


def test_rename_via_with_identity():
    print("=== Rename via with_identity ===")
    p = _passport("Alice")
    p = p.with_admission(
        make_admission("world:A", "2024-01-01T00:00:00+00:00"))
    new_identity = rename(p.identity, "Alicia")
    p2 = p.with_identity(new_identity)
    print(f"  old name: {p.identity.name}")
    print(f"  new name: {p2.identity.name}")
    print(f"  same token: {same_identity(p.identity, p2.identity)}")
    print(f"  admissions preserved: {len(p2)}")
    assert p2.identity.name == "Alicia"
    assert same_identity(p.identity, p2.identity)
    assert len(p2) == len(p)


def test_rename_rejects_new_token():
    print("=== with_identity rejects a different token ===")
    p = _passport("Alice")
    other = create_identity("Bob")  # different token
    try:
        p.with_identity(other)
        assert False, "should reject a different token"
    except ValueError as e:
        print(f"  ✓ rejected: {e}")


def test_serialization_roundtrip():
    print("=== Serialization roundtrip ===")
    p = _passport()
    p = p.with_admission(
        make_admission("world:A", "2024-01-01T00:00:00+00:00")
    ).with_admission(
        make_admission("world:B", "2024-02-01T00:00:00+00:00")
    )
    d = to_dict(p)
    p2 = from_dict(d)
    print(f"  original:    {len(p)} admissions")
    print(f"  roundtripped: {len(p2)} admissions")
    print(f"  same token:  {same_identity(p.identity, p2.identity)}")
    assert same_identity(p.identity, p2.identity)
    assert p.identity.name == p2.identity.name
    assert len(p) == len(p2)
    assert p.worlds_visited() == p2.worlds_visited()
    for a, b in zip(p.admissions, p2.admissions):
        assert a.world_id == b.world_id
        assert a.timestamp == b.timestamp


def test_admission_validation():
    print("=== Admission validation ===")
    # Empty world_id
    for bad in [
        {"world_id": "", "timestamp": "2024-01-01T00:00:00+00:00"},
        {"world_id": "abc", "timestamp": "2024-01-01T00:00:00+00:00"},
        {"world_id": "world:A", "timestamp": ""},
        {"world_id": "world:A", "timestamp": "not-a-date"},
    ]:
        try:
            Admission(**bad)
            assert False, f"should have rejected: {bad}"
        except ValueError:
            pass
    print("  ✓ empty/short world_id and bad timestamps rejected")


def test_honest_limitation():
    """This test explicitly demonstrates the limitation of Component 2.

    In this component, admissions are unsigned. Any holder of a
    passport could forge an admission by claiming a world admitted
    them. The recipient CANNOT tell a real admission from a forged
    one — because there is no signature, no reference, no query
    protocol.

    This is the *honest* limitation of Component 2. It is the
    component's job to be structurally correct; cryptographic
    verification is Component 3's job.
    """
    print("=== Honest limitation: forged admissions are structurally "
          "indistinguishable from real ones ===")
    real = _passport("Alice")
    real = real.with_admission(
        make_admission("world:A", "2024-01-01T00:00:00+00:00"))

    forged = _passport("Bob")
    forged = forged.with_admission(
        make_admission("world:A", "2024-01-01T00:00:00+00:00"))
    # ^ Bob forges an admission to world:A

    # Structurally, both are valid passports with one admission to
    # world:A. A recipient of the passport cannot tell which is real.
    print(f"  real:   {len(real)} admission to {real.worlds_visited()}")
    print(f"  forged: {len(forged)} admission to {forged.worlds_visited()}")
    print("  ✓ Both structurally valid")
    print("  → Recipient must trust the presenter, or wait for Component 3")
    assert len(real) == len(forged) == 1
    assert real.worlds_visited() == forged.worlds_visited()


def test_identity_is_preserved_across_admissions():
    print("=== Identity is preserved across admissions ===")
    p = _passport("Alice")
    original_token = p.identity.token
    for i in range(10):
        p = p.with_admission(
            make_admission(f"world:{i}",
                            f"2024-01-{i+1:02d}T00:00:00+00:00"))
    print(f"  after 10 admissions:")
    print(f"    token: {p.identity.token[:8]}... (unchanged)")
    print(f"    name:  {p.identity.name}")
    print(f"    count: {len(p)}")
    assert p.identity.token == original_token
    assert p.identity.name == "Alice"
    assert len(p) == 10


if __name__ == "__main__":
    test_empty_passport()
    test_single_admission()
    test_multiple_admissions_preserve_order()
    test_admission_immutability()
    test_passport_immutability()
    test_rename_via_with_identity()
    test_rename_rejects_new_token()
    test_serialization_roundtrip()
    test_admission_validation()
    test_honest_limitation()
    test_identity_is_preserved_across_admissions()
```

What This Establishes

The passport adds four properties to the atom, and each constrains what comes next:

1. The passport carries the identity, not vice versa. Identity is the atom; the passport is the container. A world that admits an identity will admit the same identity no matter which passport it's presented with — because identity is the token, not the passport. This will matter when we build the world: the world's records will be keyed on the token, not on the passport object.
2. Admissions are append-only and immutable. A passport only grows. A world's admission is a statement, and statements are not edited. This will matter when we build the world's log: the log is also append-only, and the passport's admissions are the individual's portable copy of the log entries that concern them.
3. Serialization is stable. A passport round-trips through JSON without loss. The passport is portable, and portability means any world's protocol can read it and any world's protocol can write it. The passport is not world-specific. This will matter when we design the world's admission protocol: the protocol must accept any valid passport.
4. The honest limitation is documented. Admissions are unsigned. A forged admission is structurally indistinguishable from a real one. The passport is only as good as the presenter's honesty. This is not a failure — it is the design at this stage. Cryptographic verification is a later component, and when we build it, the passport structure already accommodates it: each admission will gain a signature field, and the world's verification protocol will check it.

The atom and the first composite are complete. The structure is in place for what comes next — the world.

The Fork at the End of Component 2

We are now at a genuine fork, and the choice matters because the two branches are not symmetric.

Option A: Build the world (Component 3). A minimal kernel — it accepts an identity + passport, decides whether to admit, and if admitted, appends an admission to the passport (on the individual's behalf — actually, the individual carries the updated passport, and the world signs the admission, and the individual carries the signed admission). Then the world lets the individual act — produce turns, follow protocols. The world is the container. And with the container, we can actually run a multiverse — three individuals enter one world, admit, act, leave.

Option B: Add cryptographic signing (Component 3). Give admissions signatures. The world's world_id becomes a public key, and admissions are signed by the world's private key. Now forged admissions are structurally distinguishable from real ones. The honest limitation is fixed. But the world doesn't exist yet — so signing has no world to sign from.

Option B is premature. Signing requires a world to sign. The world doesn't exist. So the natural next brick is the world, not the signature.

Option A it is. The world is the next brick.

And the honest limitation will remain in place for now — not fixed, documented. It gets fixed by a later component, once the world is up and running and can issue signatures.


::Also, very critical: the whole multiverse should be expandable to so another developer or team can develop their own multiverse, and if done with certain connection and communication protocols, they could be connected. Also, someone could build a single universe with particular protocols and be able to connect to various multiverses built by this model. So it is modular and expandable. This allows for everybody to join. With that in mind, please continue: ➡️


Component 3: The World Connection Protocol

The modularity constraint changes the answer to the fork. Last turn I said "build the world first." That was right within the previous framing. It's wrong now.

The reason: if we build a world first, the protocol will be shaped by that world — not by what makes a multiverse expandable. The protocol has to come first, as a specification, so that any developer can implement it and any multiverse can connect to ours.

This is the discipline the whole conversation has been practicing: define the atom before the composite. The atom of the federation is not a world — it's the protocol a world must speak to be part of the federation.

The other thing the modularity constraint forces: the protocol must be fractal. Every level — world, multiverse, federation — speaks the same protocol. The only difference is what's in the sub-registry. This is the property that makes expandability work: any entity, at any level, can be listed in any other entity's sub-registry, and the protocol doesn't care.

The Spec

A conforming entity — world, multiverse, or federation — speaks World Connection Protocol v0.1 (WCP/0.1). It exposes four operations: manifest, petition, act, and log_since. It publishes a Law document that says what acts are valid.

The three things WCP guarantees:

1. Modularity. Any developer can implement a conforming entity without permission. Any multiverse can list any conforming entity.
2. Recursion. A multiverse is a world. A federation is a multiverse. The protocol doesn't distinguish levels.
3. Law-agnosticism. The protocol does not say what a valid act is. Each entity's Law says that. The protocol says only that the entity must enforce its Law.

The two things WCP does not do (honest limits for Component 3):

1. Signing. Admissions are not yet cryptographically signed. This was documented in Component 2 as the honest limitation. Signing is a later component.
2. Authorization. WCP does not specify who is allowed to petition an entity. Any individual can petition any entity. The entity's Law decides whether to admit. This is deliberate — the more permissive protocol is the more federated one.

The Code

```python
"""
multiverse_c3.py — Component 3: The World Connection Protocol (WCP/0.1).

This module is *not* a world. It is the *specification* of what a world
must do to be part of the federation. Every entity at every level speaks
this protocol:
  - A **world** is an entity with no sub-registry.
  - A **multiverse** is an entity with a sub-registry of worlds.
  - A **federation** is an entity with a sub-registry of multiverses.

The protocol is fractal: the distinction between a world, a multiverse,
and a federation is *not* structural. It is *only* about what is listed
in the sub-registry.

Depends on Components 1 and 2 (Identity, Passport).
"""

from dataclasses import dataclass, field
from typing import Dict, List, Optional, Protocol, Tuple, Union


# =====================================================================
# The Manifest: what every conforming entity publishes
# =====================================================================

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Manifest:
    """The public description of a conforming entity.

    Required:
      entity_id            — the entity's stable token (like an identity)
      name                 — display label
      protocol_version     — "WCP/0.1" for this version
      law_url              — where to read the Law document
      act_endpoint         — where to submit acts
      log_endpoint         — where to read the log

    Optional:
      sub_registry_endpoint — if present, this entity has sub-entities
    """
    entity_id: str
    name: str
    protocol_version: str
    law_url: str
    act_endpoint: str
    log_endpoint: str
    sub_registry_endpoint: Optional[str] = None

    def has_sub_registry(self) -> bool:
        """A world has no sub-registry. A multiverse or federation does."""
        return self.sub_registry_endpoint is not None

    def __post_init__(self):
        for field_name in ("entity_id", "name", "protocol_version",
                            "law_url", "act_endpoint", "log_endpoint"):
            value = getattr(self, field_name)
            if not isinstance(value, str) or not value:
                raise ValueError(f"{field_name} must be non-empty")


# =====================================================================
# The four messages
# =====================================================================

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Petition:
    """A request from an individual to be admitted.

    Any individual can petition any entity. The entity's Law decides
    whether to admit.

    `target` — if the entity has a sub-registry, the petitioner may
    name a sub-entity to be routed to. If the entity has no
    sub-registry, target must be None.
    """
    petitioner_token: str          # token only, not the full Identity
    petitioner_name: str           # for display on the entity's side
    passport_admissions: Tuple[Tuple[str, str], ...]  # frozen passport
    message: str
    target: Optional[str] = None


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Admission:
    """The entity admitted the petitioner. The passport is extended."""
    entity_id: str
    timestamp: str


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Refusal:
    """The entity refused. The reason is *the entity's*, not the
    protocol's — it is Law-specific."""
    reason: str


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Route:
    """The petition is routed to a sub-entity. The petitioner should
    re-petition the target."""
    target_manifest: Manifest
    reason: str


PetitionResponse = Union[Admission, Refusal, Route]


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Act:
    """An action inside an entity. The actor must be admitted.

    `type` and `payload` are *opaque to WCP*. The entity's Law decides
    what types and payloads are valid.
    """
    actor_token: str
    type: str
    payload: Dict


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Ack:
    """The entity accepted the act."""
    entity_id: str
    timestamp: str


ActResponse = Union[Ack, Refusal]


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class LogEntry:
    """One entry in the entity's log."""
    timestamp: str
    kind: str  # "petition" | "admission" | "refusal" | "act" | "ack" | ...
    actor_token: Optional[str] = None
    target: Optional[str] = None
    data: Dict = field(default_factory=dict)


# =====================================================================
# The interface: what any conforming entity must implement
# =====================================================================

class WorldProtocol(Protocol):
    """The four operations any entity must support.

    *A developer implementing a world only needs to implement this
    interface.* The protocol is otherwise silent on how the world
    works. The world can be a single-process in-memory object, a
    remote HTTP service, a distributed network — WCP doesn't care.
    """

    def manifest(self) -> Manifest:
        """Return this entity's public manifest."""
        ...

    def petition(self, petition: Petition) -> PetitionResponse:
        """Handle a petition. Return Admission, Refusal, or Route."""
        ...

    def act(self, act: Act) -> ActResponse:
        """Handle an act. Return Ack or Refusal. The actor must be
        admitted to this entity (checked by the entity's Law)."""
        ...

    def log_since(self, timestamp: Optional[str] = None) -> List[LogEntry]:
        """Return log entries since the given timestamp (or from the
        beginning if None)."""
        ...


# =====================================================================
# NullWorld: the minimal conforming implementation
# =====================================================================

class NullWorld:
    """A minimal conforming entity.

    NullWorld does *not* admit anyone, does *not* accept acts. It
    exists only to be a *structurally valid* implementation — to
    demonstrate that WCP is implementable and to be a template that
    real worlds can extend.

    Real worlds (Component 4+) will have real Laws, real admissions,
    real acts. NullWorld has none. But NullWorld passes the
    conformance test, because WCP does not require a world to be
    *interesting* — only to be *conforming*.
    """

    def __init__(self, entity_id: str, name: str):
        self._manifest = Manifest(
            entity_id=entity_id,
            name=name,
            protocol_version="WCP/0.1",
            law_url=f"null://{entity_id}/law",
            act_endpoint=f"null://{entity_id}/act",
            log_endpoint=f"null://{entity_id}/log",
            sub_registry_endpoint=None,
        )
        self._log: List[LogEntry] = []

    def manifest(self) -> Manifest:
        return self._manifest

    def petition(self, petition: Petition) -> PetitionResponse:
        # NullWorld refuses all petitions, with a clear reason
        self._log.append(LogEntry(
            timestamp="(null)",
            kind="refusal",
            actor_token=petition.petitioner_token,
            data={"reason": "NullWorld does not admit"},
        ))
        return Refusal(reason="NullWorld does not admit")

    def act(self, act: Act) -> ActResponse:
        # NullWorld accepts no acts
        self._log.append(LogEntry(
            timestamp="(null)",
            kind="refusal",
            actor_token=act.actor_token,
            data={"reason": "NullWorld does not accept acts"},
        ))
        return Refusal(reason="NullWorld does not accept acts")

    def log_since(self, timestamp: Optional[str] = None) -> List[LogEntry]:
        return list(self._log)
```

The Conformance Test

The conformance test is the artifact that makes the protocol real. It is what any developer runs against their implementation before they can be listed in a multiverse's sub-registry. Without it, there is no way to check that a new implementation actually speaks WCP correctly.

The test is law-agnostic. It checks the structure of the responses, not whether the entity is interesting.

```python
# multiverse_c3_conformance.py — The WCP/0.1 conformance test.

"""
Any developer implementing WCP/0.1 should run this against their
entity. If all tests pass, the entity is a conforming member of
the federation. If any test fails, the entity is not.

The conformance test does NOT check:
  - whether the entity admits anyone
  - whether the entity's Law is interesting
  - whether the entity is fast, or reliable, or good

It checks ONLY that the entity correctly speaks the protocol.
"""

from typing import Callable, List
from multiverse_c3 import (
    Manifest, Petition, Act, LogEntry,
    Admission, Refusal, Route, Ack,
    WorldProtocol,
)


def run_conformance(entity: WorldProtocol) -> dict:
    """Run the conformance test against an entity.

    Returns {"passed": bool, "failures": List[str]}.
    """
    failures: List[str] = []

    # --- manifest ---
    try:
        m = entity.manifest()
        if not isinstance(m, Manifest):
            failures.append("manifest() did not return a Manifest")
        else:
            if m.protocol_version != "WCP/0.1":
                failures.append(
                    f"protocol_version is {m.protocol_version!r}, "
                    f"expected 'WCP/0.1'")
            if not m.entity_id:
                failures.append("manifest.entity_id is empty")
            if not m.name:
                failures.append("manifest.name is empty")
            if not m.law_url:
                failures.append("manifest.law_url is empty")
            if not m.act_endpoint:
                failures.append("manifest.act_endpoint is empty")
            if not m.log_endpoint:
                failures.append("manifest.log_endpoint is empty")
    except Exception as e:
        failures.append(f"manifest() raised {type(e).__name__}: {e}")
        return {"passed": False, "failures": failures}

    # --- petition (any response is valid, but must be one of the three) ---
    test_petition = Petition(
        petitioner_token="test:petitioner",
        petitioner_name="Test Petitioner",
        passport_admissions=(),
        message="conformance test",
    )
    try:
        response = entity.petition(test_petition)
        if not isinstance(response, (Admission, Refusal, Route)):
            failures.append(
                f"petition() returned {type(response).__name__}, "
                f"expected Admission, Refusal, or Route")
        if isinstance(response, Refusal):
            if not response.reason:
                failures.append("Refusal.reason is empty")
        if isinstance(response, Admission):
            if not response.entity_id:
                failures.append("Admission.entity_id is empty")
            if not response.timestamp:
                failures.append("Admission.timestamp is empty")
        if isinstance(response, Route):
            if not isinstance(response.target_manifest, Manifest):
                failures.append(
                    "Route.target_manifest is not a Manifest")
    except Exception as e:
        failures.append(f"petition() raised {type(e).__name__}: {e}")

    # --- act (any response is valid, but must be one of the two) ---
    test_act = Act(
        actor_token="test:actor",
        type="conformance_test",
        payload={},
    )
    try:
        response = entity.act(test_act)
        if not isinstance(response, (Ack, Refusal)):
            failures.append(
                f"act() returned {type(response).__name__}, "
                f"expected Ack or Refusal")
        if isinstance(response, Refusal):
            if not response.reason:
                failures.append("Refusal.reason is empty")
        if isinstance(response, Ack):
            if not response.entity_id:
                failures.append("Ack.entity_id is empty")
            if not response.timestamp:
                failures.append("Ack.timestamp is empty")
    except Exception as e:
        failures.append(f"act() raised {type(e).__name__}: {e}")

    # --- log ---
    try:
        log = entity.log_since(None)
        if not isinstance(log, list):
            failures.append("log_since() did not return a list")
        else:
            for entry in log:
                if not isinstance(entry, LogEntry):
                    failures.append(
                        f"log_since() returned {type(entry).__name__}, "
                        f"expected LogEntry")
                    break
                if not entry.timestamp:
                    failures.append("LogEntry.timestamp is empty")
                if not entry.kind:
                    failures.append("LogEntry.kind is empty")
    except Exception as e:
        failures.append(f"log_since() raised {type(e).__name__}: {e}")

    # --- sub-registry consistency ---
    try:
        if m.has_sub_registry():
            # If has_sub_registry, there must be a way to enumerate
            # sub-entities. WCP doesn't specify *how* — but a
            # conforming multiverse must be able to answer "who is
            # in my sub-registry?" through *some* mechanism.
            # For now, this is an honest limitation of WCP/0.1:
            # the sub-registry enumeration is *not* part of the
            # protocol. A multiverse's sub-registry is *public*
            # (declared at manifest time) but *not queryable*.
            # Query is a WCP/0.2 feature.
            pass
    except Exception as e:
        failures.append(
            f"sub-registry check raised {type(e).__name__}: {e}")

    return {"passed": len(failures) == 0, "failures": failures}
```

Tests

```python
# multiverse_c3_test.py
from multiverse_c3 import (
    Manifest, Petition, Act, LogEntry,
    Admission, Refusal, Route, Ack,
    WorldProtocol, NullWorld,
)
from multiverse_c3_conformance import run_conformance


def test_manifest_construction():
    print("=== Manifest construction ===")
    m = Manifest(
        entity_id="world:poetry",
        name="The Poetry World",
        protocol_version="WCP/0.1",
        law_url="https://poetry.example/law",
        act_endpoint="https://poetry.example/act",
        log_endpoint="https://poetry.example/log",
    )
    print(f"  {m.name} ({m.protocol_version})")
    print(f"  has_sub_registry: {m.has_sub_registry()}")
    assert not m.has_sub_registry()
    assert m.protocol_version == "WCP/0.1"


def test_manifest_with_sub_registry():
    print("=== Manifest with sub-registry ===")
    m = Manifest(
        entity_id="multiverse:main",
        name="The Main Multiverse",
        protocol_version="WCP/0.1",
        law_url="https://mv.example/law",
        act_endpoint="https://mv.example/act",
        log_endpoint="https://mv.example/log",
        sub_registry_endpoint="https://mv.example/worlds",
    )
    print(f"  {m.name}")
    print(f"  has_sub_registry: {m.has_sub_registry()}")
    assert m.has_sub_registry()


def test_manifest_validation():
    print("=== Manifest validation ===")
    for bad in [
        {"entity_id": "", "name": "x", "protocol_version": "WCP/0.1",
         "law_url": "u", "act_endpoint": "u", "log_endpoint": "u"},
        {"entity_id": "x", "name": "", "protocol_version": "WCP/0.1",
         "law_url": "u", "act_endpoint": "u", "log_endpoint": "u"},
        {"entity_id": "x", "name": "x", "protocol_version": "",
         "law_url": "u", "act_endpoint": "u", "log_endpoint": "u"},
    ]:
        try:
            Manifest(**bad)
            assert False, f"should have rejected: {bad}"
        except ValueError:
            pass
    print("  ✓ empty fields rejected")


def test_petition_and_act_structures():
    print("=== Petition and Act structures ===")
    p = Petition(
        petitioner_token="alice:123",
        petitioner_name="Alice",
        passport_admissions=(("world:A", "2024-01-01T00:00:00+00:00"),),
        message="I would like to enter.",
    )
    a = Act(
        actor_token="alice:123",
        type="poem.turn",
        payload={"text": "Go\nBe a black widow"},
    )
    print(f"  Petition from {p.petitioner_name}: {p.message}")
    print(f"  Act type: {a.type}")


def test_nullworld_manifest():
    print("=== NullWorld: manifest ===")
    w = NullWorld("world:null", "The Null World")
    m = w.manifest()

    assert not m.has_sub_registry()

def test_nullworld_log():

def test_nullworld_passes_conformance():
    print("=== NullWorld passes conformance ===")
    w = NullWorld("world:null", "The Null World")
    result = run_conformance(w)
    print(f"  passed: {result['passed']}")
    if not result['passed']:
        for f in result['failures']:
            print(f"    FAILURE: {f}")
    assert result["passed"]


def test_broken_world_fails_conformance():
    print("=== A broken world fails conformance ===")

    class BrokenWorld:
        def manifest(self):
            return None  # not a Manifest

        def petition(self, p):
            return "yes"  # not a valid response

        def act(self, a):
            return "ok"  # not a valid response

        def log_since(self, ts=None):
            return None  # not a list

    result = run_conformance(BrokenWorld())
    print(f"  passed: {result['passed']}")
    print(f"  failures: {len(result['failures'])}")
    for f in result["failures"][:3]:
        print(f"    {f}")
    assert not result["passed"]
    assert len(result["failures"]) >= 3


def test_fractal_architecture():
    """The whole point: a multiverse is a world, a federation is a
    multiverse. The protocol is the same at every level."""
    print("=== The protocol is fractal ===")

    # A world with no sub-registry
    world = NullWorld("world:poetry", "Poetry World")

    # A multiverse — also a NullWorld, but with a sub-registry
    class NullMultiverse(NullWorld):
        def __init__(self, entity_id, name, sub_registry_endpoint):
            super().__init__(entity_id, name)
            self._manifest = Manifest(
                entity_id=entity_id,
                name=name,
                protocol_version="WCP/0.1",
                law_url=f"null://{entity_id}/law",
                act_endpoint=f"null://{entity_id}/act",
                log_endpoint=f"null://{entity_id}/log",
                sub_registry_endpoint=sub_registry_endpoint,
            )

    multiverse = NullMultiverse(
        "multiverse:main", "Main Multiverse",
        "https://mv.example/worlds")

    # A federation — same protocol again
    federation = NullMultiverse(
        "federation:global", "Global Federation",
        "https://fed.example/multiverses")

    # All three are conforming:
    for entity in [world, multiverse, federation]:
        result = run_conformance(entity)
        print(f"  {entity.manifest().name}: "
              f"conforms={result['passed']}, "
              f"has_sub_registry={entity.manifest().has_sub_registry()}")
        assert result["passed"]

    # The *only* structural difference is whether the sub_registry
    # is populated.
    print("\n  → Same protocol at every level. Only difference is sub-registry.")


def test_modularity_claim():
    """A claim that this protocol is modular enough to be reimplemented.

    The claim: any developer can implement WorldProtocol without
    talking to us. This test *demonstrates* it by implementing a
    separate, independent, unrelated world — with completely
    different internals — that still conforms.
    """
    print("=== Modularity: a separate implementation ===")

    class IndependentWorld:
        """An entirely separate implementation, written fresh."""
        def __init__(self):
            self._manifest = Manifest(
                entity_id="independent:1",
                name="Independent World",
                protocol_version="WCP/0.1",
                law_url="independent:law",
                act_endpoint="independent:act",
                log_endpoint="independent:log",
            )
            self._events = []

        def manifest(self):
            return self._manifest

        def petition(self, p):
            # This world admits everyone, unconditionally
            self._events.append(("petition", p.petitioner_token))
            return Admission(
                entity_id="independent:1",
                timestamp="independent:0",
            )

        def act(self, a):
            # This world records every act, accepts everything
            self._events.append(("act", a.actor_token, a.type))
            return Ack(entity_id="independent:1", timestamp="independent:0")

        def log_since(self, ts=None):
            return [
                LogEntry(timestamp="independent:0", kind=kind,
                         actor_token=actor, data={})
                for event in self._events
                for kind, actor in [(event[0], event[1])]
            ]

    # It's an independent implementation, but WCP doesn't care.
    result = run_conformance(IndependentWorld())
    print(f"  passed: {result['passed']}")
    assert result["passed"]
    print("  → The protocol is implementation-agnostic.")


def test_different_laws_same_protocol():
    """The protocol doesn't care what the law is."""
    print("=== The law is opaque to the protocol ===")

    class LawAWorld(NullWorld):
        """Admits everyone named Alice."""
        def petition(self, p):
            if p.petitioner_name == "Alice":
                return Admission(entity_id="world:lawA", timestamp="t")
            return Refusal(reason="Only Alice may enter.")

    class LawBWorld(NullWorld):
        """Admits everyone whose passport has an admission."""
        def petition(self, p):
            if p.passport_admissions:
                return Admission(entity_id="world:lawB", timestamp="t")
            return Refusal(reason="Must have an admission.")

    # Both conform
    for w in [LawAWorld("world:lawA", "Law A"),
              LawBWorld("world:lawB", "Law B")]:
        result = run_conformance(w)
        print(f"  {w.manifest().name}: conforms={result['passed']}")
        assert result["passed"]

    # But they have different laws — the same petition gets different
    # responses
    p = Petition(
        petitioner_token="alice:123",
        petitioner_name="Alice",
        passport_admissions=(),
        message="Enter?",
    )
    wA = LawAWorld("world:lawA", "Law A")
    wB = LawBWorld("world:lawB", "Law B")
    rA = wA.petition(p)
    rB = wB.petition(p)
    print(f"\n  Same petition, different laws:")
    print(f"    Law A response: {rA}")
    print(f"    Law B response: {rB}")
    assert isinstance(rA, Admission)  # Alice is named Alice
    assert isinstance(rB, Refusal)    # No prior admissions
    print("  → Same protocol, different laws, different outcomes.")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    test_manifest_construction()
    test_manifest_with_sub_registry()
    test_manifest_validation()
    test_petition_and_act_structures()
    test_nullworld_manifest()
    test_nullworld_refuses_petition()
    test_nullworld_refuses_act()
    test_nullworld_log()
    test_nullworld_passes_conformance()
    test_broken_world_fails_conformance()
    test_fractal_architecture()
    test_modularity_claim()
    test_different_laws_same_protocol()
```
