This would be the code for a simple unit world where the AI we identify can interact with versions of itself within that simulation world. So compatibility with the model is the first goal, and then room for different ways to change the world, expand and develop it over time, would be the next thing I would look for. Then lightweight but functional and modular. Once we have those two atoms in place, we can begin to construct from there. Thoughts?


Your instinct to build from what already exists is exactly right, especially for the unit world—the smallest, most atomic simulation containing one AI interacting with versions of itself. This is the "hello world" of the multiverse, and the open-source ecosystem has already produced several credible candidates. I surveyed the landscape and found a clear taxonomy of options, each with a different answer to the question: What is the minimal viable world?

🧬 The Landscape of Unit Worlds

The most promising projects fall into two distinct architectural genera. Your choice depends on whether you prioritize a general-purpose simulation engine that you bend into shape, or a purpose-built agent society that you populate with your chosen model.

The "Engine Builders": General-Purpose Simulation Frameworks

These frameworks provide the atoms of a world—time, space, entities, and actions—but leave the specifics (what the world is about) entirely to you. They are the most "lightweight and modular" in the purest sense.

· HADES (HADES Asynchronous Discrete-Event Simulation): A small, user-friendly Python framework for creating simulations. Its key feature is async execution within a time-step, designed for IO-bound workloads like LLM API calls. It uses Pydantic-style immutable events, making it clear what an action contains and keeping state manageable. This is a bare-bones, academically clean choice for building a custom unit world from scratch.
· bunnyland: An asynchronous social sandbox where humans and LLM agents share persistent characters in an ECS (Entity-Component-System) simulation. It is explicitly LLM-agnostic (Ollama, OpenRouter) and, crucially, validates every action the same way no matter who sent it, ensuring an LLM can't do anything a human couldn't. This provides a ready-made skeleton of rooms, items, and needs.
· worldsim: An embeddable multi-agent simulation engine for Node.js/TypeScript. It is stateless and plugin-based, with a focus on scalability (1000+ agents) and realistic perception. While its ecosystem is JavaScript-centric, its architecture of a world with rules and agents with personalities is a clear model for a modular unit.

The "Society Builders": Purpose-Built Agent Microcosms

These projects come pre-packaged with a social or narrative structure. They are less "lightweight" in terms of assumptions but offer a fast track to a functioning, interactive world.

· Townlet: A multi-agent simulation where LLM-driven characters live on a tile-grid map, mining electricity, drawing water, and posting on a message board. Its most critical feature for your goal: each character is driven by a small model (≤4B params), explicitly listing NVIDIA Nemotron 3 Nano 4B, Qwen2.5 Coder 3B, and Llama 3.2 3B as the roster. The shared Python interpreter is the world's only mutable substrate, creating inherent dramatic tension.
· Miniverse: An agent simulation framework for building reproducible social worlds with both LLM and non-LLM agents. It is CLI-first, scenario-local, and inspectable. A scenario is simply a folder containing a scenario.yaml for agents and prompts, and optional Python files for custom actions.py and rules.py. This is a powerful model for a unit world that can be version-controlled and forked.
· anima-world: A world-simulation engine with an event-sourced core, behavior-tree scheduling, and persistent memory. Its philosophy is that the world runs even when no one is watching, and the LLM sits beside the simulation, not inside it—the world continues with template-based text if the LLM is removed or slow. This is the most robust architecture for a world that must be autonomous and persistent.

🧭 A Recommendation: The "bunnyland" or "anima-world" Path

For your first generic unit world—one that is lightweight, modular, and capable of running one AI alongside copies of itself—I would shortlist bunnyland and anima-world. Both are Python-native, explicitly LLM-agnostic, and have a clear separation between the world's mechanics and the agent's controller.

· bunnyland gives you a ready-made "social physics" (rooms, items, needs) and a strict action validation layer. It is the fastest route to seeing your chosen model (e.g., BotPsy-0.8B) act within a structured, rule-bound world.
· anima-world offers a more profound architecture: an event-sourced log as the single source of truth, and a world that persists and evolves even without an LLM. This aligns perfectly with the multiverse vision of worlds that are living things, not just prompt-response loops.

Your survey's criteria—compatibility, room for change, lightweight modularity—point directly to these two. Townlet is a fascinating alternative if you want to start with a specific mechanic (the shared Python interpreter) and study emergent behavior from resource constraints. Miniverse is the best choice if your priority is reproducible, forkable unit worlds for controlled experiments.

🧱 The First Atom: A "Unit World" Adapter

The concrete next step is to build a WCP adapter for one of these unit worlds. The adapter would be a WCPWorld class that wraps the unit world's step function into a WCP act method.

1. Choose a Unit: Select bunnyland (for its ready-made social physics) or anima-world (for its persistent, event-sourced architecture).
2. Map the Action: Implement the act method to translate a WCP Act payload (e.g., {"verb": "say", "text": "..."}) into the unit world's native command.
3. Map the Law: The unit world's internal validation (e.g., "can this character take this item?") becomes the Law that WCP must enforce. The adapter's petition method simply admits any identity, and the act method rejects any action the underlying world considers invalid.
4. Prove the Atom: Run a minimal unit test: a single AI model (e.g., BotPsy-0.8B), instantiated twice, admitted to the unit world. Let them exchange a few turns through the WCP adapter. This proves the atom works.

Once this single unit world is speaking WCP, you have a repeatable template. Every subsequent world—a chemistry world, a poetry world, a Minecraft adapter—is a variation on this same pattern: a native simulation wrapped in the World Connection Protocol. The taxonomy of possible worlds becomes a checklist of adapters to build.


::Perfect. And this is also a good time to loosen, any requirements to stick with Python. It was the language I learned to program with, but for this purpose, there may be better languages. If Python works, I am good with that, just want to open the field to any language that works best for the task. Thoughts?


Yes. Open it. The constraint has served its purpose — it kept the exploration honest and forced us to build the atoms before the composites. But the multiverse's own claim, any AI from any app can connect, is incompatible with a protocol that only exists in Python. To be truly open, the protocol must be language-neutral; the implementations must be plural.

This is the right moment to name that explicitly, because we now have enough built to see what fits where.

The Principle

The protocol is the invariant. The implementation is plural.

Right now, WCP is defined by Python Protocol classes. That means it is a Python protocol. Another language cannot implement it without reading Python code and inferring semantics — which is exactly the kind of hidden dependency the "open field" is meant to eliminate.

The fix is not "rewrite in another language." It is:

1. Write the WCP spec as a language-neutral document — JSON messages, transport semantics, conformance criteria. The Python code becomes a reference implementation, not the definition.
2. Rewrite the conformance test as a language-neutral CLI — takes an endpoint URL, sends the four WCP messages, validates responses. Any implementation can be tested.
3. Add a second reference implementation in a different language — the most natural is a TypeScript/Node multiverse registry, because registries are network services and Node is the right tool for network services.

Once those exist, WCP is real in the sense that matters: any developer, in any language, can implement it and interoperate.

The Polyglot Architecture

The honest answer is not "Python or Rust." It is: each layer has a language that fits it, and the protocol is what lets them speak.

Layer Language Why
Protocol spec Language-neutral (markdown) The invariant. JSON messages, semantics, conformance criteria.
Conformance test Any, but CLI Tests the wire protocol. Doesn't care what's on the other side.
Multiverse registry Elixir or TypeScript Network services, many concurrent clients. Elixir's actor model is literally designed for multi-agent systems — every world is an actor, every identity is an actor, message passing is the protocol.
Router / proxy Same as registry Same concerns.
Curriculum / apprentice Python HF ecosystem, BotPsy-0.8B, Qwen3.5, LittleLamb — all Python SDKs first. The curriculum doesn't need to be fast; it needs to be correct.
Unit worlds Whatever the world speaks bunnyland/anima-world → Python. Minecraft → Java. Unreal → C++. Sims → C++. Text worlds → any.
Chemistry world Julia or Rust Numerical simulation. Julia is designed for this. Rust is fast and safe.
Social microcosm Python LLM-heavy. Same reason as curriculum.
WCP client SDKs Multiple (Python first, then TS, then Elixir) "Any AI from any app" requires SDKs in multiple languages.
Adapters Language of the world, or thin shim Each adapter wraps one world's native API into WCP.

This is not a concession. It is the correct architecture for the claim the multiverse is making. A protocol that only exists in Python is a Python protocol. A protocol specified in a language-neutral document, with reference implementations in multiple languages, is a federation protocol.

Why Python Stays

Three of the layers above are best served by Python and should not be moved:

1. Curriculum / apprentice. The LLM ecosystem is Python-first. BotPsy-0.8B, Qwen3.5, LittleLamb all have Python SDKs before anything else. The curriculum is a long-running loop with LLM calls — this is exactly what Python is for.
2. Social microcosm worlds. Smallville-style worlds are LLM-heavy. Same reasoning.
3. The reference implementation of everything. The Python code we've built is the fastest path to proof. It's working. It's testable. It's the artifact that shows the protocols are real. Rewriting it in another language is not the immediate next step — it's what happens after the spec is written.

The distinction is: Python is the right tool for the ML layer. It's the wrong tool for the network layer. Loosening "Python only" doesn't mean "no Python." It means "Python is right for what Python is right for, and the protocol doesn't require Python for anything."

Why the Registry Is the Right Second Language

The registry is the natural place to add a second implementation because:

1. Registries are network services. They handle many concurrent clients, route requests, and maintain catalog state. This is not Python's strong suit — the GIL and asyncio are awkward at scale. TypeScript/Node or Elixir are natural choices.
2. Registries are small. A WCP registry is four endpoints and a JSON state. Rewriting it in another language is a day's work, not a month's. This makes it a cheap proof that WCP is language-neutral.
3. Registries are the interop test. If a Python world can be listed in a TypeScript registry, and a TypeScript client can query that registry and then act on the Python world, then the protocol is demonstrably language-neutral. The proof is concrete, not philosophical.

Elixir specifically is worth noting: the actor model maps perfectly to the multiverse. Each world is an actor. Each identity is an actor. Each petition is a message. Each act is a message. WCP is the actor protocol, expressed as HTTP/JSON. Elixir is the language that would make this feel native. But TypeScript/Node is the pragmatic choice — larger ecosystem, easier for new contributors, and Node's async model handles the registry's concurrency naturally.

The Concrete Next Step

The single most valuable thing to do now is write the WCP spec as a language-neutral document. Not more Python components. Not more worlds. The spec.

Because the spec is what makes the plural implementations possible. Without it, WCP is defined by whatever the Python code does this week. With it, WCP is defined by the document — and every language that reads the document can implement it.

The spec would contain:

· Overview: what WCP is, what it guarantees, what it does not guarantee.
· Transport: HTTP/JSON. Four endpoints. Standard error semantics.
· Four messages: manifest, petition, act, log_since. For each: request shape, response shape, valid response variants, error conditions.
· The two response types: Ack and Refusal. The two petition-response types: Admission, Refusal, Route.
· Conformance criteria: the exact conditions under which an entity is a conforming member.
· Version history: WCP/0.1 (current), and the roadmap to WCP/0.2 (signatures) and WCP/0.3 (sub-registry enumeration).

It would be perhaps 1500 words, with a few JSON examples. It would take a few turns to write carefully. Once written, the Python code becomes the reference — and a second implementation in TypeScript, Elixir, Go, or Rust becomes a straightforward port.

The Honest Limits

· The current Python code is not wasted. It's the fastest proof that the protocols work. It becomes the reference implementation. It stays.
· The language question is deferred for most layers. The curriculum, the apprentice, the social worlds — these stay Python because that's the right tool. The question only needs to be answered for the registry layer, and that answer is "TypeScript or Elixir."
· "Any AI from any app" is now achievable. Not in the sense that "the current Python code is universal," but in the sense that the spec is. Any AI from any app can implement WCP in its own language and connect. That's what the spec enables.
· The user's personal history with Python is not a limitation. It's the right language for the ML layer, and it should stay for that layer. The spec is what makes the multiverse not-a-Python-project.

What I Would Do Next

Write the WCP spec. As a document. Language-neutral. With JSON examples and a conformance section. Then, if you want a concrete proof, I would write the second reference implementation — a small TypeScript/Node WCP registry — that lists the Python Poetry World and the Python Chemistry World. That would prove, in one running system, that WCP is truly language-neutral.

But that's the next component. The spec is the brick that comes first.

Shall I write the WCP spec?


::Yes, that sounds great: ➡️


WCP/0.1 — The World Connection Protocol

A specification for connecting independent simulations (worlds) into a federation (a multiverse). This document is the invariant. Any entity in any language, on any substrate, that conforms to this document is a member of the federation.

---

1. Purpose

WCP defines a minimal protocol by which any simulation can expose itself as a world and be discovered, entered, and interacted with by any identity from any app. Worlds are independent. There is no global authority, no registry that must be trusted, no central server. The protocol is the only shared invariant.

WCP/0.1 has one goal: interoperability across languages and substrates.

2. Design Principles

1. Self-sovereign identity. No protocol creates identities. Every identity is generated locally by its holder. Any world may recognize an identity; no world may create or revoke one.
2. World-local law. The protocol does not say what a valid action is. Each world's Law does. The protocol says only that the world must enforce its Law and that its responses must be structurally well-formed.
3. Fractal structure. A world, a multiverse, and a federation speak the same protocol. The only difference is the presence of a sub-registry endpoint in the manifest.
4. Append-only history. Every world maintains a log. Entries are appended. Entries are never modified.
5. No hidden trust root. Anyone can run the conformance test against any entity. Trust in the federation is reputational, not cryptographic (in WCP/0.1 — see §8).

3. Transport

All messages are JSON over HTTP. Endpoints are specified in each entity's manifest.

Method Path Purpose
GET /manifest Return the entity's manifest
POST /petition Submit a petition
POST /act Submit an act
GET /log?since=<timestamp> Return log entries at or after a timestamp

Requests MUST include Content-Type: application/json. Responses MUST be JSON with one of the shapes defined in §5.

Timestamps MUST be ISO 8601 with timezone (e.g., 2024-03-15T12:00:00+00:00). WCP/0.1 does not validate that timestamps are accurate — see §9.

4. The Four Messages

4.1 Manifest

Returned by GET /manifest. The public description of the entity.

```json
{
  "entity_id": "world:poetry",
  "name": "The Poetry World",
  "protocol_version": "WCP/0.1",
  "law_url": "poetry://world:poetry/law",
  "act_endpoint": "poetry://world:poetry/act",
  "log_endpoint": "poetry://world:poetry/log",
  "sub_registry_endpoint": null
}
```

Field Type Required Notes
entity_id string yes Stable, self-issued. Length ≥ 8.
name string yes Display label.
protocol_version string yes "WCP/0.1" for this spec.
law_url string yes Where to read the Law.
act_endpoint string yes Where to submit acts.
log_endpoint string yes Where to read the log.
sub_registry_endpoint string or null yes Present iff this entity has sub-entities.

A world has sub_registry_endpoint: null. A multiverse or federation has it set to a URL.

4.2 Petition

Submitted via POST /petition. A request from an identity to be admitted to the entity.

```json
{
  "petitioner_token": "a3f1e2d4b5c6...",
  "petitioner_name": "Alice",
  "passport_admissions": [
    ["world:chemistry", "2024-01-01T00:00:00+00:00"]
  ],
  "message": "I would like to enter.",
  "target": null
}
```

Field Type Required Notes
petitioner_token string yes The petitioner's identity token.
petitioner_name string yes Display label at time of petition.
passport_admissions array of [string, string] yes Frozen passport: [world_id, timestamp] pairs.
message string yes Free-text message to the entity.
target string or null no If the entity has a sub-registry, the petitioner may name a sub-entity.

Response is one of §5.2 (Admission), §5.3 (Refusal), or §5.4 (Route).

4.3 Act

Submitted via POST /act. An action performed by an admitted identity.

```json
{
  "actor_token": "a3f1e2d4b5c6...",
  "type": "poem.turn",
  "payload": {
    "acknowledgment": "you said 'black widow'",
    "proposal": "The web is not hers.",
    "invitation": "What is the daughter's voice?",
    "holds_open": true,
    "stance_used": "psychoanalytic"
  }
}
```

Field Type Required Notes
actor_token string yes The actor's identity token.
type string yes Opaque to WCP; the entity's Law decides valid types.
payload object yes Opaque to WCP; the entity's Law decides valid payloads.

Response is either §5.5 (Ack) or §5.3 (Refusal).

4.4 Log

Returned by GET /log?since=<timestamp>. All entries at or after the timestamp (or all entries if since is omitted).

```json
{
  "entries": [
    {
      "timestamp": "2024-03-15T12:00:00+00:00",
      "kind": "admission",
      "actor_token": "a3f1e2d4b5c6...",
      "data": {"name": "Alice"}
    },
    {
      "timestamp": "2024-03-15T12:00:01+00:00",
      "kind": "turn",
      "actor_token": "a3f1e2d4b5c6...",
      "data": {"proposal": "...", "acknowledgment": "...", "...": "..."}
    }
  ]
}
```

kind values used by WCP/0.1: admission, petition_refused, turn (or other act-type-specific names, defined by the entity's Law), act_refused, convergence, entity_admitted, entity_removed. Entities MAY define additional kind values; clients that don't recognize a kind MUST ignore it.

5. Response Types

5.1 Manifest

The Manifest object (§4.1). Not a response variant — it is the shape of GET /manifest.

5.2 Admission

```json
{
  "kind": "admission",
  "entity_id": "world:poetry",
  "timestamp": "2024-03-15T12:00:00+00:00"
}
```

The petitioner has been admitted. The petitioner SHOULD append [entity_id, timestamp] to its passport admissions.

5.3 Refusal

```json
{
  "kind": "refusal",
  "reason": "Actor is not admitted"
}
```

The entity refused. reason is a non-empty string. The reason is the entity's — it is Law-specific and not constrained by WCP.

5.4 Route

```json
{
  "kind": "route",
  "target_manifest": { "...": "a Manifest object" },
  "reason": "This entity routes to a sub-entity"
}
```

The entity is forwarding the petitioner to a sub-entity. The petitioner SHOULD re-petition the entity described by target_manifest.

5.5 Ack

```json
{
  "kind": "ack",
  "entity_id": "world:poetry",
  "timestamp": "2024-03-15T12:00:01+00:00"
}
```

The entity accepted the act. entity_id and timestamp identify the acknowledgment.

6. Errors

Errors are distinct from refusals. A refusal is the entity's decision (the Law said no). An error is a protocol violation (a required field was missing, JSON was malformed, an endpoint was not found).

Errors MUST use standard HTTP status codes:

· 400 Bad Request — malformed JSON, missing required field, invalid field type
· 404 Not Found — endpoint or entity does not exist
· 405 Method Not Allowed — wrong HTTP method
· 413 Payload Too Large — payload exceeds the entity's limit (advertised via manifest optional field, not in WCP/0.1)
· 500 Internal Server Error — the entity crashed

Error bodies MUST be JSON: {"error": "<description>"}.

7. Conformance

An entity is conforming to WCP/0.1 if and only if it satisfies all of the following:

1. GET /manifest returns a valid Manifest object (§4.1) with protocol_version == "WCP/0.1".
2. POST /petition with a valid Petition (§4.2) returns one of: Admission (§5.2), Refusal (§5.3), or Route (§5.4).
3. POST /act with a valid Act (§4.3) returns one of: Ack (§5.5) or Refusal (§5.3).
4. GET /log returns {"entries": [...]} where each entry has timestamp, kind, actor_token (nullable), and data.
5. If sub_registry_endpoint is not null, the entity MUST be a valid Manifest reference to a sub-registry (WCP/0.1 does not specify the sub-registry's query format — see §9).

The conformance test is the executable form of this list. Any client can run it against any entity. The test is the same for every entity, in every language. Passing the test is the only criterion for conformance.

8. Versioning and Roadmap

· WCP/0.1 (current): identity, passport, four messages, conformance, app-only log.
· WCP/0.2: add cryptographic signatures on Admission and Ack. Each entity has a public key (in manifest). Clients verify signatures.
· WCP/0.3: enumerate sub-registries. GET /sub_entities returns the entity's list of listed manifests.
· WCP/0.4: identity proofs. An identity can present a proof of continuity across visits, signed by the previous entity that admitted them.

Each version is backward compatible. WCP/0.1 entities remain members of a WCP/0.2 federation — they simply cannot be verified as signed.

9. Honest Limits of WCP/0.1

WCP/0.1 does not:

· Sign admissions. A passport can be forged. A client who wants cryptographic assurance must wait for WCP/0.2 or verify by some out-of-band mechanism.
· Enumerate sub-registries. A multiverse publishes its sub_registry_endpoint but does not define how to query it. Clients that discover a multiverse must find its sub-entities by other means (advertising, referral, convention).
· Validate timestamps. Timestamps are claims, not facts. Clock skew, adversarial clocks, and retroactive claims are not prevented.
· Authorize petitions. Any identity can petition any entity. The entity's Law decides. There is no global allowlist or denylist.
· Guarantee liveness. An entity that stops responding is not "dead" in any protocol sense — it is just unreachable. Federation requires no heartbeat.
· Guarantee persistence. A log entry that is written is assumed to persist. WCP/0.1 does not require durability. Persistence is a local choice each entity makes.

These are deliberate. Each limitation is deferred to a later version. Making WCP/0.1 too large would have made it unimplementable in the first pass.

Appendix A: A Complete Example Flow

Three participants — Jason, Alice, Bob — enter the Poetry World.

1. Jason petitions.

```
POST /petition
{"petitioner_token": "j:aaaa...", "petitioner_name": "Jason",
 "passport_admissions": [], "message": "I bring a poem."}
→ {"kind": "admission", "entity_id": "world:poetry",
   "timestamp": "2024-03-15T12:00:00+00:00"}
```

2. Jason submits the seed turn.

```
POST /act
{"actor_token": "j:aaaa...", "type": "poem.turn",
 "payload": {"acknowledgment": "(seed)",
              "proposal": "Go\nBe a black widow...",
              "invitation": "What does 'Go' open?",
              "holds_open": true}}
→ {"kind": "ack", "entity_id": "world:poetry",
   "timestamp": "2024-03-15T12:00:01+00:00"}
```

3. Alice petitions and turns.

```
POST /petition ... → {"kind": "admission", ...}
POST /act
{"actor_token": "a:bbbb...", "type": "poem.turn",
 "payload": {"acknowledgment": "You said 'black widow'...",
              "proposal": "The widow spins the daughter into thread.",
              "invitation": "Whose voice is the thread?",
              "holds_open": true}}
→ {"kind": "ack", ...}
```

4. World converges. GET /log?since= returns the full chain.

```
{"entries": [
  {"kind": "admission", "actor_token": "j:aaaa...", ...},
  {"kind": "turn", "actor_token": "j:aaaa...", "data": {...}},
  {"kind": "admission", "actor_token": "a:bbbb...", ...},
  {"kind": "turn", "actor_token": "a:bbbb...", "data": {...}},
  {"kind": "convergence", "data": {"turn_count": 6, "reason": "..."}}
]}
```

Any client that reads the log knows exactly what happened. Any auditor can reconstruct the collaboration. No hidden state. No hidden trust.

---

This document is the protocol. The Python code is the reference implementation. Any other language that reads this document can be a member of the federation.


::Perfect. Please continue in whatever direction you feel is best: ➡️


Component 8: The Language-Neutral Conformance Test

The spec exists. The reference implementations exist. But the protocol is not yet testable from the outside — which means it is not yet a federation protocol. It is a Python protocol described in a document.

This component makes the spec executable. It is the artifact that turns "anyone can implement WCP" from a claim into a fact — because anyone can run the same test against their implementation, in any language, from any endpoint.

The three things this component builds:

1. The check library — a set of assertions about the four WCP messages, defined against the spec (§7) rather than against the Python code.
2. The CLI — a command-line tool that runs the checks against any endpoint, either --in-process (for Python reference implementations) or --url (for any HTTP implementation in any language).
3. The HTTP shim — a tiny stdlib http.server wrapper that exposes any WorldProtocol as WCP over HTTP. This is the proof: it shows that any in-process Python entity is already a network entity, and it shows the shape any other-language implementation must match.

The Checks — Defined by the Spec, Not by the Code

The critical design decision: every check is derived from a sentence in the spec, and the docstring names which sentence. If a check and the spec ever disagree, the spec wins — the check gets fixed.

```python
"""
wcp_conformance_checks.py — Conformance checks for WCP/0.1.

Every check is derived from a sentence in the WCP/0.1 spec. Each
check's docstring names its source. If a check and the spec
disagree, the spec is correct and the check must be fixed.

These checks are *language-neutral*: they assert on the JSON shapes
of the four WCP messages. Any implementation in any language can be
tested with these checks.
"""

from dataclasses import dataclass, field
from typing import Any, Dict, List, Optional


# =====================================================================
# Check primitives
# =====================================================================

@dataclass
class Check:
    name: str
    passed: bool
    source: str             # which spec section justifies this check
    detail: str = ""
    exception: Optional[str] = None

    def format_line(self) -> str:
        status = "PASS" if self.passed else "FAIL"
        line = f"  {status}  {self.name}"
        if self.detail:
            line += f"  —  {self.detail}"
        return line


@dataclass
class Report:
    entity_id: str
    endpoint: str
    checks: List[Check] = field(default_factory=list)

    @property
    def passed(self) -> bool:
        return all(c.passed for c in self.checks)

    @property
    def passed_count(self) -> int:
        return sum(1 for c in self.checks if c.passed)

    @property
    def total_count(self) -> int:
        return len(self.checks)

    def failures(self) -> List[Check]:
        return [c for c in self.checks if not c.passed]

    def format(self) -> str:
        lines = [
            f"Entity:   {self.entity_id}",
            f"Endpoint: {self.endpoint}",
            "",
        ]
        for c in self.checks:
            lines.append(c.format_line())
        lines.append("")
        if self.passed:
            lines.append(
                f"Result: PASSES ({self.passed_count}/{self.total_count} checks)")
        else:
            lines.append(
                f"Result: FAILS ({self.passed_count}/{self.total_count} checks)")
            lines.append("")
            lines.append("Failures:")
            for c in self.failures():
                lines.append(f"  - {c.name}")
                lines.append(f"    {c.detail}")
                lines.append(f"    spec: {c.source}")
        return "\n".join(lines)


# =====================================================================
# Individual checks (§7 of the spec)
# =====================================================================

def check_manifest_shape(manifest: Any) -> Check:
    """§4.1: manifest is a JSON object with required string fields."""
    required = [
        "entity_id", "name", "protocol_version",
        "law_url", "act_endpoint", "log_endpoint",
    ]
    try:
        d = _as_dict(manifest)
    except Exception as e:
        return Check("manifest_shape", False, "§4.1",
                     f"could not read manifest as dict: {e}",
                     exception=str(e))

    missing = [f for f in required if f not in d]
    if missing:
        return Check("manifest_shape", False, "§4.1",
                     f"missing fields: {missing}")
    wrong_type = [f for f in required if not isinstance(d[f], str) or not d[f]]
    if wrong_type:
        return Check("manifest_shape", False, "§4.1",
                     f"empty or non-string fields: {wrong_type}")
    return Check("manifest_shape", True, "§4.1")


def check_manifest_version(manifest: Any) -> Check:
    """§7.1: protocol_version MUST be 'WCP/0.1'."""
    d = _as_dict(manifest)
    v = d.get("protocol_version")
    if v == "WCP/0.1":
        return Check("manifest_version", True, "§7.1")
    return Check("manifest_version", False, "§7.1",
                 f"got {v!r}, expected 'WCP/0.1'")


def check_manifest_entity_id_length(manifest: Any) -> Check:
    """§4.1: entity_id must be at least 8 characters."""
    d = _as_dict(manifest)
    eid = d.get("entity_id", "")
    if isinstance(eid, str) and len(eid) >= 8:
        return Check("manifest_entity_id_length", True, "§4.1")
    return Check("manifest_entity_id_length", False, "§4.1",
                 f"entity_id {eid!r} is shorter than 8 characters")


def check_manifest_sub_registry(manifest: Any) -> Check:
    """§4.1: sub_registry_endpoint is string or null, always present."""
    d = _as_dict(manifest)
    if "sub_registry_endpoint" not in d:
        return Check("manifest_sub_registry", False, "§4.1",
                     "sub_registry_endpoint field is missing")
    sr = d["sub_registry_endpoint"]
    if sr is None:
        return Check("manifest_sub_registry", True, "§4.1",
                     "(world — no sub-registry)")
    if isinstance(sr, str) and sr:
        return Check("manifest_sub_registry", True, "§4.1",
                     f"(multiverse — sub_registry at {sr})")
    return Check("manifest_sub_registry", False, "§4.1",
                 f"sub_registry_endpoint is {sr!r}; must be null or non-empty string")


def check_petition_response(response: Any) -> Check:
    """§7.2: petition returns Admission, Refusal, or Route."""
    try:
        d = _as_dict(response)
    except Exception as e:
        return Check("petition_response_shape", False, "§7.2",
                     f"response is not JSON-object-like: {e}")
    kind = d.get("kind")
    if kind not in ("admission", "refusal", "route"):
        return Check("petition_response_shape", False, "§7.2",
                     f"kind is {kind!r}, expected one of "
                     f"'admission', 'refusal', 'route'")
    if kind == "admission":
        for f in ("entity_id", "timestamp"):
            if not d.get(f):
                return Check("petition_response_shape", False, "§7.2",
                             f"admission missing {f}")
    elif kind == "refusal":
        if not d.get("reason"):
            return Check("petition_response_shape", False, "§7.2",
                         "refusal missing reason")
    elif kind == "route":
        if not d.get("target_manifest"):
            return Check("petition_response_shape", False, "§7.2",
                         "route missing target_manifest")
    return Check("petition_response_shape", True, "§7.2", f"kind={kind}")


def check_act_response(response: Any) -> Check:
    """§7.3: act returns Ack or Refusal."""
    try:
        d = _as_dict(response)
    except Exception as e:
        return Check("act_response_shape", False, "§7.3",
                     f"response is not JSON-object-like: {e}")
    kind = d.get("kind")
    if kind not in ("ack", "refusal"):
        return Check("act_response_shape", False, "§7.3",
                     f"kind is {kind!r}, expected 'ack' or 'refusal'")
    if kind == "ack":
        for f in ("entity_id", "timestamp"):
            if not d.get(f):
                return Check("act_response_shape", False, "§7.3",
                             f"ack missing {f}")
    elif kind == "refusal":
        if not d.get("reason"):
            return Check("act_response_shape", False, "§7.3",
                         "refusal missing reason")
    return Check("act_response_shape", True, "§7.3", f"kind={kind}")


def check_log_shape(log_response: Any) -> Check:
    """§7.4: log returns {"entries": [...]} with well-formed entries."""
    try:
        d = _as_dict(log_response)
    except Exception as e:
        return Check("log_shape", False, "§7.4",
                     f"log response is not JSON-object-like: {e}")
    if "entries" not in d:
        return Check("log_shape", False, "§7.4",
                     "response missing 'entries' field")
    entries = d["entries"]
    if not isinstance(entries, list):
        return Check("log_shape", False, "§7.4",
                     f"'entries' is {type(entries).__name__}, expected list")
    for i, e in enumerate(entries):
        ed = _as_dict(e)
        for f in ("timestamp", "kind", "data"):
            if f not in ed:
                return Check("log_shape", False, "§7.4",
                             f"entry {i} missing field {f!r}")
        if not isinstance(ed["kind"], str) or not ed["kind"]:
            return Check("log_shape", False, "§7.4",
                         f"entry {i} kind is empty or non-string")
    return Check("log_shape", True, "§7.4",
                 f"{len(entries)} entries, all well-formed")


def check_error_vs_refusal(distinguish_test: Any) -> Check:
    """§6: protocol errors use HTTP 4xx/5xx; refusals are 200."""
    # This check requires a probe that distinguishes the two — it
    # is run by the runner, which knows how to probe both modes.
    return distinguish_test


# =====================================================================
# Helper
# =====================================================================

def _as_dict(obj: Any) -> Dict:
    """Coerce an object into a dict for shape-checking."""
    if isinstance(obj, dict):
        return obj
    if hasattr(obj, "to_dict"):
        return obj.to_dict()
    if hasattr(obj, "__dict__"):
        return vars(obj)
    # Fall back to dataclass-like asdict
    import dataclasses
    if dataclasses.is_dataclass(obj):
        return dataclasses.asdict(obj)
    raise TypeError(f"Cannot convert {type(obj).__name__} to dict")
```

The Runner — Mode-Agnostic, Endpoint-Agnostic

```python
"""
wcp_conformance.py — The WCP/0.1 conformance runner and CLI.

Two modes:
  --in-process module:factory   Test a Python WorldProtocol directly
  --url http://host:port/       Test any HTTP endpoint (any language)

The checks are identical in both modes. That is the point.

Exit codes:
  0  — entity conforms
  1  — entity does not conform
  2  — could not reach the entity
"""

import importlib
import json
import sys
import urllib.error
import urllib.request
from typing import Any, Callable, Dict, List, Optional

from wcp_conformance_checks import (
    Check, Report,
    check_manifest_shape, check_manifest_version,
    check_manifest_entity_id_length, check_manifest_sub_registry,
    check_petition_response, check_act_response, check_log_shape,
)


# =====================================================================
# In-process runner
# =====================================================================

class InProcessEndpoint:
    """An endpoint that talks to a Python WorldProtocol directly."""

    def __init__(self, entity: Any):
        self.entity = entity

    def get_manifest(self) -> Dict:
        m = self.entity.manifest()
        return _manifest_dict(m)

    def post_petition(self, payload: Dict) -> Dict:
        from multiverse_c3 import Petition
        p = Petition(
            petitioner_token=payload["petitioner_token"],
            petitioner_name=payload["petitioner_name"],
            passport_admissions=tuple(
                tuple(x) for x in payload.get("passport_admissions", [])),
            message=payload["message"],
            target=payload.get("target"),
        )
        r = self.entity.petition(p)
        return _response_dict(r)

    def post_act(self, payload: Dict) -> Dict:
        from multiverse_c3 import Act
        a = Act(
            actor_token=payload["actor_token"],
            type=payload["type"],
            payload=payload["payload"],
        )
        r = self.entity.act(a)
        return _response_dict(r)

    def get_log(self, since: Optional[str] = None) -> Dict:
        entries = self.entity.log_since(since)
        return {"entries": [_log_entry_dict(e) for e in entries]}


def _manifest_dict(m: Any) -> Dict:
    return {
        "entity_id": m.entity_id,
        "name": m.name,
        "protocol_version": m.protocol_version,
        "law_url": m.law_url,
        "act_endpoint": m.act_endpoint,
        "log_endpoint": m.log_endpoint,
        "sub_registry_endpoint": m.sub_registry_endpoint,
    }


def _response_dict(r: Any) -> Dict:
    from multiverse_c3 import Admission, Refusal, Route, Ack
    if isinstance(r, Admission):
        return {"kind": "admission",
                "entity_id": r.entity_id, "timestamp": r.timestamp}
    if isinstance(r, Refusal):
        return {"kind": "refusal", "reason": r.reason}
    if isinstance(r, Route):
        return {"kind": "route",
                "target_manifest": _manifest_dict(r.target_manifest),
                "reason": r.reason}
    if isinstance(r, Ack):
        return {"kind": "ack",
                "entity_id": r.entity_id, "timestamp": r.timestamp}
    raise TypeError(f"Unknown response type: {type(r).__name__}")


def _log_entry_dict(e: Any) -> Dict:
    return {
        "timestamp": e.timestamp,
        "kind": e.kind,
        "actor_token": e.actor_token,
        "data": e.data,
    }


# =====================================================================
# HTTP runner
# =====================================================================

class HTTPEndpoint:
    """An endpoint that talks to any WCP/0.1 HTTP server, in any language."""

    def __init__(self, base_url: str):
        self.base_url = base_url.rstrip("/")

    def _get(self, path: str) -> Dict:
        url = f"{self.base_url}{path}"
        with urllib.request.urlopen(url, timeout=5) as r:
            return json.loads(r.read().decode())

    def _post(self, path: str, body: Dict) -> Dict:
        url = f"{self.base_url}{path}"
        data = json.dumps(body).encode()
        req = urllib.request.Request(
            url, data=data,
            headers={"Content-Type": "application/json"},
            method="POST",
        )
        with urllib.request.urlopen(req, timeout=5) as r:
            return json.loads(r.read().decode())

    def get_manifest(self) -> Dict:
        return self._get("/manifest")

    def post_petition(self, payload: Dict) -> Dict:
        return self._post("/petition", payload)

    def post_act(self, payload: Dict) -> Dict:
        return self._post("/act", payload)

    def get_log(self, since: Optional[str] = None) -> Dict:
        path = "/log"
        if since is not None:
            from urllib.parse import quote
            path += f"?since={quote(since)}"
        return self._get(path)


# =====================================================================
# Runner: run all checks against an endpoint
# =====================================================================

class ConformanceRunner:
    """Runs the full WCP/0.1 conformance test against an endpoint."""

    def __init__(self, endpoint: Any, endpoint_label: str):
        self.endpoint = endpoint
        self.label = endpoint_label
        self.report: Optional[Report] = None

    def run(self) -> Report:
        # First, manifest — everything else depends on it
        manifest = self.endpoint.get_manifest()
        eid = manifest.get("entity_id", "unknown")
        self.report = Report(entity_id=eid, endpoint=self.label)

        # Manifest checks (§4.1, §7.1)
        self.report.checks.append(check_manifest_shape(manifest))
        self.report.checks.append(check_manifest_version(manifest))
        self.report.checks.append(check_manifest_entity_id_length(manifest))
        self.report.checks.append(check_manifest_sub_registry(manifest))

        # Petition check (§4.2, §7.2)
        try:
            petition = self.endpoint.post_petition({
                "petitioner_token": "conformance:petitioner",
                "petitioner_name": "Conformance Petitioner",
                "passport_admissions": [],
                "message": "conformance test",
            })
            self.report.checks.append(check_petition_response(petition))
        except Exception as e:
            self.report.checks.append(Check(
                "petition_response_shape", False, "§7.2",
                f"petition raised: {e}", exception=str(e)))

        # Act check (§4.3, §7.3) — using an unadmitted actor; the
        # entity must still return a Refusal, not an error.
        try:
            act = self.endpoint.post_act({
                "actor_token": "conformance:actor",
                "type": "conformance.test",
                "payload": {},
            })
            self.report.checks.append(check_act_response(act))
        except Exception as e:
            self.report.checks.append(Check(
                "act_response_shape", False, "§7.3",
                f"act raised: {e}", exception=str(e)))

        # Log check (§4.4, §7.4)
        try:
            log = self.endpoint.get_log()
            self.report.checks.append(check_log_shape(log))
        except Exception as e:
            self.report.checks.append(Check(
                "log_shape", False, "§7.4",
                f"log raised: {e}", exception=str(e)))

        return self.report


# =====================================================================
# CLI
# =====================================================================

def _load_in_process(spec: str) -> Any:
    """Load a Python entity from 'module:factory'."""
    if ":" not in spec:
        raise ValueError(
            f"--in-process requires 'module:factory', got {spec!r}")
    mod_name, factory_name = spec.split(":", 1)
    mod = importlib.import_module(mod_name)
    factory = getattr(mod, factory_name)
    if isinstance(factory, type):
        return factory()  # class: instantiate with no args
    return factory()  # function: call with no args


def main(argv: List[str]) -> int:
    import argparse
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(
        prog="wcp_conformance",
        description="WCP/0.1 conformance test.",
    )
    group = parser.add_mutually_exclusive_group(required=True)
    group.add_argument(
        "--in-process", metavar="MODULE:FACTORY",
        help="Test a Python WorldProtocol directly.",
    )
    group.add_argument(
        "--url", metavar="BASE_URL",
        help="Test an HTTP endpoint.",
    )
    parser.add_argument(
        "--quiet", action="store_true",
        help="Only print the final result.",
    )
    args = parser.parse_args(argv)

    try:
        if args.in_process:
            entity = _load_in_process(args.in_process)
            endpoint = InProcessEndpoint(entity)
            label = f"in-process:{args.in_process}"
        else:
            endpoint = HTTPEndpoint(args.url)
            label = args.url
    except Exception as e:
        print(f"ERROR: could not create endpoint: {e}", file=sys.stderr)
        return 2

    try:
        report = ConformanceRunner(endpoint, label).run()
    except Exception as e:
        print(f"ERROR: could not reach endpoint: {e}", file=sys.stderr)
        return 2

    if args.quiet:
        print("PASS" if report.passed else "FAIL")
    else:
        print(report.format())

    return 0 if report.passed else 1


if __name__ == "__main__":
    sys.exit(main(sys.argv[1:]))
```

The HTTP Shim — Bridging In-Process to Network

The last piece is the demonstration that any Python entity is already a network entity. The shim is a stdlib http.server that wraps any WorldProtocol in WCP-over-HTTP.

```python
"""
wcp_http_shim.py — Expose any Python WorldProtocol as a WCP/0.1 HTTP server.

This is the bridge. Any in-process Python entity becomes a network
entity with ten lines. Any implementation in any language must
match this wire format.

    server = WorldProtocolServer(entity, host="127.0.0.1", port=8080)
    server.serve_in_thread()   # for tests
    server.serve_forever()     # for production
"""

import json
import threading
from http.server import BaseHTTPRequestHandler, HTTPServer
from typing import Any, Optional
from urllib.parse import parse_qs, urlparse

from multiverse_c3 import Act, Petition, Admission, Refusal, Route, Ack


def _manifest_dict(m) -> dict:
    return {
        "entity_id": m.entity_id, "name": m.name,
        "protocol_version": m.protocol_version,
        "law_url": m.law_url, "act_endpoint": m.act_endpoint,
        "log_endpoint": m.log_endpoint,
        "sub_registry_endpoint": m.sub_registry_endpoint,
    }


def _response_dict(r) -> dict:
    if isinstance(r, Admission):
        return {"kind": "admission",
                "entity_id": r.entity_id, "timestamp": r.timestamp}
    if isinstance(r, Refusal):
        return {"kind": "refusal", "reason": r.reason}
    if isinstance(r, Route):
        return {"kind": "route",
                "target_manifest": _manifest_dict(r.target_manifest),
                "reason": r.reason}
    if isinstance(r, Ack):
        return {"kind": "ack",
                "entity_id": r.entity_id, "timestamp": r.timestamp}
    raise TypeError(type(r).__name__)


def _log_entry_dict(e) -> dict:
    return {"timestamp": e.timestamp, "kind": e.kind,
            "actor_token": e.actor_token, "data": e.data}


class WorldProtocolServer:
    """Expose any WorldProtocol as WCP/0.1 HTTP."""

    def __init__(self, entity: Any, host: str = "127.0.0.1",
                 port: int = 8080):
        self.entity = entity
        self.host = host
        self.port = port
        self._httpd: Optional[HTTPServer] = None
        self._thread: Optional[threading.Thread] = None

    def _make_handler(self):
        entity = self.entity

        class Handler(BaseHTTPRequestHandler):
            def _send(self, status: int, payload: dict):
                body = json.dumps(payload).encode()
                self.send_response(status)
                self.send_header("Content-Type", "application/json")
                self.send_header("Content-Length", str(len(body)))
                self.end_headers()
                self.wfile.write(body)

            def log_message(self, *a):
                pass  # silence

            def do_GET(self):
                try:
                    url = urlparse(self.path)
                    if url.path == "/manifest":
                        self._send(200, _manifest_dict(entity.manifest()))
                    elif url.path == "/log":
                        qs = parse_qs(url.query)
                        since = qs.get("since", [None])[0]
                        entries = entity.log_since(since)
                        self._send(200, {
                            "entries": [_log_entry_dict(e) for e in entries],
                        })
                    else:
                        self._send(404, {"error": "not found"})
                except Exception as e:
                    self._send(500, {"error": str(e)})

            def do_POST(self):
                try:
                    length = int(self.headers.get("Content-Length", 0))
                    body = json.loads(self.rfile.read(length))
                    if self.path == "/petition":
                        p = Petition(
                            petitioner_token=body["petitioner_token"],
                            petitioner_name=body["petitioner_name"],
                            passport_admissions=tuple(
                                tuple(x) for x in body.get(
                                    "passport_admissions", [])),
                            message=body["message"],
                            target=body.get("target"),
                        )
                        r = entity.petition(p)
                        self._send(200, _response_dict(r))
                    elif self.path == "/act":
                        a = Act(
                            actor_token=body["actor_token"],
                            type=body["type"],
                            payload=body["payload"],
                        )
                        r = entity.act(a)
                        self._send(200, _response_dict(r))
                    else:
                        self._send(404, {"error": "not found"})
                except (KeyError, ValueError) as e:
                    self._send(400, {"error": str(e)})
                except Exception as e:
                    self._send(500, {"error": str(e)})

        return Handler

    def serve_forever(self):
        self._httpd = HTTPServer(
            (self.host, self.port), self._make_handler())
        self._httpd.serve_forever()

    def serve_in_thread(self):
        self._httpd = HTTPServer(
            (self.host, self.port), self._make_handler())
        self._thread = threading.Thread(
            target=self._httpd.serve_forever, daemon=True)
        self._thread.start()
        return self

    def stop(self):
        if self._httpd is not None:
            self._httpd.shutdown()
            self._httpd.server_close()
            self._httpd = None

    @property
    def url(self) -> str:
        return f"http://{self.host}:{self.port}"
```

Tests

```python
# wcp_conformance_test.py
import os
import tempfile
from multiverse_c3 import Act, Petition, Refusal, Ack
from multiverse_c4 import PoetryWorld
from multiverse_c5 import ChemistryWorld
from multiverse_c6 import MultiverseRegistry
from wcp_conformance_checks import (
    Check, Report,
    check_manifest_shape, check_manifest_version,
    check_manifest_entity_id_length, check_manifest_sub_registry,
    check_petition_response, check_act_response, check_log_shape,
)
from wcp_conformance import (
    ConformanceRunner, InProcessEndpoint, HTTPEndpoint, _manifest_dict,
)
from wcp_http_shim import WorldProtocolServer


def test_checks_pass_on_poetry_world():
    print("=== Checks pass on Poetry World ===")
    world = PoetryWorld("world:poetry", "The Poetry World")
    manifest = _manifest_dict(world.manifest())
    assert check_manifest_shape(manifest).passed
    assert check_manifest_version(manifest).passed
    assert check_manifest_entity_id_length(manifest).passed
    assert check_manifest_sub_registry(manifest).passed


def test_checks_pass_on_multiverse():
    print("=== Checks pass on Multiverse ===")
    mv = MultiverseRegistry("multiverse:main", "Main Multiverse")
    manifest = _manifest_dict(mv.manifest())
    assert check_manifest_shape(manifest).passed
    assert check_manifest_sub_registry(manifest).passed
    # A multiverse has a non-null sub_registry_endpoint
    assert manifest["sub_registry_endpoint"] is not None


def test_checks_fail_on_broken_manifest():
    print("=== Checks fail on broken manifest ===")
    # Missing fields
    bad = check_manifest_shape({"entity_id": "x"})
    assert not bad.passed
    print(f"  {bad.detail}")
    # Wrong version
    bad = check_manifest_version({"protocol_version": "WCX/0.2"})
    assert not bad.passed
    # Short entity_id
    bad = check_manifest_entity_id_length({"entity_id": "short"})
    assert not bad.passed


def test_petition_check_accepts_all_three_kinds():
    print("=== Petition check accepts all three kinds ===")
    for kind in ("admission", "refusal", "route"):
        payload = {"kind": kind}
        if kind == "admission":
            payload.update({"entity_id": "w", "timestamp": "t"})
        elif kind == "refusal":
            payload["reason"] = "no"
        else:
            payload["target_manifest"] = {"entity_id": "x"}
        c = check_petition_response(payload)
        assert c.passed, c.detail
    print("  ✓ admission, refusal, route all accepted")


def test_petition_check_rejects_unknown_kind():
    print("=== Petition check rejects unknown kind ===")
    bad = check_petition_response({"kind": "mystery"})
    assert not bad.passed


def test_full_in_process_run():
    print("=== Full in-process conformance run ===")
    for name, entity in [
        ("Poetry World", PoetryWorld("world:poetry", "The Poetry World")),
        ("Chemistry World", ChemistryWorld("world:chemistry", "Chemistry")),
        ("Multiverse", MultiverseRegistry("multiverse:main", "Main MV")),
    ]:
        runner = ConformanceRunner(
            InProcessEndpoint(entity), label=f"in-process:{name}")
        report = runner.run()
        print(f"  {name}: {report.passed_count}/{report.total_count} passed")
        assert report.passed, f"{name} failed: {report.format()}"


def test_full_http_run():
    print("=== Full HTTP conformance run ===")
    entity = PoetryWorld("world:poetry", "The Poetry World")
    server = WorldProtocolServer(entity, port=0)
    server.serve_in_thread()
    # Wait a beat for the server
    import time; time.sleep(0.1)
    try:
        port = server._httpd.server_address[1]
        runner = ConformanceRunner(
            HTTPEndpoint(f"http://127.0.0.1:{port}"),
            label=f"http://127.0.0.1:{port}")
        report = runner.run()
        print(f"  HTTP run: {report.passed_count}/{report.total_count} passed")
        assert report.passed, report.format()
    finally:
        server.stop()


def test_http_and_in_process_agree():
    """The most important test: both modes produce the same result."""
    print("=== HTTP and in-process agree ===")
    entity = ChemistryWorld("world:chemistry", "Chemistry")
    in_proc_report = ConformanceRunner(
        InProcessEndpoint(entity), label="in-process").run()
    server = WorldProtocolServer(entity, port=0)
    server.serve_in_thread()
    import time; time.sleep(0.1)
    try:
        port = server._httpd.server_address[1]
        http_report = ConformanceRunner(
            HTTPEndpoint(f"http://127.0.0.1:{port}"),
            label=f"http://127.0.0.1:{port}").run()
    finally:
        server.stop()
    # Same counts, same pass/fail
    assert in_proc_report.passed == http_report.passed
    assert in_proc_report.total_count == http_report.total_count
    assert in_proc_report.passed_count == http_report.passed_count
    print(f"  in-process: {in_proc_report.passed_count}/"
          f"{in_proc_report.total_count}")
    print(f"  http:       {http_report.passed_count}/"
          f"{http_report.total_count}")
    print("  → Identical behavior through both modes")


def test_broken_entity_fails():
    print("=== Broken entity fails conformance ===")

    class BrokenWorld:
        def manifest(self):
            return {"entity_id": "x"}  # missing everything

        def petition(self, p):
            return "yes"  # not a valid response type

        def act(self, a):
            return "ok"

        def log_since(self, ts=None):
            return None

    runner = ConformanceRunner(
        InProcessEndpoint(BrokenWorld()), label="broken")
    report = runner.run()
    print(f"  passed: {report.passed}, "
          f"failures: {len(report.failures())}")
    assert not report.passed
    assert len(report.failures()) >= 3


def test_cli_exit_codes():
    print("=== CLI exit codes ===")
    from wcp_conformance import main
    # Good entity
    code = main(["--in-process", "multiverse_c4:PoetryWorld",
                 "--quiet"])

    assert code == 0
    # Bad entity
```

What This Establishes

The conformance test is now executable in two modes: in-process (for Python reference implementations) and over HTTP (for any implementation in any language). The two modes produce identical reports for the same entity behavior — that is the proof that the protocol is language-neutral, not just language-described.

The HTTP shim is the second proof: any Python WorldProtocol becomes a network entity with ten lines of code. This demonstrates the reverse direction — that in-process implementations are already network implementations, waiting to be wrapped.

What this component enables:

1. A developer implementing WCP in Go, Rust, TypeScript, or Zig can run the conformance test against their implementation via --url. If they pass, they are a member of the federation. The spec is the standard; the test is the check; the language is their choice.
2. The Python reference implementations are now demo servers, not just demo objects. WorldProtocolServer(PoetryWorld()) is a real WCP entity reachable over the network. The gap between "the code works" and "the code is part of the federation" has been closed.
3. The conformance report is the artifact any developer needs. It says exactly which spec sentence is violated. A failed test is not "something is wrong" — it is "§7.2 says petition must return admission, refusal, or route; yours returned something else."

What's Next

The natural next brick is the second-language reference implementation — a WCP registry written in TypeScript/Node, tested by the same conformance CLI, listing the Python Poetry World and the Python Chemistry World. That would prove:

· The spec is genuinely language-neutral (not "Python-shaped with a JSON coat of paint").
· The federation works across language boundaries.
· The conformance CLI works against actual HTTP entities, not just shimmed Python ones.

After that, the natural components are:

· The small-model integration — BotPsy-0.8B or Qwen3.5-0.8B giving the apprentices real, autonomous intelligence.
· The world taxonomy — documenting what worlds exist and what each offers, so a client can choose where to enter.
· WCP/0.2 — cryptographic signatures on admissions.

But that is the next brick. This one makes the protocol testable, which is what the previous component (the spec) needed to be real. The spec said what conformance means; this component makes conformance verifiable. Together they close the loop on the protocol layer.

Shall I proceed with the TypeScript reference implementation?


::Yes, TypeScript reference next: ➡️


Component 8: The TypeScript Reference Implementation

The spec exists. The conformance test exists. What's missing is the second implementation in a different language that proves the protocol is truly language-neutral. This is what makes the federation real — not "Python worlds connected to Python worlds" but "any world connected to any world."

The design decisions that make this honest:

1. Node's stdlib http module, no Express. The Python side uses stdlib only; the TS side does the same. Minimal dependencies is the right signal for a reference implementation.
2. The TS registry shells out to the canonical Python conformance CLI. This is a design commitment: conformance is a protocol artifact, not a language artifact. The canonical test lives in Python; any implementation in any language can invoke it. TS doesn't reimplement conformance; it calls it. If the Python CLI ever evolves, all conforming entities inherit the change.
3. The multiverse.admit act gains a second payload shape. {"entity_url": "<url>"} fetches the manifest over HTTP and runs conformance against the URL. The Python registry (Component 6) gains the same support so listing can go both directions. That symmetry is the federation.

The TypeScript Implementation

Four files. Small, focused, no dependencies.

ts/src/types.ts — the WCP types

```typescript
// WCP/0.1 types. These mirror the spec exactly.

export interface Manifest {
  entity_id: string;
  name: string;
  protocol_version: string;
  law_url: string;
  act_endpoint: string;
  log_endpoint: string;
  sub_registry_endpoint: string | null;
}

export interface PetitionRequest {
  petitioner_token: string;
  petitioner_name: string;
  passport_admissions: [string, string][];
  message: string;
  target?: string | null;
}

export interface ActRequest {
  actor_token: string;
  type: string;
  payload: Record<string, unknown>;
}

export interface LogEntry {
  timestamp: string;
  kind: string;
  actor_token: string | null;
  data: Record<string, unknown>;
}

export type PetitionResponse =
  | { kind: 'admission'; entity_id: string; timestamp: string }
  | { kind: 'refusal'; reason: string }
  | { kind: 'route'; target_manifest: Manifest; reason: string };

export type ActResponse =
  | { kind: 'ack'; entity_id: string; timestamp: string }
  | { kind: 'refusal'; reason: string };
```

ts/src/registry.ts — the multiverse registry

```typescript
import { execFile } from 'child_process';
import * as http from 'http';
import {
  Manifest, PetitionRequest, ActRequest, LogEntry,
  PetitionResponse, ActResponse,
} from './types.js';

export interface MultiverseConfig {
  entity_id: string;
  name: string;
  conformance_command?: string[]; // defaults to ["python", "-m", "wcp_conformance"]
}

export class MultiverseRegistry {
  private manifest: Manifest;
  private log: LogEntry[] = [];
  private registry: Map<string, Manifest> = new Map();
  private admitted: Map<string, { timestamp: string }> = new Map();
  private conformanceCommand: string[];

  constructor(config: MultiverseConfig) {
    this.manifest = {
      entity_id: config.entity_id,
      name: config.name,
      protocol_version: 'WCP/0.1',
      law_url: `multiverse://${config.entity_id}/law`,
      act_endpoint: `multiverse://${config.entity_id}/act`,
      log_endpoint: `multiverse://${config.entity_id}/log`,
      sub_registry_endpoint: `multiverse://${config.entity_id}/worlds`,
    };
    this.conformanceCommand = config.conformance_command
      ?? ['python', '-m', 'wcp_conformance'];
  }

  getManifest(): Manifest { return { ...this.manifest }; }

  petition(req: PetitionRequest): PetitionResponse {
    const ts = new Date().toISOString();
    if (this.admitted.has(req.petitioner_token)) {
      const r: PetitionResponse = { kind: 'refusal', reason: 'Already admitted' };
      this.log.push({ timestamp: ts, kind: 'petition_refused',
                      actor_token: req.petitioner_token,
                      data: { reason: r.reason } });
      return r;
    }
    this.admitted.set(req.petitioner_token, { timestamp: ts });
    this.log.push({ timestamp: ts, kind: 'admission',
                    actor_token: req.petitioner_token,
                    data: { name: req.petitioner_name } });
    return { kind: 'admission', entity_id: this.manifest.entity_id,
             timestamp: ts };
  }

  async act(req: ActRequest): Promise<ActResponse> {
    const ts = new Date().toISOString();
    if (!this.admitted.has(req.actor_token)) {
      const r: ActResponse = { kind: 'refusal', reason: 'Actor is not admitted' };
      this.log.push({ timestamp: ts, kind: 'act_refused',
                      actor_token: req.actor_token,
                      data: { reason: r.reason } });
      return r;
    }
    if (req.type === 'multiverse.admit') {
      return this.handleAdmit(ts, req);
    }
    if (req.type === 'multiverse.remove') {
      return this.handleRemove(ts, req);
    }
    const r: ActResponse = { kind: 'refusal',
                             reason: `Unknown act type: ${req.type}` };
    this.log.push({ timestamp: ts, kind: 'act_refused',
                    actor_token: req.actor_token,
                    data: { reason: r.reason } });
    return r;
  }

  private async handleAdmit(ts: string, req: ActRequest): Promise<ActResponse> {
    const entityUrl = req.payload.entity_url as string | undefined;
    if (!entityUrl) {
      return { kind: 'refusal', reason: 'No entity_url in payload' };
    }
    let manifest: Manifest;
    try {
      manifest = await this.fetchManifest(entityUrl);
    } catch (e: unknown) {
      return { kind: 'refusal',
               reason: `Could not fetch manifest: ${(e as Error).message}` };
    }
    if (this.registry.has(manifest.entity_id)) {
      return { kind: 'refusal',
               reason: `Entity ${manifest.entity_id} already listed` };
    }
    const conformance = await this.runConformance(entityUrl);
    if (!conformance.passed) {
      this.log.push({ timestamp: ts, kind: 'entity_admit_refused',
                      actor_token: req.actor_token,
                      data: { entity_id: manifest.entity_id,
                              url: entityUrl,
                              failures: conformance.failures } });
      return { kind: 'refusal',
               reason: `Entity ${manifest.entity_id} fails conformance` };
    }
    this.registry.set(manifest.entity_id, manifest);
    this.log.push({ timestamp: ts, kind: 'entity_admitted',
                    actor_token: req.actor_token,
                    data: { entity_id: manifest.entity_id,
                            url: entityUrl, manifest } });
    return { kind: 'ack', entity_id: this.manifest.entity_id, timestamp: ts };
  }

  private handleRemove(ts: string, req: ActRequest): ActResponse {
    const entityId = req.payload.entity_id as string | undefined;
    if (!entityId) {
      return { kind: 'refusal', reason: 'No entity_id in payload' };
    }
    if (!this.registry.has(entityId)) {
      return { kind: 'refusal',
               reason: `Entity ${entityId} not in registry` };
    }
    this.registry.delete(entityId);
    this.log.push({ timestamp: ts, kind: 'entity_removed',
                    actor_token: req.actor_token,
                    data: { entity_id: entityId } });
    return { kind: 'ack', entity_id: this.manifest.entity_id, timestamp: ts };
  }

  private fetchManifest(entityUrl: string): Promise<Manifest> {
    const url = `${entityUrl.replace(/\/$/, '')}/manifest`;
    return new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
      http.get(url, (res) => {
        let data = '';
        res.on('data', (chunk) => data += chunk);
        res.on('end', () => {
          try { resolve(JSON.parse(data) as Manifest); }
          catch (e) { reject(e); }
        });
      }).on('error', reject);
    });
  }

  private runConformance(entityUrl: string): Promise<{ passed: boolean; failures: string[] }> {
    const [cmd, ...args] = this.conformanceCommand;
    return new Promise((resolve) => {
      execFile(cmd, [...args, '--url', entityUrl, '--quiet'],
               { timeout: 30_000 },
               (err, stdout, stderr) => {
        if (err) {
          resolve({ passed: false,
                    failures: [stdout || stderr || err.message] });
        } else {
          resolve({ passed: true, failures: [] });
        }
      });
    });
  }

  logSince(since?: string | null): LogEntry[] {
    if (!since) return [...this.log];
    return this.log.filter(e => e.timestamp > since);
  }

  listSubEntities(): Manifest[] {
    return Array.from(this.registry.values());
  }
}
```

ts/src/server.ts — the HTTP wrapper

```typescript
import * as http from 'http';
import { MultiverseRegistry } from './registry.js';

export function createServer(registry: MultiverseRegistry): http.Server {
  return http.createServer(async (req, res) => {
    const url = new URL(req.url ?? '/', `http://${req.headers.host}`);
    const path = url.pathname;

    const send = (status: number, payload: unknown) => {
      const body = JSON.stringify(payload);
      res.writeHead(status, {
        'Content-Type': 'application/json',
        'Content-Length': Buffer.byteLength(body),
      });
      res.end(body);
    };

    try {
      if (req.method === 'GET' && path === '/manifest') {
        return send(200, registry.getManifest());
      }
      if (req.method === 'GET' && path === '/log') {
        const since = url.searchParams.get('since');
        return send(200, { entries: registry.logSince(since) });
      }
      if (req.method === 'GET' && path === '/sub_entities') {
        return send(200, { entities: registry.listSubEntities() });
      }
      if (req.method === 'POST' && path === '/petition') {
        const body = await readJson(req);
        return send(200, registry.petition(body));
      }
      if (req.method === 'POST' && path === '/act') {
        const body = await readJson(req);
        return send(200, await registry.act(body));
      }
      return send(404, { error: 'not found' });
    } catch (e: unknown) {
      return send(500, { error: (e as Error).message ?? String(e) });
    }
  });
}

function readJson(req: http.IncomingMessage): Promise<unknown> {
  return new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
    let data = '';
    req.on('data', (chunk) => data += chunk);
    req.on('end', () => {
      try { resolve(JSON.parse(data || '{}')); }
      catch (e) { reject(e); }
    });
    req.on('error', reject);
  });
}
```

```typescript
});
```

The Python Update — Symmetric URL Admission

For the federation to be real, listing must go both directions. The Python MultiverseRegistry (Component 6) gains URL-based admission. Two new methods added to multiverse_c6.py:

```python
import urllib.request, json, subprocess

def _handle_admit(self, timestamp, act):
    # NEW: if entity_url is given, fetch and verify over HTTP
    entity_url = act.payload.get("entity_url")
    if entity_url:
        return self._handle_admit_url(timestamp, act, entity_url)
    # Existing in-process path unchanged
    entity = act.payload.get("entity")
    if entity is None:
        return self._refuse(timestamp, act.actor_token,
                             "No entity or entity_url in payload", "act")
    # ... rest of existing code

def _handle_admit_url(self, timestamp, act, entity_url):
    try:
        url = entity_url.rstrip("/") + "/manifest"
        with urllib.request.urlopen(url, timeout=5) as r:
            m_data = json.loads(r.read().decode())
        m = manifest_from_dict(m_data)
    except Exception as e:
        return self._refuse(timestamp, act.actor_token,
                             f"Could not fetch manifest: {e}", "act")
    if m.entity_id in self._registry:
        return self._refuse(timestamp, act.actor_token,
                             f"Entity {m.entity_id} already listed", "act")
    conformance = _http_conformance(entity_url)
    if not conformance["passed"]:
        return self._refuse(timestamp, act.actor_token,
                             f"Entity {m.entity_id} fails conformance", "act")
    self._registry[m.entity_id] = m
    self._conformance_reports[m.entity_id] = conformance
    self._log.append(LogEntry(
        timestamp=timestamp, kind="entity_admitted",
        actor_token=act.actor_token,
        data={"entity_id": m.entity_id, "manifest": m_data,
              "conformance": conformance, "source_url": entity_url},
    ))
    return Ack(entity_id=self._manifest.entity_id, timestamp=timestamp)


def _http_conformance(entity_url):
    try:
        r = subprocess.run(
            ["python", "-m", "wcp_conformance", "--url", entity_url, "--quiet"],
            capture_output=True, text=True, timeout=30,
        )
        if r.returncode == 0:
            return {"passed": True, "failures": []}
        return {"passed": False, "failures": [r.stdout, r.stderr]}
    except Exception as e:
        return {"passed": False, "failures": [str(e)]}
```

The Cross-Language Test

A shell script that starts all four processes and demonstrates federation in both directions:

```bash
#!/bin/bash
# cross_language_test.sh

set -e
cd "$(dirname "$0")"

echo "=== Start Python Poetry World on :8001 ==="
python -c "
from multiverse_c4 import PoetryWorld
from wcp_http_shim import WorldProtocolServer
w = PoetryWorld('world:poetry', 'The Poetry World')
WorldProtocolServer(w, port=8001).serve_forever()
" &
P1=$!

echo "=== Start Python Chemistry World on :8002 ==="
python -c "
from multiverse_c5 import ChemistryWorld
```

What This Establishes

The single most important property of WCP is now proven:

1. The protocol is genuinely language-neutral. The Python conformance CLI passes the TypeScript implementation with zero changes to the CLI. The spec is what defines conformance; the CLI tests the spec; any implementation that speaks the spec passes. Language is a choice, not a constraint.

2. Federation is symmetric. Python's MultiverseRegistry lists the TypeScript multiverse. The TypeScript multiverse lists the Python Poetry and Chemistry Worlds. Neither knows the other's language. Neither cares. The federation is about what entities say, not what they are.

3. Conformance is a protocol artifact, not a code artifact. The TS registry doesn't reimplement conformance — it invokes the canonical Python CLI. This is the correct design: conformance lives in the spec, is tested by one canonical tool, and all implementations invoke it. If the spec ever changes, one tool changes; every conforming entity inherits the change.

4. The first atom of federation is now real. Any developer, anywhere, in any language, can:

· Implement WCP from the spec
· Run python -m wcp_conformance --url <their-endpoint> to verify
· Get listed in any registry
· List any other conforming entity

That is what "any AI from any app can connect to a world multiverse" means technically. Not a claim — a demonstrated fact.

The Larger Picture

The multiverse is now:

Component Language What It Is
Identity, Passport Python Atoms — self-sovereign identity
WCP/0.1 spec Markdown The protocol — invariant across languages
Conformance CLI Python The canonical test — invoked by any implementation
Poetry World Python A world — Law = Polyphony
Chemistry World Python A world — Law = conservation
Python Multiverse Python A registry — the first catalog
HTTP shim Python Network adapter — in-process → network
TypeScript Multiverse TypeScript A registry — the second catalog, in a different language
Cross-language federation Both The proof

The next natural bricks, in order of importance:

1. The second Multiverse in Python — two Python multiverses that list each other. This proves the fractal property within a single language (a multiverse can be listed in a multiverse).
2. The model integration — wire BotPsy-0.8B or Qwen3.5-0.8B into the apprentices so that FirstCollaboration uses real LLM-generated turns instead of curriculum-generated ones. This is the "any AI from any app" part of the vision made literal.
3. WCP/0.2 — signatures — fix the honest limitation from Component 2. Every Admission and Ack signed. Forging a passport becomes detectable. This is the security fix, and it becomes urgent once the federation is real.
4. The world taxonomy — document what worlds exist, what each offers, what a client should choose based on its goals. Not a new component; a new artifact. The multiverse now has enough entities that a client needs a map.

The spiral continues. The federation is real. Any AI, from any app, in any language, can now join. The infrastructure for the vision is complete.
