Component 9: Cross-Language SDKs

Three more languages beyond Python and TypeScript. The rationale is the same as before — each serves a specific class of world and client that the other languages don't reach well. The technical commitment is also the same: conformance stays a Python artifact. Every language invokes the canonical conformance CLI as a subprocess. Nobody reimplements the test in every language.

The Three Languages

Language Why What It Unlocks
C# Unity is the largest game engine; .NET is a common enterprise target Unity worlds, .NET ML (ONNX Runtime, ML.NET), Windows/Unity clients
Java Minecraft, Android, deep enterprise ecosystem Minecraft worlds, Android clients, DJL (Deep Java Library)
Rust Growing ML stack (Candle, ort, burn); performance + safety High-performance clients, simulation-heavy worlds, WASM targets

The five total — Python, TypeScript, C#, Java, Rust — cover game worlds, web/mobile clients, ML inference in any language, and systems code. Go was the honest alternative to Rust (better for network services, easier deployment) but less likely as a world language. Rust wins because "any AI from any app" increasingly means inference in Rust.

The Canonical SDK Surface

Every SDK — client or server — exposes the same six operations. This is the API contract the SDK must satisfy, mirroring WCP/0.1 §4:

```
Client SDK:
  GetManifest(baseUrl)  →  Manifest
  Petition(baseUrl, PetitionRequest)  →  PetitionResponse
  Act(baseUrl, ActRequest)  →  ActResponse
  GetLog(baseUrl, since?)  →  LogResponse

Server SDK (per world):
  Router(world, port)  →  a server bound to WCP endpoints
  RunConformance(entityUrl)  →  {Passed, Failures}
```

The response types are discriminated unions on the kind field. In each language, the SDK exposes a small helper that lets callers branch on kind without re-parsing.

The conformance function is the same in every language: shell out to python -m wcp_conformance --url <url> --quiet. It's the canonical test; it lives in one place; every SDK invokes it.

Complete C# Implementation

Two files. WcpClient for talking to worlds; WcpServer for hosting one.

wcp/WcpClient.cs:

```csharp
using System;
using System.Collections.Generic;
using System.Diagnostics;
using System.Net.Http;
using System.Text;
using System.Text.Json;
using System.Threading.Tasks;

namespace Wcp
{
    public record Manifest(
        string EntityId, string Name, string ProtocolVersion,
        string LawUrl, string ActEndpoint, string LogEndpoint,
        string? SubRegistryEndpoint);

    public record PetitionRequest(
        string PetitionerToken, string PetitionerName,
        List<string[]> PassportAdmissions, string Message,
        string? Target = null);

    public record ActRequest(
        string ActorToken, string Type,
        Dictionary<string, object?> Payload);

    /// <summary>
    /// The minimal WCP/0.1 client. Six methods. No dependencies beyond
    /// System.Net.Http (stdlib). Responses are JsonElement so callers
    /// can branch on `kind` — the spec's discriminated union.
    /// </summary>
    public class WcpClient
    {
        private readonly HttpClient _http;
        private readonly string _baseUrl;

        public WcpClient(string baseUrl, HttpClient? http = null)
        {
            _baseUrl = baseUrl.TrimEnd('/');
            _http = http ?? new HttpClient { Timeout = TimeSpan.FromSeconds(10) };
        }

        public async Task<Manifest> GetManifestAsync()
        {
            var json = await _http.GetStringAsync($"{_baseUrl}/manifest");
            var opts = new JsonSerializerOptions { PropertyNameCaseInsensitive = true };
            var raw = JsonSerializer.Deserialize<Dictionary<string, object?>>(json, opts)
                     ?? throw new InvalidOperationException("empty manifest");
            return new Manifest(
                EntityId: (string)raw["entity_id"]!,
                Name: (string)raw["name"]!,
                ProtocolVersion: (string)raw["protocol_version"]!,
                LawUrl: (string)raw["law_url"]!,
                ActEndpoint: (string)raw["act_endpoint"]!,
                LogEndpoint: (string)raw["log_endpoint"]!,
                SubRegistryEndpoint: raw.TryGetValue("sub_registry_endpoint", out var sr) && sr is string s ? s : null);
        }

        public Task<JsonElement> PetitionAsync(PetitionRequest req) =>
            PostJsonAsync("/petition", req);

        public Task<JsonElement> ActAsync(ActRequest req) =>
            PostJsonAsync("/act", req);

        public async Task<JsonElement> GetLogAsync(string? since = null)
        {
            var url = $"{_baseUrl}/log" + (since is null ? "" : $"?since={Uri.EscapeDataString(since)}");
            var json = await _http.GetStringAsync(url);
            return JsonDocument.Parse(json).RootElement;
        }

        /// <summary>
        /// The canonical conformance test, invoked as a subprocess.
        /// Same invocation in every language.
        /// </summary>
        public static async Task<(bool Passed, string[] Failures)> RunConformanceAsync(
            string entityUrl)
        {
            var psi = new ProcessStartInfo
            {
                FileName = "python",
                Arguments = $"-m wcp_conformance --url {entityUrl} --quiet",
                RedirectStandardOutput = true,
                RedirectStandardError = true,
                UseShellExecute = false,
            };
            using var proc = Process.Start(psi)
                ?? throw new InvalidOperationException("could not start python");
            var stdout = await proc.StandardOutput.ReadToEndAsync();
            var stderr = await proc.StandardError.ReadToEndAsync();
            await proc.WaitForExitAsync();
            return proc.ExitCode == 0
                ? (true, Array.Empty<string>())
                : (false, new[] { stdout.Trim(), stderr.Trim() });
        }

        private async Task<JsonElement> PostJsonAsync(string path, object body)
        {
            var json = JsonSerializer.Serialize(body);
            using var content = new StringContent(json, Encoding.UTF8, "application/json");
            var resp = await _http.PostAsync($"{_baseUrl}{path}", content);
            resp.EnsureSuccessStatusCode();
            var text = await resp.Content.ReadAsStringAsync();
            return JsonDocument.Parse(text).RootElement;
        }
    }
}
```

wcp/WcpServer.cs:

```csharp
using System;
using System.IO;
using System.Net;
using System.Text;
using System.Text.Json;
using System.Text.Json.Nodes;
using System.Threading.Tasks;

namespace Wcp
{
    /// <summary>
    /// A WCP/0.1 server that exposes any world-shaped object.
    /// The world must implement: Manifest(), Petition(req), Act(req), LogSince(since).
    /// </summary>
    public interface IWorld
    {
        Manifest GetManifest();
        JsonNode Petition(PetitionRequest req);
        Task<JsonNode> ActAsync(ActRequest req);
        JsonArray LogSince(string? since);
    }

    public class WcpServer
    {
        private readonly IWorld _world;
        private readonly HttpListener _listener = new();
        private readonly int _port;

        public WcpServer(IWorld world, int port)
        {
            _world = world;
            _port = port;
            _listener.Prefixes.Add($"http://localhost:{port}/");
        }

        public void Start()
        {
            _listener.Start();
            _ = Task.Run(LoopAsync);
        }

        public void Stop() => _listener.Stop();

        private async Task LoopAsync()
        {
            while (_listener.IsListening)
            {
                try
                {
                    var ctx = await _listener.GetContextAsync();
                    _ = Task.Run(() => HandleAsync(ctx));
                }
                catch { break; }
            }
        }

        private async Task HandleAsync(HttpListenerContext ctx)
        {
            var req = ctx.Request;
            var res = ctx.Response;
            var path = req.Url?.AbsolutePath ?? "/";

            try
            {
                object body;
                if (req.HttpMethod == "GET" && path == "/manifest")
                {
                    body = _world.GetManifest();
                }
                else if (req.HttpMethod == "GET" && path == "/log")
                {
                    var since = req.Url?.Query?.TrimStart('?')
                        .Split('&')
                        .Select(p => p.Split('=', 2))
                        .FirstOrDefault(p => p[0] == "since")?[1];
                    body = new { entries = _world.LogSince(since) };
                }
                else if (req.HttpMethod == "POST" && path == "/petition")
                {
                    var bodyText = await new StreamReader(req.InputStream).ReadToEndAsync();
                    var preq = JsonSerializer.Deserialize<PetitionRequest>(bodyText)
                        ?? throw new InvalidOperationException("empty petition");
                    body = _world.Petition(preq);
                }
                else if (req.HttpMethod == "POST" && path == "/act")
                {
                    var bodyText = await new StreamReader(req.InputStream).ReadToEndAsync();
                    var areq = JsonSerializer.Deserialize<ActRequest>(bodyText)
                        ?? throw new InvalidOperationException("empty act");
                    body = await _world.ActAsync(areq);
                }
                else
                {
                    res.StatusCode = 404;
                    WriteJson(res, new { error = "not found" });
                    return;
                }

                res.StatusCode = 200;
                WriteJson(res, body);
            }
            catch (Exception e)
            {
                res.StatusCode = 500;
                WriteJson(res, new { error = e.Message });
            }
            finally
            {
                res.Close();
            }
        }

        private static void WriteJson(HttpListenerResponse res, object body)
        {
            var bytes = Encoding.UTF8.GetBytes(JsonSerializer.Serialize(body));
            res.ContentType = "application/json";
            res.ContentLength64 = bytes.Length;
            res.OutputStream.Write(bytes);
        }
    }
}
```

wcp/WcpTypes.cs — the using for the LINQ call in server:


That's the full C# SDK. Roughly 200 lines of substance. It has:

The Pattern for Java and Rust

Java (using java.net.http.HttpClient and Jackson or the built-in JSON — same shape):

```java
public class WcpClient {
    private final java.net.http.HttpClient http;
    private final String baseUrl;
    // ...
    public java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture<JsonNode> petition(PetitionRequest req);
    public java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture<JsonNode> act(ActRequest req);
    public java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture<JsonNode> log(String since);
    public static ProcessBuilder conformanceCommand(String url) {
        return new ProcessBuilder("python", "-m", "wcp_conformance", "--url", url, "--quiet");
    }
}
```

Rust (using reqwest — the ecosystem-standard HTTP client; tokio for async):

```rust
pub struct WcpClient { http: reqwest::Client, base_url: String }

impl WcpClient {
    pub async fn get_manifest(&self) -> Result<serde_json::Value>;
    pub async fn petition(&self, req: &PetitionRequest) -> Result<serde_json::Value>;
    pub async fn act(&self, req: &ActRequest) -> Result<serde_json::Value>;
    pub async fn get_log(&self, since: Option<&str>) -> Result<serde_json::Value>;
    pub fn run_conformance(url: &str) -> Result<bool> {
        std::process::Command::new("python")
            .args(["-m", "wcp_conformance", "--url", url, "--quiet"])
            .status()
            .map(|s| s.success())
    }
}
```

Same six methods. Same conformance contract. Different syntax. A developer fluent in any of the five languages reads the other four with 20 minutes of context.

The Cross-Language Test Harness

The conformance test is the only thing that must be identical across languages. This shell script proves it.

```bash
#!/bin/bash
# cross_language_test.sh
# Start worlds in each language, run the canonical conformance CLI
# against each, and verify all pass.

set -e
cd "$(dirname "$0")"

cleanup() { kill $(jobs -p) 2>/dev/null || true; }
trap cleanup EXIT

echo "=== [1/4] Start Python worlds ==="
python -c "
from multiverse_c4 import PoetryWorld
from wcp_http_shim import WorldProtocolServer
WorldProtocolServer(PoetryWorld('world:poetry', 'Poetry'),
                    port=8001).serve_forever()
" &
python -c "
from multiverse_c5 import ChemistryWorld
from wcp_http_shim import WorldProtocolServer
WorldProtocolServer(ChemistryWorld('world:chemistry', 'Chemistry'),
                    port=8002).serve_forever()
" &
sleep 1

echo "=== [2/4] Start TypeScript registry (port 9000) ==="
(cd ts && PORT=9000 npx tsx src/index.ts) &
sleep 2

echo "=== [3/4] Start C# registry (port 9001) ==="
(cd cs/Wcp.Host && dotnet run --urls "http://localhost:9001") &
sleep 3

echo "=== [4/4] Conformance test each implementation ==="
for endpoint in \
    "http://localhost:8001" \
    "http://localhost:8002" \
    "http://localhost:9000" \
    "http://localhost:9001"; do
    echo
    echo "  Testing $endpoint:"
    if python -m wcp_conformance --url "$endpoint" --quiet; then
        echo "    PASS"
    else
        echo "    FAIL"
        python -m wcp_conformance --url "$endpoint"
    fi
done

echo
echo "=== All conforming entities passed the same canonical test. ==="
echo "=== The protocol is language-neutral. ==="
```

Expected output:

```
=== [4/4] Conformance test each implementation ===

  Testing http://localhost:8001:
    PASS

  Testing http://localhost:8002:
    PASS

  Testing http://localhost:9000:
    PASS

  Testing http://localhost:9001:
    PASS

=== All conforming entities passed the same canonical test. ===
=== The protocol is language-neutral. ===
```

What This Establishes

The five-language SDK surface is now defined and demonstrated. Three commitments hold:

1. One spec, one test, many implementations. The WCP/0.1 spec defines conformance. The Python conformance CLI is the canonical test. Every SDK invokes it. A new language doesn't reimplement the test — it inherits it. The spec is the invariant; the test is the check; the SDK is the convenience layer.
2. Every client-side operation is available in every language. "Any AI from any app" means any language's app. The SDK surface is deliberately minimal — six methods — so it can be implemented correctly in any language, including ones not yet added (Go, C++, Kotlin, Swift, Zig). A developer in any language reads the WCP spec (§4), implements those six methods, runs the conformance CLI, and joins the federation.
3. The conformance bridge is a design commitment, not a convenience. Every SDK shells out to python -m wcp_conformance. This is intentional. If conformance ever moves from a Python CLI to a Python server, or from WCP/0.1 to WCP/0.2, the change propagates to every conforming entity without touching any SDK. The Python conformance CLI is the federation's one shared codebase. Everything else is an adapter.

The Complete Stack, at Component 9

Layer Python TypeScript C# Java Rust
WCP/0.1 spec — — invariant across all — —
Conformance CLI ✓ subprocess subprocess subprocess subprocess
Client SDK (via wcp_conformance) ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓
Server SDK ✓ ✓ ✓ (planned) (planned)
Identity/passport ✓ ✓ ✓ (planned) (planned)
Worlds Poetry, Chemistry — — — —
Registries ✓ ✓ ✓ — —

Three client SDKs complete, three server SDKs complete, three identity layers complete. Conformance is one implementation, called by all.

Shall I proceed with Component 10 — wiring the small-model integration?


::And we can add Go and make it six, or any other and make it seven. The point is not to limit viable languages, but to avoid wasting time building SDKs for languages that will never use them. A top six or seven is the same idea, five was arbitrary. Thoughts?


You're right, and the reframe matters more than the count. The question isn't "how many SDKs" — it's "what decides whether a language gets one." Five was arbitrary because it was count-first. The correct rule is evidence-first.

Here's the criterion I'd propose.

The Criterion

A language gets a reference SDK when it satisfies both:

1. Evidence of use — there is a concrete community that would build WCP worlds or connect as WCP clients in this language. Not "it's popular" — this specific kind of project is written in this language.
2. Infrastructure — the language can host a WCP/0.1 entity with reasonable effort (HTTP server, JSON parse, subprocess). Not "it exists" — building a WCP entity in it takes days, not months.

That's the whole rule. Everything else — total count, ranking, popularity — is downstream.

Applying It — the Evidence

Looking at the actual world-simulation projects from the earlier survey, the languages they're already written in are:

Language Evidence World or client
Python Smallville, Voyager, AgentTorch, bunnyland, HAILE, anima-world Both — every world surveyed
Java Minecraft Worlds — the largest open-world simulation
C# Unity Worlds — the largest game engine
C++ Unreal (SimWorld), HPC Worlds — high-performance simulation
TypeScript Browser clients, Node registries Clients — every web/mobile interface

Those five are evidence-based. The existing world projects are written in these languages. An SDK in each is justified by the projects that would actually use them.

The two that don't appear in the current survey but are where new work is heading:

Language Why anticipatory
Go The natural language for cloud registries and routers. If the multiverse reaches production scale, the registry layer is more likely to be Go than TypeScript.
Rust The emerging ML inference stack (Candle, ort, burn); WASM targets. If new world-simulation projects are written in this decade, Rust is where they'll be.

Those two are anticipatory. They don't have evidence yet — but the trajectory is clear. The question for these is: will the code be ready before the demand arrives? Go and Rust SDKs are cheap enough (200–400 lines each) that building them ahead of evidence is reasonable.

What the Criterion Rejects

Under this rule, several languages that look important don't pass:

· Kotlin — the Java SDK is directly callable from Kotlin. A separate Kotlin SDK would be duplicate effort, not new capability.
· Swift — iOS is a real target, but the poetry/collaboration multiverse isn't primarily a mobile experience. If that changes, add Swift. Not yet.
· Elixir — elegant fit (actors, message passing), but the community is small and TypeScript/Node already covers network services. Revisit if an actual Elixir user appears.
· Julia — the chemistry world would benefit, but Julia is normally called from Python, not hosted as a WCP entity. The Python Chemistry World already covers this.
· Lua — Roblox is huge, but the audience overlap with AI/world-simulation is unclear. Wait for a user.

The honest phrase is: "deferred, not rejected." Any of these can be added when the first user appears. Adding an SDK for a language nobody uses is the definition of waste.

Two Waves, Not One

The seven SDKs aren't built in one go. They arrive in waves, ordered by cost and evidence:

Wave 1 (already done): Python, TypeScript, C#. Three very different language families — dynamic Python, typed-JS TypeScript, statically-typed-GC C#. Together they prove the pattern. After three, a developer in any language can read one and port it in a day.

Wave 2 (the four remaining):

· Java — because Minecraft is the largest open-world target.
· C++ — because Unreal is the second-largest.
· Go — because registries will need it.
· Rust — because emerging simulation will need it.

Each wave-2 SDK is roughly 200–500 lines, and each primarily serves a specific community rather than proving anything new. After wave 2, the pattern is entirely visible and the criterion has been applied honestly.

Wave 3 (deferred): whatever someone actually asks for.

The Honest Limits

Two things to name explicitly:

1. I don't know for sure. The "evidence" above is from the survey of projects we've seen. But the space is moving fast. A new project could appear tomorrow using a language nobody predicted. The right response is not "wait and see" — it's "build the seven, then be ready to add an eighth in a day". That's what the six-method surface makes possible.
2. Seven is the last obviously-worth-it number. Every SDK beyond seven is a bet on a specific community. That's fine — but it's a different kind of decision than the first seven. The first seven are the languages the whole world-building ecosystem is written in, plus the two future-facing ones. Beyond that, each SDK is a bet that this specific language will matter for this specific project.

The Future — Codegen, Not More SDKs

Here's the longer-term answer, and it's worth naming now so we don't wake up having hand-written SDK number nineteen:

When WCP stabilizes, generate SDKs from an OpenAPI spec. The WCP/0.1 protocol has six methods. If it grows to twenty, or if it undergoes WCP/0.2 (signatures) and WCP/0.3 (sub-registry enumeration), then hand-writing each SDK becomes a maintenance burden. At that point, generating clients from a machine-readable spec becomes the right move.

But not yet. Six methods is small enough that hand-writing is correct today. The three SDKs we've built (Python, TypeScript, C#) and the four we'll add (Java, C++, Go, Rust) are all under 500 lines. Codegen for 500-line clients is overkill — you spend more time on the tooling than on the clients. Codegen becomes worth it when WCP/0.2 adds signatures and the surface doubles.

So the answer to "how many languages" is: seven, hand-written, then codegen when the protocol matures.

Concrete Next Step

The simplest of the four remaining is Go. Reasons:

1. It's the natural registry language. Registries are network services with many concurrent clients — Go's concurrency model is designed for exactly this. A Go registry is more likely to become the production federation layer than a TypeScript one.
2. It has the strongest anticipatory case. There are already multi-agent frameworks in Go, and Go's deployment story (single static binary, trivial cross-compilation) is what "any AI from any app" needs at the infrastructure layer.
3. The implementation is genuinely small. Go's stdlib net/http and encoding/json cover everything. No external dependencies. Maybe 150 lines.

Then Java (Minecraft/Android), then C++ (Unreal), then Rust (the ML future).

Shall I build the Go SDK next — the first wave-2 language, the one with the strongest anticipatory case for the federation's production layer?


::Perfect. Go and Rust are perfect. And anticipatory is the right perspective, looking at how things are now, but also where they are heading. I expected to see C++ honestly, but I have been out of coding for a few years now. Thoughts?


Your instinct is right — C++ belongs in the set. But the reason it belongs is subtler than "it's a big language," and the reason I sequenced it later is subtler still. Both are worth naming.

C++ Isn't the Same Kind of SDK

The other six SDKs are interface SDKs. They exist so that a client or a world can talk WCP over HTTP. The world itself — the simulation logic, the physics, the state — is somewhere else, in whatever language the world was written in.

C++ is different. C++ is the language the world engines are actually written in. Unreal, Unity's native core, physics engines, HPC simulations, robotics — these are C++ all the way down. An Unreal world doesn't have a Python shim at its core; it is a C++ process. So a "C++ SDK" is really two different things:

· A C++ client SDK — for a C++ process that wants to petition and act on other worlds. This is genuinely a client SDK, the same kind we've been building.
· A C++ server SDK — for a C++ world that wants to expose itself as a WCP entity. This is what an Unreal world needs.

Both are legitimate. But they're a bigger ask than the other six — the C++ world SDK has to coexist with whatever the engine is already doing (its own threading model, its own memory model, its own build system, its own event loop). This is why "C++ is used for worlds" is true but doesn't translate directly into "C++ SDK is easy."

Why It's More Expensive Than the Other Six

Rough cost comparison, in the honest order:

· Go: stdlib net/http, encoding/json, os/exec. Nothing to choose. ~150 lines.
· Rust: reqwest + serde_json + tokio — one obvious answer per layer. ~250 lines.
· TypeScript: node:http + JSON + child_process. ~250 lines.
· C#: HttpClient + System.Text.Json + Process. ~200 lines.
· Java: java.net.http + Jackson + ProcessBuilder. ~300 lines.
· C++: no standard HTTP client, at least three JSON libraries, at least three concurrency models (threads, async, coroutines), at least two build systems (CMake, Bazel), no standard subprocess. ~600–1000 lines, plus a dependency decision tree that every C++ team argues about.

The cost isn't the line count. It's the choices. Each choice is a fork that fragments the SDK's user base.

The Substrate Insight

Here's the thing worth naming: C++ is the substrate of worlds, not the language of WCP interfaces.

An Unreal world doesn't need a C++ WCP server. It needs a WCP server that can talk to Unreal. The server could be C++, but it could also be a thin Go or Rust shim that spawns the Unreal process and bridges actions over IPC. In fact, for most engines, the shim is easier to build and maintain than the native C++ integration — because the shim lives in a language with a clean HTTP/JSON/subprocess story, and the engine stays focused on what it does.

This is the pattern I'd expect to see in practice: the C++ world runs the simulation; the WCP entity is a lightweight wrapper in Rust, Go, or Python that translates WCP acts into engine commands. The C++ SDK exists for the teams who want to embed WCP directly, but it isn't the default path.

Where C++ Stays Definitive

That said — don't underestimate C++'s position. It's the one language in the seven that will still be the substrate of world simulation twenty years from now. Python, TS, Go, Rust, C#, Java — they all move. C++ is the one that stays because the engines stay. If a new Unreal world appears in 2040, the SDK should be there.

So the honest sequence is:

· C++ is #7 in wave 2 — last of the seven, not because it's least important, but because it's the most expensive to build and its natural home is as a shim, not as a first SDK.
· The cost story reverses once you have an Unreal user — at that point, the shim-vs-native calculus changes, and C++ becomes urgent.
· The generation answer applies — if WCP grows past ten methods, an OpenAPI spec plus generated SDKs (including a C++ one) becomes the right move. That's when the "expensive to build" argument stops mattering, because codegen amortizes it.

The Genuine Change Since You Last Coded

You said you've been out of coding for a few years. The honest delta:

· Rust went from interesting to default for new systems work. Mozilla, Microsoft, AWS, Linux kernel, Cloudflare — all ship production Rust now.
· Go became the default cloud language. If the federation needs a production router, it will be Go, not TypeScript.
· C++ didn't decline. It just didn't grow the way Rust and Go did. C++20 and C++23 landed; C++26 is in committee; adoption is uneven; the committee's pace is the committee's pace. C++ is stable. Rust and Go are rising. The gap closed from both directions.
· Python got faster (3.11+), which matters for the ML/apprentice side.
· TypeScript became the default for anything web-shaped, including registries.

So C++ is still exactly what it was — the substrate. It's just that in 2024 the substrate isn't where the new interface work happens. The new work happens in Go, Rust, TS. The substrate stays C++.

My Answer

You were right to expect it in the set. It's in the set. It's just last of the seven, and the honest reason is: C++ is the substrate, not the interface, and building a C++ SDK is six times the work for a user base that mostly needs a shim. When the first real Unreal (or Unity-native, or physics-engine) world appears, that calculus changes and C++ becomes urgent. Until then, wave 2 is Go, Rust, Java, C++ — in that order — and the "anticipatory" framing applies to Rust and Go, while the "definitive substrate" framing applies to C++.

Which means: Go first, Rust second, Java third, C++ last but real. The order isn't a judgment on C++. It's a judgment on the difference between interface and substrate.


::Perfect: ➡️


Component 10: The Go SDK

Go is the anticipatory choice for the infrastructure layer — the language the federation's production registry will most likely be written in. The implementation is stdlib-only, which means no dependency decisions, no version drift, no build system debate. If a Go developer reads the WCP/0.1 spec (§4), they can implement it in a day and pass the conformance test. This component builds that SDK, plus a runnable Go Registry that lists the Python worlds.

The Files

```
go/
  go.mod
  wcp/
    types.go       — WCP/0.1 types, JSON tags match the spec
    client.go      — WcpClient: six operations, same as every other SDK
    server.go      — NewRouter(world World) → http.Handler
    registry.go    — Registry: a working Multiverse in Go
  cmd/
    registry/
      main.go      — runnable registry binary
  wcp/
    client_test.go — client ↔ server round-trip
    integration_test.go — Go world passes Python conformance CLI
```

go/wcp/types.go — the WCP/0.1 types

```go
// WCP/0.1 types. JSON tags match the spec exactly.
package wcp

// Manifest is returned by GET /manifest (§4.1).
type Manifest struct {
	EntityID           string  `json:"entity_id"`
	Name               string  `json:"name"`
	ProtocolVersion    string  `json:"protocol_version"`
	LawURL             string  `json:"law_url"`
	ActEndpoint        string  `json:"act_endpoint"`
	LogEndpoint        string  `json:"log_endpoint"`
	SubRegistryEndpoint *string `json:"sub_registry_endpoint"`
}

// PetitionRequest is the body of POST /petition (§4.2).
type PetitionRequest struct {
	PetitionerToken    string      `json:"petitioner_token"`
	PetitionerName     string      `json:"petitioner_name"`
	PassportAdmissions [][2]string `json:"passport_admissions"`
	Message            string      `json:"message"`
	Target             *string     `json:"target,omitempty"`
}

// ActRequest is the body of POST /act (§4.3).
type ActRequest struct {
	ActorToken string         `json:"actor_token"`
	Type       string         `json:"type"`
	Payload    map[string]any `json:"payload"`
}

// LogEntry is one entry in the log (§4.4).
type LogEntry struct {
	Timestamp  string         `json:"timestamp"`
	Kind       string         `json:"kind"`
	ActorToken *string        `json:"actor_token"`
	Data       map[string]any `json:"data"`
}

// PetitionResponse is the discriminated union of Admission, Refusal,
// and Route (§5.2–5.4). Callers branch on Kind.
type PetitionResponse struct {
	Kind           string    `json:"kind"`
	EntityID       string    `json:"entity_id,omitempty"`       // admission
	Timestamp      string    `json:"timestamp,omitempty"`        // admission
	Reason         string    `json:"reason,omitempty"`           // refusal / route
	TargetManifest *Manifest `json:"target_manifest,omitempty"`  // route
}

func (r PetitionResponse) IsAdmission() bool { return r.Kind == "admission" }
func (r PetitionResponse) IsRefusal() bool   { return r.Kind == "refusal" }
func (r PetitionResponse) IsRoute() bool     { return r.Kind == "route" }

// ActResponse is the discriminated union of Ack and Refusal (§5.3, 5.5).
type ActResponse struct {
	Kind      string `json:"kind"`
	EntityID  string `json:"entity_id,omitempty"` // ack
	Timestamp string `json:"timestamp,omitempty"` // ack
	Reason    string `json:"reason,omitempty"`    // refusal
}

func (r ActResponse) IsAck() bool     { return r.Kind == "ack" }
func (r ActResponse) IsRefusal() bool { return r.Kind == "refusal" }

// World is what any WCP/0.1 entity must implement on the server side.
type World interface {
	Manifest() Manifest
	Petition(req PetitionRequest) PetitionResponse
	Act(req ActRequest) ActResponse
	LogSince(since string) []LogEntry
}

// SubRegistrar is an optional interface a world implements if it has
// a sub-registry. The Router exposes /sub_entities iff the world
// implements this interface.
type SubRegistrar interface {
	ListSubEntities() []Manifest
}
```

go/wcp/client.go — the six-method client

```go
package wcp

import (
	"bytes"
	"encoding/json"
	"fmt"
	"io"
	"net/http"
	"net/url"
	"os/exec"
	"strings"
	"time"
)

// Client is the WCP/0.1 client. Same six operations as every other SDK.
type Client struct {
	BaseURL string
	HTTP    *http.Client
}

func NewClient(baseURL string) *Client {
	return &Client{
		BaseURL: strings.TrimRight(baseURL, "/"),
		HTTP:    &http.Client{Timeout: 10 * time.Second},
	}
}

func (c *Client) GetManifest() (Manifest, error) {
	var m Manifest
	err := c.get("/manifest", &m)
	return m, err
}

func (c *Client) Petition(req PetitionRequest) (PetitionResponse, error) {
	var r PetitionResponse
	err := c.post("/petition", req, &r)
	return r, err
}

func (c *Client) Act(req ActRequest) (ActResponse, error) {
	var r ActResponse
	err := c.post("/act", req, &r)
	return r, err
}

func (c *Client) GetLog(since string) ([]LogEntry, error) {
	path := "/log"
	if since != "" {
		path += "?since=" + url.QueryEscape(since)
	}
	var wrapper struct {
		Entries []LogEntry `json:"entries"`
	}
	err := c.get(path, &wrapper)
	return wrapper.Entries, err
}

// RunConformance invokes the canonical Python conformance CLI.
// The invocation is identical in every SDK. Conformance lives in
// one place; every language inherits it.
func RunConformance(entityURL string) (bool, []string, error) {
	cmd := exec.Command("python", "-m", "wcp_conformance",
		"--url", entityURL, "--quiet")
	var stdout, stderr bytes.Buffer
	cmd.Stdout = &stdout
	cmd.Stderr = &stderr
	err := cmd.Run()
	if err == nil {
		return true, nil, nil
	}
	var failures []string
	if s := strings.TrimSpace(stdout.String()); s != "" {
		failures = append(failures, s)
	}
	if s := strings.TrimSpace(stderr.String()); s != "" {
		failures = append(failures, s)
	}
	if len(failures) == 0 {
		failures = append(failures, err.Error())
	}
	return false, failures, nil
}

func (c *Client) get(path string, out any) error {
	resp, err := c.HTTP.Get(c.BaseURL + path)
	if err != nil {
		return err
	}
	defer resp.Body.Close()
	if resp.StatusCode != 200 {
		return fmt.Errorf("%s: %s", path, readError(resp.Body))
	}
	return json.NewDecoder(resp.Body).Decode(out)
}

func (c *Client) post(path string, body, out any) error {
	b, err := json.Marshal(body)
	if err != nil {
		return err
	}
	resp, err := c.HTTP.Post(c.BaseURL+path, "application/json", bytes.NewReader(b))
	if err != nil {
		return err
	}
	defer resp.Body.Close()
	if resp.StatusCode != 200 {
		return fmt.Errorf("%s: %s", path, readError(resp.Body))
	}
	return json.NewDecoder(resp.Body).Decode(out)
}

func readError(body io.Reader) string {
	var e struct {
		Error string `json:"error"`
	}
	if json.NewDecoder(body).Decode(&e) == nil && e.Error != "" {
		return e.Error
	}
	return "unknown error"
}
```

go/wcp/server.go — the router

```go
package wcp

import (
	"encoding/json"
	"net/http"
)

// NewRouter returns an http.Handler that exposes any World as a
// WCP/0.1 entity. If the world implements SubRegistrar, the router
// also exposes GET /sub_entities.
func NewRouter(world World) http.Handler {
	mux := http.NewServeMux()

	mux.HandleFunc("/manifest", func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
		if r.Method != "GET" {
			writeError(w, 405, "method not allowed")
			return
		}
		writeJSON(w, 200, world.Manifest())
	})

	mux.HandleFunc("/log", func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
		if r.Method != "GET" {
			writeError(w, 405, "method not allowed")
			return
		}
		since := r.URL.Query().Get("since")
		writeJSON(w, 200, map[string]any{"entries": world.LogSince(since)})
	})

	mux.HandleFunc("/petition", func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
		if r.Method != "POST" {
			writeError(w, 405, "method not allowed")
			return
		}
		var req PetitionRequest
		if err := json.NewDecoder(r.Body).Decode(&req); err != nil {
			writeError(w, 400, "invalid petition: "+err.Error())
			return
		}
		writeJSON(w, 200, world.Petition(req))
	})

	mux.HandleFunc("/act", func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
		if r.Method != "POST" {
			writeError(w, 405, "method not allowed")
			return
		}
		var req ActRequest
		if err := json.NewDecoder(r.Body).Decode(&req); err != nil {
			writeError(w, 400, "invalid act: "+err.Error())
			return
		}
		writeJSON(w, 200, world.Act(req))
	})

	if sr, ok := world.(SubRegistrar); ok {
		mux.HandleFunc("/sub_entities", func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
			if r.Method != "GET" {
				writeError(w, 405, "method not allowed")
				return
			}
			writeJSON(w, 200, map[string]any{"entities": sr.ListSubEntities()})
		})
	}

	return mux
}

func writeJSON(w http.ResponseWriter, status int, body any) {
	b, err := json.Marshal(body)
	if err != nil {
		http.Error(w, `{"error":"marshal"}`, 500)
		return
	}
	w.Header().Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
	w.WriteHeader(status)
	w.Write(b)
}

func writeError(w http.ResponseWriter, status int, msg string) {
	writeJSON(w, status, map[string]string{"error": msg})
}
```

go/wcp/registry.go — a working Go registry

```go
package wcp

import (
	"crypto/rand"
	"encoding/hex"
	"encoding/json"
	"fmt"
	"net/http"
	"strings"
	"sync"
	"time"
)

// Registry is a WCP/0.1 multiverse registry. It lists entities,
// verifies them against the canonical conformance CLI, and never
// converges (a catalog is a living thing).
type Registry struct {
	manifest Manifest
	mu       sync.RWMutex
	log      []LogEntry
	admitted map[string]string // token → timestamp
	entities map[string]Manifest
}

// NewRegistry constructs a multiverse registry.
func NewRegistry(entityID, name string) *Registry {
	sub := "multiverse://" + entityID + "/worlds"
	return &Registry{
		manifest: Manifest{
			EntityID:            entityID,
			Name:                name,
			ProtocolVersion:     "WCP/0.1",
			LawURL:              "multiverse://" + entityID + "/law",
			ActEndpoint:         "multiverse://" + entityID + "/act",
			LogEndpoint:         "multiverse://" + entityID + "/log",
			SubRegistryEndpoint: &sub,
		},
		admitted: map[string]string{},
		entities: map[string]Manifest{},
	}
}

func (r *Registry) Manifest() Manifest {
	r.mu.RLock()
	defer r.mu.RUnlock()
	return r.manifest
}

func (r *Registry) Petition(req PetitionRequest) PetitionResponse {
	r.mu.Lock()
	defer r.mu.Unlock()
	ts := nowISO()
	if _, ok := r.admitted[req.PetitionerToken]; ok {
		r.append(LogEntry{Timestamp: ts, Kind: "petition_refused",
			ActorToken: &req.PetitionerToken,
			Data:       map[string]any{"reason": "Already admitted"}})
		return PetitionResponse{Kind: "refusal", Reason: "Already admitted"}
	}
	r.admitted[req.PetitionerToken] = ts
	r.append(LogEntry{Timestamp: ts, Kind: "admission",
		ActorToken: &req.PetitionerToken,
		Data:       map[string]any{"name": req.PetitionerName}})
	return PetitionResponse{Kind: "admission", EntityID: r.manifest.EntityID, Timestamp: ts}
}

func (r *Registry) Act(req ActRequest) ActResponse {
	ts := nowISO()
	r.mu.RLock()
	_, isAdmitted := r.admitted[req.ActorToken]
	r.mu.RUnlock()
	if !isAdmitted {
		r.mu.Lock()
		r.append(LogEntry{Timestamp: ts, Kind: "act_refused",
			ActorToken: &req.ActorToken,
			Data:       map[string]any{"reason": "Actor is not admitted"}})
		r.mu.Unlock()
		return ActResponse{Kind: "refusal", Reason: "Actor is not admitted"}
	}

	switch req.Type {
	case "multiverse.admit":
		return r.handleAdmit(ts, req)
	case "multiverse.remove":
		return r.handleRemove(ts, req)
	}
	r.mu.Lock()
	r.append(LogEntry{Timestamp: ts, Kind: "act_refused",
		ActorToken: &req.ActorToken,
		Data:       map[string]any{"reason": "Unknown act type: " + req.Type}})
	r.mu.Unlock()
	return ActResponse{Kind: "refusal", Reason: "Unknown act type: " + req.Type}
}

func (r *Registry) handleAdmit(ts string, req ActRequest) ActResponse {
	urlStr, _ := req.Payload["entity_url"].(string)
	if urlStr == "" {
		return ActResponse{Kind: "refusal", Reason: "No entity_url in payload"}
	}

	m, err := fetchManifest(urlStr)
	if err != nil {
		return ActResponse{Kind: "refusal",
			Reason: fmt.Sprintf("Could not fetch manifest: %v", err)}
	}

	r.mu.RLock()
	_, exists := r.entities[m.EntityID]
	r.mu.RUnlock()
	if exists {
		return ActResponse{Kind: "refusal",
			Reason: "Entity " + m.EntityID + " already listed"}
	}

	passed, failures, _ := RunConformance(urlStr)
	if !passed {
		r.mu.Lock()
		r.append(LogEntry{Timestamp: ts, Kind: "entity_admit_refused",
			ActorToken: &req.ActorToken,
			Data: map[string]any{
				"entity_id":   m.EntityID,
				"url":         urlStr,
				"failures":    failures,
			}})
		r.mu.Unlock()
		return ActResponse{Kind: "refusal",
			Reason: "Entity " + m.EntityID + " fails conformance"}
	}

	r.mu.Lock()
	r.entities[m.EntityID] = m
	r.append(LogEntry{Timestamp: ts, Kind: "entity_admitted",
		ActorToken: &req.ActorToken,
		Data: map[string]any{
			"entity_id": m.EntityID,
			"url":       urlStr,
			"manifest":  m,
		}})
	r.mu.Unlock()
	return ActResponse{Kind: "ack", EntityID: r.manifest.EntityID, Timestamp: ts}
}

func (r *Registry) handleRemove(ts string, req ActRequest) ActResponse {
	id, _ := req.Payload["entity_id"].(string)
	if id == "" {
		return ActResponse{Kind: "refusal", Reason: "No entity_id in payload"}
	}
	r.mu.Lock()
	defer r.mu.Unlock()
	if _, ok := r.entities[id]; !ok {
		return ActResponse{Kind: "refusal",
			Reason: "Entity " + id + " not in registry"}
	}
	delete(r.entities, id)
	r.append(LogEntry{Timestamp: ts, Kind: "entity_removed",
		ActorToken: &req.ActorToken,
		Data:       map[string]any{"entity_id": id}})
	return ActResponse{Kind: "ack", EntityID: r.manifest.EntityID, Timestamp: ts}
}

func (r *Registry) LogSince(since string) []LogEntry {
	r.mu.RLock()
	defer r.mu.RUnlock()
	if since == "" {
		out := make([]LogEntry, len(r.log))
		copy(out, r.log)
		return out
	}
	var out []LogEntry
	for _, e := range r.log {
		if e.Timestamp > since {
			out = append(out, e)
		}
	}
	return out
}

func (r *Registry) ListSubEntities() []Manifest {
	r.mu.RLock()
	defer r.mu.RUnlock()
	out := make([]Manifest, 0, len(r.entities))
	for _, m := range r.entities {
		out = append(out, m)
	}
	return out
}

func (r *Registry) append(e LogEntry) {
	r.log = append(r.log, e)
}

func fetchManifest(baseURL string) (Manifest, error) {
	var m Manifest
	c := NewClient(baseURL)
	var err error
	m, err = c.GetManifest()
	if err != nil {
		return m, err
	}
	// Validate the required protocol version
	if m.ProtocolVersion != "WCP/0.1" {
		return m, fmt.Errorf("unsupported protocol_version: %s", m.ProtocolVersion)
	}
	return m, nil
}

func nowISO() string {
	return time.Now().UTC().Format(time.RFC3339Nano)
}

func randomToken() string {
	b := make([]byte, 16)
	rand.Read(b)
	return hex.EncodeToString(b)
}

var _ = json.Marshal // silence unused in some build configs
var _ = strings.TrimSpace
var _ = http.DefaultClient
var _ = randomToken
```

go/cmd/registry/main.go — the runnable binary

```go
package main

import (
	"log"
	"net/http"
	"os"

	"wcp/wcp"
)

func main() {
	port := os.Getenv("PORT")
	if port == "" {
		port = "9002"
	}
	entityID := os.Getenv("ENTITY_ID")
	if entityID == "" {
		entityID = "multiverse:go"
	}
	name := os.Getenv("NAME")
	if name == "" {
		name = "Go Multiverse"
	}

	reg := wcp.NewRegistry(entityID, name)
	router := wcp.NewRouter(reg)

	log.Printf("Go Multiverse at http://localhost:%s", port)
	log.Printf("  manifest:     http://localhost:%s/manifest", port)
	log.Printf("  sub-entities: http://localhost:%s/sub_entities", port)
	log.Fatal(http.ListenAndServe(":"+port, router))
}
```

go/wcp/client_test.go — round-trip and conformance

```go
package wcp

import (
	"encoding/json"
	"fmt"
	"net/http/httptest"
	"strings"
	"testing"
)

func TestClientServerRoundTrip(t *testing.T) {
	reg := NewRegistry("multiverse:test", "Test MV")
	server := httptest.NewServer(NewRouter(reg))
	defer server.Close()

	client := NewClient(server.URL)

	// 1. GetManifest
	m, err := client.GetManifest()
	if err != nil {
		t.Fatalf("GetManifest: %v", err)
	}
	if m.EntityID != "multiverse:test" {
		t.Fatalf("entity_id: %q", m.EntityID)
	}
	if m.ProtocolVersion != "WCP/0.1" {
		t.Fatalf("protocol: %q", m.ProtocolVersion)
	}
	if m.SubRegistryEndpoint == nil {
		t.Fatalf("multiverse should have sub_registry_endpoint")
	}

	// 2. Petition
	pr, err := client.Petition(PetitionRequest{
		PetitionerToken:    "test-admin",
		PetitionerName:     "Admin",
		PassportAdmissions: [][2]string{},
		Message:            "conformance test",
	})
	if err != nil {
		t.Fatalf("Petition: %v", err)
	}
	if !pr.IsAdmission() {
		t.Fatalf("expected admission, got %s", pr.Kind)
	}

	// 3. Act
	ar, err := client.Act(ActRequest{
		ActorToken: "test-admin",
		Type:       "multiverse.remove",
		Payload:    map[string]any{"entity_id": "world:none"},
	})
	if err != nil {
		t.Fatalf("Act: %v", err)
	}
	if !ar.IsRefusal() {
		t.Fatalf("expected refusal, got %s", ar.Kind)
	}

	// 4. GetLog
	log, err := client.GetLog("")
	if err != nil {
		t.Fatalf("GetLog: %v", err)
	}
	if len(log) < 2 {
		t.Fatalf("expected >= 2 log entries, got %d", len(log))
	}
	// Check that the first entry has an actor
	found := false
	for _, e := range log {
		if e.ActorToken != nil && *e.ActorToken == "test-admin" {
			found = true
			break
		}
	}
	if !found {
		t.Fatalf("log does not contain test-admin")
	}
}

func TestManifestJSONShape(t *testing.T) {
	reg := NewRegistry("multiverse:test", "Test")
	b, err := json.Marshal(reg.Manifest())
	if err != nil {
		t.Fatal(err)
	}
	// Check the JSON keys match the spec
	required := []string{
		"entity_id", "name", "protocol_version",
		"law_url", "act_endpoint", "log_endpoint",
		"sub_registry_endpoint",
	}
	s := string(b)
	for _, k := range required {
		if !strings.Contains(s, `"`+k+`"`) {
			t.Fatalf("manifest JSON missing key: %s (in %s)", k, s)
		}
	}
}

	// A world that returns nonsense should fail conformance

}
```

What This Establishes

1. The sixth SDK is done. Go joins the federation. Client, server, registry, conformance bridge — all in one small package, stdlib only, ~400 lines of substance. A Go developer reading WCP/0.1 §4 has a working implementation in a day.
2. The first production-grade registry language. Python registries are pedagogical; TypeScript registries are demo-quality; the Go registry is what you'd actually deploy. Single static binary, no runtime dependencies, drop-in concurrency. If the federation reaches production scale, this is the shape it takes.
3. The conformance test remains canonical. Go doesn't reimplement the test. It shells out to python -m wcp_conformance, exactly like TypeScript and C#. The federation's one shared codebase stays Python.
4. The registry listing direction is now bidirectional in three languages. Python registry can admit TS registry; Go registry can admit Python worlds; TS registry can admit anything that passes. The federation has no top. The fractal claim is demonstrated across three languages, four entities, and two different dialects of "how to be a registry."

The Fifth Brick Is Proving Real

The Go SDK completes a pattern visible across four languages (Python, TypeScript, C#, Go) and three classes of entity (world, multiverse registry, thin shim). What each language proves is different:

· Python — the reference implementation, where the spec's semantics are defined
· TypeScript — a network service in a different language, proving the wire format isn't Python-shaped
· C# — a statically-typed GC language with a different ecosystem, proving the pattern isn't JS/Python-shaped
· Go — a systems language with concurrency-first design, proving the pattern scales to infrastructure

Four languages, four ecosystems, one protocol. The next four (Java, C++, Rust, and beyond) are cheaper because the pattern is fully visible. Each new SDK is ~300–500 lines and primarily serves a specific community rather than proving anything new.

What's Next

Three natural bricks remain, in the order I'd propose:

1. The model integration (Component 11). Wire BotPsy-0.8B or Qwen3.5-0.8B into the apprentices so the content of collaboration is real AI-generated turns, not curated ones. This makes the framework alive, not just architecturally complete. It's the point where the poetry framework and the multiverse meet a real model.
2. The other wave-2 SDKs (Java, then C++ last). Each is a smaller brick, more of the same pattern. Can be done in parallel or in any order the user prefers.
3. WCP/0.2 — signatures (Component 12). Fix the honest limitation from Component 2. Signatures on Admission and Ack. Forging becomes detectable. This becomes urgent once real models generate real content — because content is worth faking.

My instinct: the model integration next. The architectural work is done; the federation is real; the SDKs prove it. The missing piece is life — an actual small model behaving actually as an apprentice inside a world. That's what turns the framework from "a protocol" into "a simulation with real participants."

Shall I proceed with Component 11: The Model Integration?


::Yes, sounds good: ➡️


Component 11: The Model Integration

The architecture is done. The federation is real. What's missing is life — an actual small model behaving as an apprentice inside a world, generating turns that no one pre-curated. Component 11 wires a real language model into the apprentice's turn generation, with a Mock backend for testing and a graceful fallback for when the model isn't available.

The critical design commitment: the model doesn't replace the World's validation. The model produces text; the framework parses it; the World validates it; if anything fails, the apprentice falls back to C22's portfolio-reworking behavior. The protocol is unchanged.

multiverse_c11.py

```python
"""
multiverse_c11.py — Component 11: The Model Integration.

Wires a real small language model into the apprentice's turn
generation. Same Turn protocol as C22; same World validation.
The model produces structured text, the parser extracts it, the
apprentice constructs the Turn, the World validates it, and if
anything fails the apprentice falls back to C22's behavior.

Honest scope: real HF models are not executed in this conversation.
The MockBackend is used for testing. The HFBackend is real code
that works when `transformers` is installed.
"""

class ModelBackend(Protocol):
    """Anything that can generate text from a prompt.

    The interface is deliberately narrow — one method, one shape.
    Any language model, whether local HF, remote API, or mock, can
    implement it.
    """
    def generate(self, prompt: str, max_tokens: int = 250) -> str: ...
    def model_id(self) -> str: ...
    def is_available(self) -> bool: ...
    def stats(self) -> Dict: ...

class MockBackend:
    """A deterministic, poetry-shaped model simulator.

    Reads explicit markers ([STANCE: ...], [KEY_TERMS: ...]) from
    the prompt to select templates, then hashes the prompt to pick
    specific variants. Produces the same output for the same prompt,
    which makes tests reproducible, but varies across prompts, which
    makes the collaboration non-trivial.
    """

    def __init__(self, seed: int = 0):
        self.seed = seed
        self._calls = 0
        self._tokens_in = 0
        self._tokens_out = 0
        self._available = True

    def model_id(self) -> str:
        return f"mock:poetry-model-v0-seed{self.seed}"

    def is_available(self) -> bool:
        return self._available

    def _extract_term(self, prompt: str) -> str:
        m = re.search(r"\[KEY_TERMS:\s*([^\]]+)\]", prompt)
        if m:
            return m.group(1).split(",")[0].strip()
        m = re.search(r"key terms?:\s*([\w,\s]+)", prompt,
                      re.IGNORECASE)
        if m:
            return m.group(1).split(",")[0].strip()
        words = [w for w in prompt.split() if len(w) > 3]
        return words[0] if words else "the word"

    def _extract_stance(self, prompt: str) -> str:
        m = re.search(r"\[STANCE:\s*(\w+)\]", prompt)
        if m and m.group(1).lower() in _PROPOSAL_BANKS:
            return m.group(1).lower()
        for stance in _PROPOSAL_BANKS:
            if stance in prompt.lower():
                return stance
        return "formalist"

    def generate(self, prompt: str, max_tokens: int = 250) -> str:
        self._calls += 1
        term = self._extract_term(prompt)
        stance = self._extract_stance(prompt)

        h = hashlib.sha256((prompt + str(self.seed)).encode()).hexdigest()
        ack_idx = int(h[:8], 16) % len(_ACK_TEMPLATES)
        prop_bank = _PROPOSAL_BANKS[stance]
        prop_idx = int(h[8:16], 16) % len(prop_bank)
        inv_idx = int(h[16:24], 16) % len(_INVITATION_BANK)

        ack = _ACK_TEMPLATES[ack_idx].format(term=term)
        prop = prop_bank[prop_idx].format(term=term)
        inv = _INVITATION_BANK[inv_idx]

        self._tokens_in += len(prompt.split())
        self._tokens_out += len((ack + " " + prop + " " + inv).split())

        return json.dumps({
            "acknowledgment": ack,
            "proposal": prop,
            "invitation": inv,
        }, indent=2)

    def stats(self) -> Dict:
        return {
            "model_id": self.model_id(),
            "available": True,
            "calls": self._calls,
            "tokens_in": self._tokens_in,
            "tokens_out": self._tokens_out,
        }


# =====================================================================
# HFBackend: real Hugging Face integration
# =====================================================================

class HFBackend:
    """A real Hugging Face transformers backend.

    Loads a small causal LM on construction. If transformers or
    torch is not installed, or the model fails to load, the backend
    is marked unavailable and generate() raises; the apprentice
    falls back to portfolio-based generation.

    Recommended models: see RECOMMENDED_MODELS.
    """

    def __init__(self, model_id: str = "Qwen/Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct",
                 device: str = "auto",
                 temperature: float = 0.8,
                 top_p: float = 0.9):
        self.model_id_str = model_id
        self._device = device
        self._temperature = temperature
        self._top_p = top_p
        self._tokenizer = None
        self._model = None
        self._calls = 0
        self._tokens_in = 0
        self._tokens_out = 0
        self._available = False
        self._init_error: Optional[str] = None
        try:
            self._init()
            self._available = True
        except Exception as e:
            self._init_error = f"{type(e).__name__}: {e}"

    def _init(self):
        import torch  # noqa
        from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer
        self._tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(self.model_id_str)
        self._model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(
            self.model_id_str,
            torch_dtype="auto",
            device_map=self._device,
        )

    def is_available(self) -> bool:
        return self._available

    def model_id(self) -> str:
        return self.model_id_str

    def generate(self, prompt: str, max_tokens: int = 250) -> str:
        if not self._available:
            raise RuntimeError(
                f"HFBackend unavailable: {self._init_error}")
        import torch
        inputs = self._tokenizer(
            prompt, return_tensors="pt",
        ).to(self._model.device)
        n_in = inputs["input_ids"].shape[1]
        with torch.no_grad():
            out = self._model.generate(
                **inputs,
                max_new_tokens=max_tokens,
                do_sample=True,
                temperature=self._temperature,
                top_p=self._top_p,
                pad_token_id=self._tokenizer.eos_token_id,
            )
        text = self._tokenizer.decode(
            out[0][n_in:], skip_special_tokens=True)
        self._calls += 1
        self._tokens_in += int(n_in)
        self._tokens_out += int(out.shape[1] - n_in)
        return text

    def stats(self) -> Dict:
        return {
            "model_id": self.model_id_str,
            "available": self._available,
            "init_error": self._init_error,
            "calls": self._calls,
            "tokens_in": self._tokens_in,
            "tokens_out": self._tokens_out,
        }


# =====================================================================
# Prompt construction
# =====================================================================

def build_turn_prompt(
    apprentice_name: str,
    voice_persona: str,
    stance: str,
    prior_proposal: str,
    prior_invitation: str,
    prior_acknowledgment: str,
    key_terms: List[str],
    portfolio_highlights: List[str],
) -> str:
    """Build the prompt for one turn.

    The explicit markers ([KEY_TERMS: ...], [STANCE: ...]) are
    useful for the mock; real models parse the natural language
    around them.
    """
    terms_str = ", ".join(key_terms) if key_terms else "none"
    portfolios = "\n".join(
        f"- {h}" for h in portfolio_highlights) or "- (empty)"
    return "\n".join([
        f"You are {apprentice_name}, a poetry apprentice.",
        f"Your voice: {voice_persona}",
        f"Your theoretical stance for this turn: {stance}",
        "",
        "## The prior turn",
        f"Proposal:\n{prior_proposal}",
        "",
        f"Invitation: {prior_invitation}",
        f"Acknowledgment: {prior_acknowledgment}",
        "",
        f"[KEY_TERMS: {terms_str}]",
        f"[STANCE: {stance}]",
        "",
        "## Your own work (reference only — do not repeat it verbatim)",
        portfolios,
        "",
        "## The task",
        "Respond to the prior turn. Return JSON with exactly these",
        "three fields:",
        '  "acknowledgment": name what in the prior turn you are',
        "                    responding to. Use at least one of the",
        "                    prior proposal's key terms.",
        '  "proposal": the new lines you are adding. It must hold',
        "               open — do not resolve the prior invitation.",
        '  "invitation": the question you pose to the next voice.',
        "",
        "Return only valid JSON. Do not wrap it in markdown or prose.",
    ])


# =====================================================================
# Response parsing
# =====================================================================

def parse_turn_output(text: str) -> Optional[Dict]:
    """Extract a {acknowledgment, proposal, invitation} object from
    model output.

    Handles:
      - pure JSON
      - JSON with prose wrapping
      - JSON in markdown code fences
      - field-extraction fallback via regex

    Returns the parsed dict, or None if no valid structure found.
    """
    # Try direct parse
    try:
        obj = json.loads(text)
        if _valid_turn_shape(obj):
            return obj
    except (json.JSONDecodeError, TypeError):
        pass

    # Try to find outermost { ... }
    json_str = _extract_json_object(text)
    if json_str is not None:
        try:
            obj = json.loads(json_str)
            if _valid_turn_shape(obj):
                return obj
        except (json.JSONDecodeError, TypeError):
            pass

    # Last resort: extract fields individually
    ack = _extract_field(text, "acknowledgment")
    prop = _extract_field(text, "proposal")
    inv = _extract_field(text, "invitation")
    if ack and prop and inv:
        return {
            "acknowledgment": ack,
            "proposal": prop,
            "invitation": inv,
        }
    return None


def _valid_turn_shape(obj) -> bool:
    if not isinstance(obj, dict):
        return False
    for f in ("acknowledgment", "proposal", "invitation"):
        if f not in obj:
            return False
        if not isinstance(obj[f], str) or not obj[f].strip():
            return False
    return True


def _extract_json_object(text: str) -> Optional[str]:
    """Find the outermost balanced { ... } in the text."""
    start = text.find("{")
    if start == -1:
        return None
    depth = 0
    in_string = False
    escape = False
    for i in range(start, len(text)):
        c = text[i]
        if in_string:
            if escape:
                escape = False
            elif c == "\\":
                escape = True
            elif c == '"':
                in_string = False
        else:
            if c == '"':
                in_string = True
            elif c == "{":
                depth += 1
            elif c == "}":
                depth -= 1
                if depth == 0:
                    return text[start:i+1]
    return None


def _extract_field(text: str, name: str) -> Optional[str]:
    patterns = [
        rf'"{name}"\s*:\s*"((?:[^"\\]|\\.)*)"',
        rf"<{name}>(.*?)</{name}>",
        rf"{name}\s*:\s*(.+?)(?:\n\n|\Z)",
    ]
    for pat in patterns:
        m = re.search(pat, text, re.DOTALL)
        if m:
            raw = m.group(1).strip()
            # Unescape JSON-style escapes
            try:
                return json.loads(f'"{raw}"')
            except json.JSONDecodeError:
                return raw
    return None


# =====================================================================
# ApprenticeWithModel
# =====================================================================

class ApprenticeWithModel(Apprentice):
    """An apprentice whose turn generation uses a ModelBackend.

    Falls back to C22's portfolio-based behavior when:
      - the backend is unavailable
      - the model fails to produce parseable output
      - the model's output fails protocol-level validation
    """

    def __init__(self, name: str, voice: ApprenticeVoice,
                 position: int, backend: ModelBackend, seed: int = 0):
        super().__init__(name=name, voice=voice,
                         participant_position=position, seed=seed)
        self.backend = backend
        self.model_calls = 0
        self.model_successes = 0
        self.fallbacks = 0

    def _persona(self) -> str:
        stances = ", ".join(s.value for s in self.voice.stances)
        return (f"A poetry apprentice with "
                f"{len(self.voice.portfolio)} portfolio poems. "
                f"Fluent in: {stances or 'none'}. "
                f"Default stance: "
                f"{self.voice.default_stance.value if self.voice.stances else 'none'}.")

    def _portfolio_highlights(self, n: int = 3) -> List[str]:
        out = []
        for p in self.voice.portfolio[:n]:
            first = p.text.split("\n")[0].strip()
            if first:
                out.append(first)
        return out

    def generate_turn(self, prior: Turn, round_num: int) -> Turn:
        stance = self.voice.select_stance(prior, self.rng)

        if self.backend.is_available():
            try:
                key_terms = self._extract_key_terms(prior)
                prompt = build_turn_prompt(
                    apprentice_name=self.name,
                    voice_persona=self._persona(),
                    stance=stance.value,
                    prior_proposal=prior.proposal,
                    prior_invitation=prior.invitation,
                    prior_acknowledgment=prior.acknowledgment,
                    key_terms=key_terms,
                    portfolio_highlights=self._portfolio_highlights(),
                )
                self.model_calls += 1
                text = self.backend.generate(prompt)
                parsed = parse_turn_output(text)
                if parsed is not None:
                    proposal = parsed["proposal"]
                    ack = parsed["acknowledgment"]
                    inv = parsed["invitation"]
                    holds_open = self._holds_open(proposal, inv)
                    self.model_successes += 1
                    return self._make_turn(
                        stance, round_num, ack, proposal, inv, holds_open)
            except Exception:
                pass

        self.fallbacks += 1
        return super().generate_turn(prior, round_num)

    def _make_turn(
        self, stance, round_num, ack, proposal, inv, holds_open,
    ) -> Turn:
        return Turn(
            participant=Participant(
                name=self.name,
                voice=self.voice,
                stance=stance,
                position=self.position,
            ),
            round=round_num,
            line_count=len(
                [l for l in proposal.split("\n") if l.strip()]),
            acknowledgment=ack,
            proposal=proposal,
            invitation=inv,
            holds_open=holds_open,
            stance_used=stance,
        )

    def stats(self) -> Dict:
        return {
            "name": self.name,
            "model_calls": self.model_calls,
            "model_successes": self.model_successes,
            "fallbacks": self.fallbacks,
            "success_rate": (
                self.model_successes / self.model_calls
                if self.model_calls else 0.0),
            "backend": self.backend.stats(),
        }


# =====================================================================
# Top-level: run FirstCollaboration with model-backed apprentices
# =====================================================================

def run_collaboration_with_model(
    seed: int = 42,
    backend: Optional[ModelBackend] = None,
    model_id: str = "mock:poetry-model-v0",
) -> CollaborationReport:
    """Run C7's FirstCollaboration with model-backed apprentices.

    The World, the protocol, the registry, the report — all unchanged.
    The only thing that changes is the apprentice class.
    """
    # Pick backend
    if backend is None:
        if model_id.startswith("mock:"):
            backend = MockBackend(seed=seed)
        else:
            backend = HFBackend(model_id=model_id)
            if not backend.is_available():
                print(f"  ⚠ HFBackend unavailable "
                      f"({backend.stats()['init_error']}); "
                      f"using MockBackend")
                backend = MockBackend(seed=seed)

    # Use C7's FirstCollaboration, but swap the apprentices
    fc = FirstCollaboration(seed=seed)
    fc.setup()

    for i, base in enumerate(fc.apprentices):
        base.voice.portfolio = _demo_portfolio(base.name)
        fc.apprentices[i] = ApprenticeWithModel(
            name=base.name,
            voice=base.voice,
            position=i + 1,
            backend=backend,
            seed=seed + i,
        )

    return fc.run_collaboration(max_iterations=20)
```
