Component 61: The Ledger-as-Commitment-Store Specification

This component is a document, not code. The arc is now mature enough that some decisions are about deployment rather than protocol. The ledger question — "how do we share information across worlds that don't trust each other?" — is the largest one, and it deserves a specification rather than an ad hoc implementation.

The spec is written in the same discipline as WCP/0.1 (the protocol spec): precise, honest about what it does and doesn't do, with the same "operational, not prescriptive" tone.

---

LCS/0.1 — The Ledger-as-Commitment-Store Specification

A deployment specification for sharing commitments to signed artifacts across a federation of worlds. This document is not part of the World Connection Protocol. It is a deployment option — how a federation may choose to operate its collective memory. Every artifact a conforming world produces is already verifiable without a ledger. The ledger is a convenience: canonical ordering and discovery. It is not required for correctness.

---

1. Purpose

A federation of worlds has a problem, and it is not the one blockchains usually solve. The problem is not shared state. Worlds are self-sovereign; they do not share state, and should not. The problem is collective memory: when a world needs to know "has anyone else seen this contract?" or "what happened first?" — there is no place to look.

LCS defines that place. It is not a store of artifacts; it is a store of commitments to artifacts. What it commits to is a hash. What it can answer is: "was this artifact seen by the federation, and when?" What it cannot answer is: "what does this artifact say?" — that requires the artifact itself.

This is the difference between a chain and a log. A chain is a state machine. A log is a memory of events. The federation needs a log.

2. The Problem the Ledger Solves

Three problems the substrate currently has no answer for:

Ordering. C57's bilateral revocation is timestamped by both parties. If one party revokes at T=10 and another cites at T=5, was the citation valid? In a pure offline world, the answer depends on who you ask — the timestamps are claims, and different worlds may have different clocks. A ledger gives a federation-wide order of when the network learned of each event. This is a different and weaker claim than when the event occurred, but it is one that can be checked by anyone.

Discovery. C59's announcement flows through C56's signed relay, but a relay chain does not reach every world. A world that hears no announcement has no way to learn of a contract it wasn't told about. A ledger is one place to look: query for artifacts by kind, by world, by contract_id, and learn what exists without needing a specific relay path.

First-seen time. When two worlds propose contracts with identical terms (C57's same-terms collision), the contract ID is the terms hash. Which one "came first" is unanswerable from artifacts alone. The ledger records first-seen: the earliest commit of a hash. This is a fact about the network, not about the artifact — and it's honest.

These three problems are real. None of them require a ledger to be trusted — they require a ledger to be available and ordered. That's a different design constraint.

3. What a Ledger Is Not

A ledger is not:

· A state store. It commits to hashes, not contents. It does not contain the artifacts.
· An authority. It does not verify artifacts. Verification happens offline, against the caller's trust anchors, using the same code paths C13 through C60 already provide.
· A trust root. Whoever controls the ledger's consensus can reorder its commits. The spec must name this and provide a way to reason about it. The federation's trust assumptions are not moved to the ledger; they are layered on top of it.
· A requirement. Worlds that operate without a ledger are conforming. They lose the three problems' solutions but keep everything else.

4. The Commitment Protocol

A ledger is an append-only sequence of commitment records. Any participant may append. The ledger, in turn, promises:

1. Immutability. A committed record never changes.
2. Total order. Every commit has a strict sequence number, and no two commits share a sequence number.
3. Availability. Given a commit sequence number, the record is retrievable.
4. Auditability. Any participant may read the full history.

Everything else — who may commit, what the commits mean, whether they're true — is out of scope. The ledger records claims, not truths.

5. The Commitment Record

The ledger's unit is the commitment record. Its shape:

```
{
  "kind": "commitment",
  "commit_index": <int, monotonically increasing from 0>,
  "artifact_hash": <64 hex chars>,
  "artifact_kind": <string — one of the arc's kinds>,
  "committer_world_id": <string>,
  "committer_public_key": <64 hex chars>,
  "timestamp_claimed": <ISO 8601>,
  "signature": <128 hex chars>,
  "previous_commit_hash": <64 hex chars or null for index 0>,
  "ledger_commit_hash": <64 hex chars>
}
```

Fields:

· commit_index — assigned by the ledger. Total order.
· artifact_hash — the hash of the committed artifact. This is the canonical hash of the artifact, defined per kind (see §10).
· artifact_kind — one of the arc's kinds (signed_admission, passport, dag_link, signed_manifest, person_binding, chain_link, attestation, attested_rumor, relay_chain, contract_offer, contract_acceptance, contract_announcement, contract_revocation, ...). Kinds are open; new kinds are defined by future components.
· committer_world_id — the world making the commitment. Self-sovereign.
· committer_public_key — the committer's public key, matching the artifact's world key (per C55's framing: the world is the holder of its key).
· timestamp_claimed — the committer's claim about when they committed. Unverified.
· signature — the committer's signature over (artifact_hash, artifact_kind, committer_world_id, committer_public_key, timestamp_claimed, previous_commit_hash). This is not the artifact's signature (which is inside the artifact); it is the committer's assertion that they committed.
· previous_commit_hash — the hash of the previous commitment record. This chains the ledger; recomputation from the head produces the ledger's history.
· ledger_commit_hash — the hash of this record.

The record is self-containing — it can be verified offline, given the artifact and the ledger's neighborhood of records around it.

6. The Query Model

The ledger exposes three queries:

A. get_commit(artifact_hash) → List[CommitmentRecord]
Returns all commitment records for a given artifact. There may be zero (artifact not committed), one (committed once), or many (committed by multiple worlds). The list is ordered by commit_index.

B. get_commits_by_kind(kind, since_index) → List[CommitmentRecord]
Returns all commitment records of a kind, from a given index. For discovery.

C. get_commit_chain(start_index, end_index) → List[CommitmentRecord]
Returns the commitment chain from start to end. For verification; each record's previous_commit_hash must chain correctly.

That's it. No queries by artifact content, no queries by policy, no queries by anything else. Those would require the ledger to understand artifacts, which it does not.

7. Verification with the Ledger

The ledger is additive to the arc's verification. It is never required. When a client wants to verify a claim, it does the existing verification, then optionally consults the ledger:

Without the ledger: verify the artifact against its declared trust anchors, per its kind's own rules (C13 for signatures, C24 for chains, C27 for DAGs, C56 for relay chains, etc.).

With the ledger:

1. Verify the artifact offline, as above. If the artifact is invalid, the ledger is irrelevant.
2. If valid, query the ledger for the artifact's commits. If none, note "the federation has no record of this artifact's existence."
3. If some, check that at least one commit record is signed by a key the caller trusts. (The caller decides whom to trust — the ledger does not aggregate trust.)
4. If desired, query for the artifact's first commit index and record it as "first-seen time."
5. If the artifact references another artifact (e.g., a revocation cites a contract), query for that artifact's first commit and compare indices. This gives a federation-wide order of events.

The ledger does not replace any check the arc already performs. It only adds ordering and discovery, both of which are optional.

8. What the Ledger Adds

Three things, and only three:

1. Order. A total order of commit indices, federation-wide. An event at index 100 occurred (was first-seen) before an event at index 101 — no matter what the artifacts' claimed timestamps say.
2. First-seen time. For any artifact, the earliest commit index and its associated timestamp_claimed. This is a fact about the network, not about the artifact. It answers the "which one came first?" question without pretending to know what "actually happened first" means.
3. Discovery. A place to ask "what artifacts of kind K have been committed since index N?" without contacting every world.

9. What the Ledger Does Not Add

· Enforcement. The ledger does not enforce anything. It records what was committed.
· State. The ledger does not know "current status" of anything. To learn if a contract is revoked, a client queries for commitments of kind contract_revocation with the contract's ID. Multiple revocation announcements may exist; the client decides which to trust.
· Truth. The ledger does not verify that a committed artifact is honest. It verifies that a committer signed a commitment to it. That's a weaker claim, and the caller is responsible for the trust chain (C13 through C60) that makes the artifact meaningful.
· Data availability. If the artifact itself is lost, the ledger's commitment proves it once existed. It does not prove what it said. The federation must maintain its own data-availability policy (federation relays, IPFS, archival nodes, etc.); the ledger is not one.
· Anonymity. A committer's world ID is public. There is no unlinkable commitment in LCS/0.1.
· Cost reduction. Public ledgers cost gas. Permissioned ledgers cost compute. Local logs cost nothing but provide no cross-world ordering. The cost-performance tradeoff is real and is not hidden.

10. Interaction with Existing Components

Every component in the arc produces artifacts with canonical hashes. Those hashes are the ledger's payload. The mapping is:

Component Artifact Canonical hash
C13 Signed admission / ack / leave canonical_bytes(artifact.payload)
C15 Passport entry entry.canonical_payload() hashed
C24 Signed report signed.canonical_payload() hashed
C25 Chain link link.link_hash()
C27 DAG link link.link_hash()
C28 Signed manifest manifest.canonical_payload() hashed
C36 Person binding binding.binding_hash()
C38 Person manifest manifest.canonical_payload() hashed
C40 Cross-world attestation att.canonical_payload() hashed
C48 Federation attestation att.content_hash
C54 Attested rumor attested.rumor_id (= attestation.content_hash)
C56 Signed relay chain chain.attestation.content_hash (per chain); relays and receipts individually by their own hashes
C57 Contract offer/acceptance/revocation offer.offer_hash(), acc.canonical_payload() hashed, rev.canonical_payload() hashed
C59/C60 Announcements announcement.announcement_hash()

Every one of these is defined by the artifact's own code. The ledger does not need to know what they mean — it just stores their hashes.

11. Failure Modes

If the ledger is unavailable. Every offline verification still works. The ledger's three additions (order, first-seen, discovery) are lost until it's back. This is the correct degradation.

If the ledger is forked. There are two histories. The spec says: pick one, note that the other exists, let social consensus determine which matters. This is not a solved problem in distributed systems; LCS does not try to solve it. A federation that cares about forks must run its own consensus — the ledger is a transport, not a consensus mechanism.

If a committer commits a lie. The commitment is signed by the committer. Its validity is: "this committer claimed, at this time, that they committed to this artifact." Whether the artifact is true is a separate question, answered by the artifact's own verification. A lying committer is an unreliable index, not an invalid one. Clients should trust a committer only if they trust the world the committer represents.

If the ledger reorders commits retroactively. A ledger that reorders its commits is dishonest. There is no cryptographic protection against this in LCS/0.1 — the trust in the ledger is trust in the ledger's operators. This is exactly what any blockchain's consensus layer is for; LCS punts to the deployment.

If the artifact's hash collides. The spec assumes hash collision resistance for SHA-256 (or whatever hash the deployment chooses). It does not defend against an adversary who can break the hash; no commitment scheme can.

If the ledger is spammed with garbage commitments. The ledger stores hashes and signatures; garbage commitments cost the same as valid ones. A permissioned ledger can filter by committer; a public ledger cannot. This is a real cost of the "anyone can commit" model; the spec acknowledges it and leaves the answer to the deployment.

12. Deployment Options

The spec is deployment-agnostic. Four options, in ascending order of cost and trust:

A. Local commitment log (per-world). A single world maintains a Merkle chain of its own commitments. Zero cross-world ordering. Useful for audit trails of what a world has done. Trivial to implement.

B. Federation-operated permissioned ledger. The federation runs a consensus protocol (Tendermint, Raft, etc.) over a shared log. Cross-world ordering via the federation's consensus. Cheap and fast, but requires federation coordination. Appropriate for a small number of participating worlds.

C. Merkle-checkpointed public log. Like Certificate Transparency. The ledger is a public append-only log; the federation periodically publishes a signed tree head that participants can verify against. Cross-world ordering via the log; integrity via the tree heads. Cheap; auditable by anyone; no consensus needed for the log itself, only for what a "valid" tree head is.

D. Public blockchain (Ethereum, etc.). Each commitment is a transaction; cross-world ordering via the chain's consensus. Highest trust (in the chain's consensus) and highest cost (gas). Appropriate only if the federation cares about public verifiability more than cost, or if commitments are infrequent enough that gas is acceptable.

The spec recommends C for most federations. It provides public auditability without the cost of a full blockchain, and it makes the trust assumption explicit (the tree-head signers, not the log itself). This is a design commitment that the deployment can override.

13. Honest Limits

· LCS/0.1 does not solve consensus. It assumes a ledger whose operators can be trusted to provide an ordered log. Choosing the ledger is choosing your trust assumptions.
· LCS/0.1 does not solve data availability. The artifact must be retrievable by whoever needs to verify it. The ledger's commitment is not the artifact.
· LCS/0.1 does not solve ordering of events. It solves ordering of commits. The order in which the federation learned of things is a weaker claim than the order in which they happened. The artifacts' own timestamps are the only source for "what happened first"; LCS provides "what was seen first."
· LCS/0.1 does not add privacy. Every commit is public and linkable to a world ID. Applications that need privacy must layer it themselves (e.g., by committing to a salted hash and revealing the salt selectively).
· LCS/0.1 does not modify WCP. A WCP world that doesn't commit to any ledger is a fully conforming member of the federation. Ledger participation is optional.
· LCS/0.1 does not add arbitration. If two worlds disagree about whether an event happened "before" or "after" a ledger commit, the ledger's ordering is one input, not a final answer. Arbitration — if a federation wants it — is the job of a C44-style council (see C58's dispute-resolution thread, not in the arc yet).

---

Appendix A: A Worked Example — C59/C60 Lifecycle Committed to a Ledger

Alice's world (world:poetry) and Bob's world (world:chemistry) establish a contract at artifact timestamp 2024-03-01T12:00:00+00:00, then revoke it at 2024-03-05T18:00:00+00:00.

Meanwhile, Carol's world (world:other) creates a citation of the contract in an act at 2024-03-05T17:00:00+00:00 — one hour before the revocation was announced, but the act's timestamp precedes it.

Without a ledger:

Alice sees the citation is revoked — the citation fails against current state.
Carol sees the citation was made before revocation — she argues it's valid.
Neither can settle.

With LCS:

1. Alice commits her establishment announcement at index 100.
2. Alice commits her revocation announcement at index 250.
3. Carol commits her citation act at index 240.

The ledger's total order says:

· 100 < 240 < 250: the establishment, then the citation, then the revocation.

Now a client with the artifacts can answer:

"The citation was committed at index 240, which is after the establishment (100) and before the revocation (250). Depending on which policy applies — current status as of commit or current status as of timestamp — the citation is either valid or void."

The ledger gives the order; the policy is the world's choice. This is the correct division of labor. A world that says "citations are valid if the contract was in force at the citation's committed time" reaches a different conclusion than one that says "at the citation's claimed time." Both are defensible; the ledger's contribution is that the facts (indices 100, 240, 250) are recorded and checkable, so the disagreement is about policy, not about facts.

That's the answer to the user's blockchain question. The ledger doesn't resolve disputes; it makes the facts of dispute common knowledge. The policy remains local.

---

What This Establishes

Component 61 adds no code. It establishes a contract between the arc and its deployments: "Here is what the substrate will and won't promise about shared memory. Here is how you can add ordering and discovery without adding shared state. Here is what remains — and must remain — local."

The user's blockchain question is now answered at the right level: a commitment store is compatible with everything the arc has built; a state store is not. The substrate supports the first without modification. The second would require C1–C60 to be redesigned. The spec makes the choice explicit, so future work doesn't accidentally choose the wrong one.

What Was Run

Nothing. This is a specification document, not a code component. There is no multiverse_c61.py, no tests, and no makefile target. The document itself is the artifact.

The honest status: the spec is complete and internally consistent; it composes over C1–C60 without modification; it defers consensus and data availability to deployment; and it names its own limits. It has not been validated against a live ledger because no deployment exists yet.

The arc is now complete in a specific sense: it can answer what the substrate is, how artifacts are verified, what architectures it supports, how worlds communicate, and how the federation's memory is shared. What's Next

Three directions remain, each now clearly in the deployment or application domain rather than the protocol domain:

1. Component 62: A reference LCS implementation. A small, testable implementation of the commitment store, using the Merkle-checkpointed public log option (§12.C). Two append-only logs, one Merkle tree, one signed tree head. This would take the spec from "here's how it should work" to "here's a working instance," without changing any of the arc's primitives.
2. Component 62: The demonstration runner, updated for the diplomatic layer. C51's survey shows seven architectures and four extensions. The diplomatic layer (C55–C60) has its own demos, each with its own output. A make diplomatic-survey or an extended make all-layers would make the whole arc visible in one command. Packaging, not substance.
3. Component 62: Policy-driven disputes. The Appendix A example shows a real question — "is a citation valid by current status or by claimed time?" — with two defensible answers. A ContractPolicyText (C50-style signed policy) could let a world declare its answer, so a citation's validity is determined by the world's published policy, not by the reader's assumption. This is the natural consumer of C58, C59, C60 and C61 together.

My instinct: the reference LCS implementation. It's the piece that takes the spec from "a good design" to "a real thing." It's small, self-contained, and it doesn't touch any existing component. It's the same move the arc made at C8 (reference conformance CLI), C49 (reference persistence), and C56 (reference relay): a working instance that makes the abstract claim concrete.

Shall I proceed with Component 62: The Reference LCS Implementation?


::➡️


Component 62: The Reference LCS Implementation

C61 was the specification. C62 is the working artifact — a Merkle-log commitment store with offline inclusion proofs and signed tree heads. It doesn't resolve consensus, doesn't store artifacts, doesn't enforce anything. It does exactly three things C61 promised: total order, first-seen time, discovery — and nothing else.

The one design commitment that keeps this honest: the ledger's verification is separate from the federation's verification. A commitment record verifies against its committer's key (one C13 check). A tree head verifies against the federation's checkpoint key (one C13 check). Whether the artifact the commitment refers to is meaningful is a completely different question, answered by C13–C60, and the ledger doesn't participate. Two independent verifications; two independent trust anchors.

The one infrastructure extension worth naming: a Merkle-tree inclusion proof. Nothing like it has been in the arc before. It's a small amount of code (about 60 lines) and it's what makes "the commit is in the log" a checkable property without trusting the log operator.

multiverse_c62.py

```python
"""
multiverse_c62.py — Component 62: The Reference LCS Implementation.

A working instance of C61's ledger-as-commitment-store spec.

What it provides:
  - CommitmentRecord: one signed append to the log.
  - CommitmentLog: append + three queries (get_commit,
    get_commits_by_kind, get_commit_chain).
  - Merkle tree helpers: leaf_hash, internal_hash, merkle_root,
    inclusion_proof, verify_inclusion.
  - SignedTreeHead: a federation-signed checkpoint over a
    specific tree size.
  - CheckpointPublisher: signs the current root.
  - verify_commitment: single-record offline check.
  - verify_commitment_chain: whole-log chain check
    (previous_commit_hash linkage).
  - verify_tree_head: check a checkpoint against a federation
    public key.
  - verify_inclusion: check that a commit is in a checkpoint.

What it deliberately does NOT provide:
  - Consensus (C61 §11, §13).
  - Persistence to disk (serialization is trivial; kept out).
  - Network transport (in-process).
  - Consistency proofs (C61 §13 — real CT property, not in
    scope for the reference; inclusion proofs are).
  - Artifact verification (that's C13–C60's job).
  - Data availability (the caller must retain artifacts).

Composition:
  - Uses C13's Ed25519 for commitment signatures and
    tree-head signatures.
  - Commitments reference artifact hashes computed by the
    artifact's own canonical_payload() / *_hash() methods.
  - A tree head is a signed blob that a caller can pin or
    publish; commits are included via Merkle proofs against
    the head's root.

House rules honored:
  - "Every behaviour has a test that fails if the behaviour
    breaks" — one per: append/order, query by hash, query by
    kind, chain integrity, empty root, one-leaf root, odd-leaf
    root, inclusion proof verify, tampered proof rejected,
    tree head sign/verify, full flow.
  - "A world never raises on what a visitor sends" — verifiers
    return verdicts; append raises only on caller error.
  - "History, not rank" — the log is append-only; commits are
    factual.

Honest limits (documented, tested):
  - No consistency proofs. A log operator who rewinds and
    re-signs a *different* tree with the same size would need
    an out-of-band check to detect. Inclusion proofs alone
    prove a commit is in *a* tree, not that the tree is
    consistent with earlier ones.
  - No fork detection. Two operators could sign two different
    trees of the same size. The federation's checkpoint
    policy (C61 §12.C) is what prevents this; the reference
    implementation just produces the signed head.
  - No data availability. The commitment record is not the
    artifact; a caller that lost the artifact can still prove
    it *was* committed, but cannot re-verify its content.
  - commit_index is a client-visible number. In a real
    distributed log, indices would be agreed by the log's
    consensus. Here they are `len(entries)` because the log
    is single-writer.
  - No time verification. `timestamp_claimed` is a claim
    covered by the committer's signature but not checked
    against any clock.
"""

import hashlib
from dataclasses import dataclass
from datetime import datetime, timezone
from typing import Any, Dict, List, Optional, Tuple

from multiverse_c13 import (
    HAS_CRYPTO, KeyPair, canonical_bytes, verify_signature,
)


def _now() -> str:
    return datetime.now(timezone.utc).isoformat()


def _hash_payload(p: bytes) -> str:
    return hashlib.sha256(p).hexdigest()


# =====================================================================
# CommitmentRecord
# =====================================================================

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class CommitmentRecord:
    """One append to the log. Signed by the committer.

    The signature covers (artifact_hash, artifact_kind,
    committer_world_id, committer_public_key,
    timestamp_claimed, previous_commit_hash). Not commit_index
    — the log assigns that.
    """
    commit_index: int
    artifact_hash: str
    artifact_kind: str
    committer_world_id: str
    committer_public_key: str
    timestamp_claimed: str
    signature: str
    previous_commit_hash: Optional[str]

    def __post_init__(self):
        if self.commit_index < 0:
            raise ValueError("commit_index must be >= 0")
        for f in ("artifact_hash", "artifact_kind",
                  "committer_world_id", "committer_public_key",
                  "timestamp_claimed", "signature"):
            v = getattr(self, f)
            if not isinstance(v, str) or not v:
                raise ValueError(f"{f} required")
        if len(self.artifact_hash) != 64:
            raise ValueError(
                "artifact_hash must be 64 hex chars")
        if len(self.committer_public_key) != 64:
            raise ValueError(
                "committer_public_key must be 64 hex chars")
        if self.previous_commit_hash is not None:
            if len(self.previous_commit_hash) != 64:
                raise ValueError(
                    "previous_commit_hash must be 64 hex chars "
                    "or None")

    def commitment_payload(self) -> bytes:
        """The bytes the committer signs. Not commit_index."""
        return canonical_bytes({
            "kind": "commitment_signature",
            "artifact_hash": self.artifact_hash,
            "artifact_kind": self.artifact_kind,
            "committer_world_id": self.committer_world_id,
            "committer_public_key": self.committer_public_key,
            "timestamp_claimed": self.timestamp_claimed,
            "previous_commit_hash": self.previous_commit_hash,
        })

    def ledger_commit_hash(self) -> str:
        """The hash of the whole record (includes commit_index)."""
        return _hash_payload(canonical_bytes({
            "kind": "commitment",
            "commit_index": self.commit_index,
            "artifact_hash": self.artifact_hash,
            "artifact_kind": self.artifact_kind,
            "committer_world_id": self.committer_world_id,
            "committer_public_key": self.committer_public_key,
            "timestamp_claimed": self.timestamp_claimed,
            "signature": self.signature,
            "previous_commit_hash": self.previous_commit_hash,
        }))

    def to_dict(self) -> Dict:
        return {
            "commit_index": self.commit_index,
            "artifact_hash": self.artifact_hash,
            "artifact_kind": self.artifact_kind,
            "committer_world_id": self.committer_world_id,
            "committer_public_key": self.committer_public_key,
            "timestamp_claimed": self.timestamp_claimed,
            "signature": self.signature,
            "previous_commit_hash": self.previous_commit_hash,
        }

    @classmethod
    def from_dict(cls, d: Dict) -> "CommitmentRecord":
        return cls(
            commit_index=d["commit_index"],
            artifact_hash=d["artifact_hash"],
            artifact_kind=d["artifact_kind"],
            committer_world_id=d["committer_world_id"],
            committer_public_key=d["committer_public_key"],
            timestamp_claimed=d["timestamp_claimed"],
            signature=d["signature"],
            previous_commit_hash=d.get("previous_commit_hash"),
        )


def verify_commitment(record: CommitmentRecord) -> bool:
    """Verify one commitment's signature. Never raises."""
    if not HAS_CRYPTO:
        return False
    try:
        if not isinstance(record, CommitmentRecord):
            return False
        return verify_signature(
            record.committer_public_key,
            record.commitment_payload(),
            record.signature)
    except Exception:
        return False


# =====================================================================
# Merkle helpers
# =====================================================================

def _leaf_hash(commit_hash: str) -> str:
    """Leaf domain separator: 0x00 prefix prevents second-preimage
    attacks where a leaf is confused with an internal node."""
    return _hash_payload(
        b"\x00" + bytes.fromhex(commit_hash))


def _internal_hash(left: str, right: str) -> str:
    """Internal domain separator: 0x01 prefix."""
    return _hash_payload(
        b"\x01" + bytes.fromhex(left) + bytes.fromhex(right))


def _level_sizes(n: int) -> List[int]:
    """The size of each Merkle level. Sizes shrink by half, rounded
    up, until 1. E.g., n=3 → [3, 2, 1]; n=5 → [5, 3, 2, 1]."""
    if n <= 0:
        return []
    sizes = [n]
    while sizes[-1] > 1:
        sizes.append((sizes[-1] + 1) // 2)
    return sizes


def merkle_root(leaves: List[str]) -> str:
    """Compute the Merkle root of a list of commit hashes.

    Odd-sized levels promote their last node up without hashing
    it (CT-style, not Bitcoin-style). Empty input → empty string.
    """
    if not leaves:
        return ""
    level = [_leaf_hash(l) for l in leaves]
    while len(level) > 1:
        next_level: List[str] = []
        for i in range(0, len(level), 2):
            if i + 1 < len(level):
                next_level.append(
                    _internal_hash(level[i], level[i + 1]))
            else:
                next_level.append(level[i])  # promote
        level = next_level
    return level[0]


def inclusion_proof(leaves: List[str], index: int) -> List[str]:
    """The sibling hashes needed to prove leaves[index] is in the
    tree with the given leaves.

    The proof has no fixed length — promoted nodes contribute
    no sibling at their level. The verifier derives the same
    shape from `len(leaves)`.
    """
    n = len(leaves)
    if n == 0:
        raise ValueError("empty tree has no inclusion proofs")
    if index < 0 or index >= n:
        raise IndexError(
            f"index {index} out of range for tree of size {n}")
    proof: List[str] = []
    level = [_leaf_hash(l) for l in leaves]
    i = index
    while len(level) > 1:
        # Sibling exists unless this is the last node on an
        # odd-sized level (promoted).
        is_last = (i == len(level) - 1)
        is_odd_level = (len(level) % 2 == 1)
        if not (is_last and is_odd_level):
            if i % 2 == 0:
                proof.append(level[i + 1])
            else:
                proof.append(level[i - 1])
        # Move up
        next_level: List[str] = []
        for j in range(0, len(level), 2):
            if j + 1 < len(level):
                next_level.append(
                    _internal_hash(level[j], level[j + 1]))
            else:
                next_level.append(level[j])
        level = next_level
        i //= 2
    return proof


def verify_inclusion(
    leaf: str, proof: List[str], index: int, n: int,
    expected_root: str,
) -> bool:
    """Verify that `leaf` at position `index` (of a tree with
    `n` leaves) hashes up to `expected_root` using `proof`.

    The verifier computes the tree shape from `n`, so it knows
    whether each level has a sibling for this node or is a
    promoted last node. Never raises.
    """
    try:
        if not HAS_CRYPTO:
            return False
        if n <= 0 or index < 0 or index >= n:
            return False
        if not isinstance(leaf, str) or len(leaf) != 64:
            return False
        sizes = _level_sizes(n)
        h = _leaf_hash(leaf)
        i = index
        proof_iter = iter(proof)
        for level_idx in range(len(sizes) - 1):
            size_at_level = sizes[level_idx]
            is_last = (i == size_at_level - 1)
            is_odd_level = (size_at_level % 2 == 1)
            is_promoted = is_last and is_odd_level
            if not is_promoted:
                sibling = next(proof_iter, None)
                if sibling is None:
                    return False
                if i % 2 == 0:
                    h = _internal_hash(h, sibling)
                else:
                    h = _internal_hash(sibling, h)
            i //= 2
        # No extra hashes allowed in the proof
        if next(proof_iter, None) is not None:
            return False
        return h == expected_root
    except Exception:
        return False


# =====================================================================
# CommitmentLog
# =====================================================================

class CommitmentLog:
    """The append-only log.

    The reference implementation is single-writer. A production
    ledger with multiple writers needs consensus (C61 §12); the
    log's interface here is what the consensus would produce.
    """

    def __init__(self):
        self._entries: List[CommitmentRecord] = []

    def size(self) -> int:
        return len(self._entries)

    def entries(self) -> List[CommitmentRecord]:
        return list(self._entries)

    def append(
        self,
        artifact_hash: str,
        artifact_kind: str,
        committer_world_id: str,
        committer_kp: KeyPair,
        timestamp_claimed: Optional[str] = None,
    ) -> CommitmentRecord:
        """Append a commitment. Signs it with the committer's key.

        The caller supplies `artifact_hash` — computed from the
        actual artifact using the artifact's own canonical hash
        method. The log does not (and cannot) compute it, since
        it does not know the artifact's kind's hash semantics.
        """
        if not HAS_CRYPTO:
            raise RuntimeError(
                "CommitmentLog.append requires cryptography")
        if not isinstance(artifact_hash, str) \
                or len(artifact_hash) != 64:
            raise ValueError(
                "artifact_hash must be 64 hex chars")
        if not isinstance(artifact_kind, str) or not artifact_kind:
            raise ValueError("artifact_kind required")
        if not isinstance(committer_world_id, str) \
                or not committer_world_id:
            raise ValueError("committer_world_id required")
        if timestamp_claimed is None:
            timestamp_claimed = _now()
        commit_index = len(self._entries)
        previous_hash = (
            self._entries[-1].ledger_commit_hash()
            if self._entries else None)
        public_key = committer_kp.public_key_hex()
        payload = canonical_bytes({
            "kind": "commitment_signature",
            "artifact_hash": artifact_hash,
            "artifact_kind": artifact_kind,
            "committer_world_id": committer_world_id,
            "committer_public_key": public_key,
            "timestamp_claimed": timestamp_claimed,
            "previous_commit_hash": previous_hash,
        })
        record = CommitmentRecord(
            commit_index=commit_index,
            artifact_hash=artifact_hash,
            artifact_kind=artifact_kind,
            committer_world_id=committer_world_id,
            committer_public_key=public_key,
            timestamp_claimed=timestamp_claimed,
            signature=committer_kp.sign(payload).hex(),
            previous_commit_hash=previous_hash,
        )
        self._entries.append(record)
        return record

    # -- Queries -------------------------------------------------

    def get_commit(
        self, artifact_hash: str,
    ) -> List[CommitmentRecord]:
        """All commitments of a given artifact hash, by index."""
        return [e for e in self._entries
                if e.artifact_hash == artifact_hash]

    def get_commits_by_kind(
        self, artifact_kind: str, since_index: int = 0,
    ) -> List[CommitmentRecord]:
        return [e for e in self._entries
                if e.artifact_kind == artifact_kind
                and e.commit_index >= since_index]

    def get_commit_chain(
        self, start_index: int, end_index: int,
    ) -> List[CommitmentRecord]:
        """Entries in [start, end). Indices are clamped to bounds."""
        start = max(0, start_index)
        end = min(len(self._entries), end_index)
        if start >= end:
            return []
        return list(self._entries[start:end])

    def first_commit_index(
        self, artifact_hash: str,
    ) -> Optional[int]:
        """The earliest commit index for an artifact, or None."""
        for e in self._entries:
            if e.artifact_hash == artifact_hash:
                return e.commit_index
        return None

    # -- Merkle / checkpoint -------------------------------------

    def all_leaf_hashes(self) -> List[str]:
        return [e.ledger_commit_hash() for e in self._entries]

    def merkle_root(self) -> str:
        return merkle_root(self.all_leaf_hashes())

    def inclusion_proof_for(
        self, commit_index: int,
    ) -> List[str]:
        return inclusion_proof(
            self.all_leaf_hashes(), commit_index)


# =====================================================================
# Chain verification
# =====================================================================

@dataclass
class ChainVerdict:
    valid: bool
    reason: str
    bad_index: Optional[int] = None

    def to_dict(self) -> Dict:
        return {
            "valid": self.valid,
            "reason": self.reason,
            "bad_index": self.bad_index,
        }


def verify_commitment_chain(
    entries: List[CommitmentRecord],
) -> ChainVerdict:
    """Verify a whole log's chain of commitments. Never raises.

    Checks, in order:
      1. Each record's commit_index equals its position.
      2. Record 0's previous_commit_hash is None.
      3. Record i>0's previous_commit_hash equals
         record i-1's ledger_commit_hash.
      4. Each record's signature verifies.
    """
    if not HAS_CRYPTO:
        return ChainVerdict(
            valid=False, reason="cryptography not installed")
    if not isinstance(entries, list):
        return ChainVerdict(
            valid=False, reason="entries must be a list")
    for i, e in enumerate(entries):
        if not isinstance(e, CommitmentRecord):
            return ChainVerdict(
                valid=False,
                reason=f"entry {i} is not a CommitmentRecord",
                bad_index=i)
        if e.commit_index != i:
            return ChainVerdict(
                valid=False,
                reason=(f"entry {i} has commit_index "
                         f"{e.commit_index}"),
                bad_index=i)
        if i == 0:
            if e.previous_commit_hash is not None:
                return ChainVerdict(
                    valid=False,
                    reason="first entry has "
                            "previous_commit_hash",
                    bad_index=0)
        else:
            prev = entries[i - 1]
            if e.previous_commit_hash != \
                    prev.ledger_commit_hash():
                return ChainVerdict(
                    valid=False,
                    reason=(f"entry {i} previous_commit_hash "
                             f"does not match entry {i-1}"),
                    bad_index=i)
        if not verify_commitment(e):
            return ChainVerdict(
                valid=False,
                reason=f"entry {i} signature INVALID",
                bad_index=i)
    return ChainVerdict(
        valid=True, reason="chain verifies")


# =====================================================================
# SignedTreeHead
# =====================================================================

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class SignedTreeHead:
    """A federation-signed checkpoint over a specific tree size."""
    tree_size: int
    root_hash: str
    timestamp: str
    federation_public_key: str
    signature: str

    def __post_init__(self):
        if self.tree_size < 0:
            raise ValueError("tree_size must be >= 0")
        if self.tree_size == 0 and self.root_hash != "":
            raise ValueError(
                "empty tree must have empty root")
        if self.tree_size > 0 and len(self.root_hash) != 64:
            raise ValueError(
                "root_hash must be 64 hex chars")
        for f in ("timestamp", "federation_public_key",
                  "signature"):
            v = getattr(self, f)
            if not isinstance(v, str) or not v:
                raise ValueError(f"{f} required")
        if len(self.federation_public_key) != 64:
            raise ValueError(
                "federation_public_key must be 64 hex chars")

    def canonical_payload(self) -> bytes:
        return canonical_bytes({
            "kind": "signed_tree_head",
            "tree_size": self.tree_size,
            "root_hash": self.root_hash,
            "timestamp": self.timestamp,
            "federation_public_key": self.federation_public_key,
        })

    def to_dict(self) -> Dict:
        return {
            "tree_size": self.tree_size,
            "root_hash": self.root_hash,
            "timestamp": self.timestamp,
            "federation_public_key": self.federation_public_key,
            "signature": self.signature,
        }

    @classmethod
    def from_dict(cls, d: Dict) -> "SignedTreeHead":
        return cls(
            tree_size=d["tree_size"],
            root_hash=d["root_hash"],
            timestamp=d["timestamp"],
            federation_public_key=d["federation_public_key"],
            signature=d["signature"],
        )


def verify_tree_head(
    head: SignedTreeHead,
    expected_public_key: Optional[str] = None,
) -> bool:
    """True iff the tree head's signature verifies. Never raises."""
    if not HAS_CRYPTO:
        return False
    try:
        if not isinstance(head, SignedTreeHead):
            return False
        key = (expected_public_key
                or head.federation_public_key)
        return verify_signature(
            key, head.canonical_payload(), head.signature)
    except Exception:
        return False


# =====================================================================
# CheckpointPublisher
# =====================================================================

class CheckpointPublisher:
    """Sign the current state of a log as a tree head.

    Each call produces a new SignedTreeHead for the log's current
    size. Old heads stay valid; new heads cover a superset of
    commits. (Consistency proofs between heads are future work —
    see the module docstring.)
    """

    def __init__(
        self, log: CommitmentLog, federation_kp: KeyPair,
    ):
        if not HAS_CRYPTO:
            raise RuntimeError(
                "CheckpointPublisher requires cryptography")
        self._log = log
        self._kp = federation_kp

    def publish(self) -> SignedTreeHead:
        timestamp = _now()
        size = self._log.size()
        root = self._log.merkle_root()
        public_key = self._kp.public_key_hex()
        payload = canonical_bytes({
            "kind": "signed_tree_head",
            "tree_size": size,
            "root_hash": root,
            "timestamp": timestamp,
            "federation_public_key": public_key,
        })
        return SignedTreeHead(
            tree_size=size,
            root_hash=root,
            timestamp=timestamp,
            federation_public_key=public_key,
            signature=self._kp.sign(payload).hex(),
        )


# =====================================================================
# Artifact hash helpers (convenience, not core)
# =====================================================================

def artifact_hash(artifact: Any) -> str:
    """Compute a canonical hash for an arc artifact.

    Dispatches on the artifact's own shape: if it has
    `.canonical_payload()`, hash that; elif it has
    `.ledger_commit_hash()`, use that; elif it has
    `.content_hash`, use that; elif it has `.offer_hash()`, use
    that; else raise. This lets a caller compute a stable hash
    for any of the arc's artifacts with one function, while
    keeping the *ledger* ignorant of artifact kinds.
    """
    if hasattr(artifact, "offer_hash") \
            and callable(artifact.offer_hash):
        return artifact.offer_hash()
    if hasattr(artifact, "ledger_commit_hash") \
            and callable(artifact.ledger_commit_hash):
        return artifact.ledger_commit_hash()
    if hasattr(artifact, "announcement_hash") \
            and callable(artifact.announcement_hash):
        return artifact.announcement_hash()
    if hasattr(artifact, "binding_hash") \
            and callable(artifact.binding_hash):
        return artifact.binding_hash()
    if hasattr(artifact, "link_hash") \
            and callable(artifact.link_hash):
        return artifact.link_hash()
    if hasattr(artifact, "content_hash"):
        v = artifact.content_hash
        if isinstance(v, str) and len(v) == 64:
            return v
    if hasattr(artifact, "canonical_payload") \
            and callable(artifact.canonical_payload):
        return _hash_payload(artifact.canonical_payload())
    raise TypeError(
        f"cannot compute canonical hash for "
        f"{type(artifact).__name__}")
```

Demo — the Appendix A scenario from C61, made real

```python
def demo(artifact_dir: Optional[str] = None) -> Dict:
    """Appendix A of C61, as a working example.

    Alice's world and Bob's world establish a contract (commit
    at some index). Carol's world cites the contract (commit
    at a later index). Alice and Bob revoke the contract (commit
    at a still later index). The ledger gives the *order of
    commits*, which is what a reader needs.

    Two versions of the same three events:

      Case A — commit order matches claimed order.
      Case B — commit order differs from claimed order.

    Case B is the point of the ledger: the two orders are
    different facts, and the ledger makes the *commit order*
    checkable without claiming the *claimed order* is wrong.

    Anchor: Dickinson, 'Forever – is composed of Nows –'
    (the ledger orders the Nows).
    """
    import json
    from pathlib import Path
    from multiverse_c1 import create_identity
    from multiverse_c13 import KeyPair

    if not HAS_CRYPTO:
        raise RuntimeError("demo requires `cryptography`")

    if artifact_dir is None:
        artifact_dir = "artifacts"
    path = Path(artifact_dir)
    path.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)

    # Fake but representative hashes for the three artifacts
    # (in a real run, these would come from C57/C59/C60 artifacts)
    establishment_hash = _hash_payload(b"establishment")
    citation_hash = _hash_payload(b"citation")
    revocation_hash = _hash_payload(b"revocation")

    # -- Case A: commit order matches claimed order ------------
    log_a = CommitmentLog()
    alice_kp = KeyPair.generate()
    bob_kp = KeyPair.generate()
    carol_kp = KeyPair.generate()

    # Commit 0: establishment
    log_a.append(
        establishment_hash,
        "contract_announcement",
        "world:poetry",
        alice_kp,
        timestamp_claimed="2024-03-01T12:00:00+00:00",
    )
    # Commit 1: citation
    log_a.append(
        citation_hash,
        "citation_act",
        "world:other",
        carol_kp,
        timestamp_claimed="2024-03-05T17:00:00+00:00",
    )
    # Commit 2: revocation
    log_a.append(
        revocation_hash,
        "contract_revocation",
        "world:poetry",
        alice_kp,
        timestamp_claimed="2024-03-05T18:00:00+00:00",
    )

    # Publish a checkpoint
    federation_kp = KeyPair.generate()
    publisher_a = CheckpointPublisher(log_a, federation_kp)
    head_a = publisher_a.publish()

    # Generate and verify inclusion proofs for all three
    proofs_a = []
    for i in range(3):
        proof = log_a.inclusion_proof_for(i)
        leaf = log_a.all_leaf_hashes()[i]
        ok = verify_inclusion(
            leaf, proof, i, log_a.size(), head_a.root_hash)
        proofs_a.append({
            "index": i,
            "kind": log_a.entries()[i].artifact_kind,
            "claimed": log_a.entries()[i].timestamp_claimed,
            "proof_length": len(proof),
            "verified": ok,
        })

    # -- Case B: same events, different commit order ----------
    log_b = CommitmentLog()
    # Commit 0: establishment
    log_b.append(
        establishment_hash,
        "contract_announcement",
        "world:poetry",
        alice_kp,
        timestamp_claimed="2024-03-01T12:00:00+00:00",
    )
    # Commit 1: revocation (claimed LATER but committed FIRST)
    log_b.append(
        revocation_hash,
        "contract_revocation",
        "world:poetry",
        alice_kp,
        timestamp_claimed="2024-03-05T18:00:00+00:00",
    )
    # Commit 2: citation (claimed EARLIER but committed LATER)
    log_b.append(
        citation_hash,
        "citation_act",
        "world:other",
        carol_kp,
        timestamp_claimed="2024-03-05T17:00:00+00:00",
    )
    publisher_b = CheckpointPublisher(log_b, federation_kp)
    head_b = publisher_b.publish()
    proofs_b = []
    for i in range(3):
        proof = log_b.inclusion_proof_for(i)
        leaf = log_b.all_leaf_hashes()[i]
        ok = verify_inclusion(
            leaf, proof, i, log_b.size(), head_b.root_hash)
        proofs_b.append({
            "index": i,
            "kind": log_b.entries()[i].artifact_kind,
            "claimed": log_b.entries()[i].timestamp_claimed,
            "proof_length": len(proof),
            "verified": ok,
        })

    # Verify both chains and both heads
    chain_a = verify_commitment_chain(log_a.entries())
    chain_b = verify_commitment_chain(log_b.entries())
    head_a_ok = verify_tree_head(
        head_a, federation_kp.public_key_hex())
    head_b_ok = verify_tree_head(
        head_b, federation_kp.public_key_hex())

    # First-seen queries
    first_seen = {
        "establishment": log_a.first_commit_index(
            establishment_hash),
        "citation": log_a.first_commit_index(citation_hash),
        "revocation": log_a.first_commit_index(revocation_hash),
    }
    first_seen_b = {
        "establishment": log_b.first_commit_index(
            establishment_hash),
        "citation": log_b.first_commit_index(citation_hash),
        "revocation": log_b.first_commit_index(revocation_hash),
    }

    # -- Print -----------------------------------------------
    print("=" * 70)
    print("LCS Reference Implementation — order is what the ledger adds")
    print("=" * 70)
    print()
    print(f"  Case A: commit order matches claimed order")
    print(f"    chain valid:  {chain_a.valid}")
    print(f"    head signed:  {head_a_ok}")
    print(f"    entries:")
    for p in proofs_a:
        print(f"      [{p['index']}] {p['kind']:25s} "
              f"claimed={p['claimed'][:19]} "
              f"proof_ok={p['verified']}")
    print(f"    first-seen: {first_seen}")
    print()
    print(f"  Case B: commit order differs from claimed order")
    print(f"    chain valid:  {chain_b.valid}")
    print(f"    head signed:  {head_b_ok}")
    print(f"    entries:")
    for p in proofs_b:
        print(f"      [{p['index']}] {p['kind']:25s} "
              f"claimed={p['claimed'][:19]} "
              f"proof_ok={p['verified']}")
    print(f"    first-seen: {first_seen_b}")
    print()
    print("  What this demonstrates:")
    print("    - The ledger commits to *artifact hashes*, not artifacts.")
    print("    - The ledger records the *order of commits*, not the")
    print("      order of events. In Case B, the citation was claimed")
    print("      before the revocation but committed after it.")
    print("    - Inclusion proofs let a client prove a specific")
    print("      commit is in a specific tree head without trusting")
    print("      the log operator.")
    print("    - The tree head is federation-signed; a client that")
    print("      pins the federation key knows the head is authentic.")
    print("    - The artifact itself (its meaning, its signature,")
    print("      its truth) is NOT in the ledger's scope. That's")
    print("      C13–C60's job.")
    print()
    print("  Anchor (public domain, Emily Dickinson):")
    print("    'Forever – is composed of Nows –'")
    print("    'Tis not a different time –'")

    audit = {
        "case_a": {
            "chain_valid": chain_a.valid,
            "head_signed": head_a_ok,
            "tree_size": log_a.size(),
            "root_hash": head_a.root_hash,
            "proofs": proofs_a,
            "first_seen": first_seen,
        },
        "case_b": {
            "chain_valid": chain_b.valid,
            "head_signed": head_b_ok,
            "tree_size": log_b.size(),
            "root_hash": head_b.root_hash,
            "proofs": proofs_b,
            "first_seen": first_seen_b,
        },
    }
    (path / "lcs_demo.json").write_text(
        json.dumps(audit, indent=2))
    print(f"\n  → {path}/lcs_demo.json")
    return audit
```

Tests (multiverse_c62_test.py)

```python
import json
import tempfile
from pathlib import Path

import pytest

from multiverse_c13 import HAS_CRYPTO, KeyPair, canonical_bytes
from multiverse_c62 import (
    CommitmentRecord, verify_commitment,
    _leaf_hash, _internal_hash, _level_sizes,
    merkle_root, inclusion_proof, verify_inclusion,
    CommitmentLog, ChainVerdict, verify_commitment_chain,
    SignedTreeHead, verify_tree_head,
    CheckpointPublisher,
    artifact_hash,
    demo,
    _hash_payload,
)


pytestmark = pytest.mark.skipif(
    not HAS_CRYPTO, reason="cryptography not installed")


# =====================================================================
# Helpers
# =====================================================================

def _make_log(n=3):
    log = CommitmentLog()
    kp = KeyPair.generate()
    records = []
    for i in range(n):
        r = log.append(
            artifact_hash=_hash_payload(f"art-{i}".encode()),
            artifact_kind=f"kind-{i}",
            committer_world_id=f"world:{i}",
            committer_kp=kp,
        )
        records.append(r)
    return log, kp, records


# =====================================================================
# CommitmentRecord
# =====================================================================

def test_record_validates_fields():
    print("=== CommitmentRecord: validates fields ===")
    with pytest.raises(ValueError):
        CommitmentRecord(
            commit_index=-1,
            artifact_hash="aa" * 32,
            artifact_kind="x",
            committer_world_id="w",
            committer_public_key="aa" * 32,
            timestamp_claimed="t",
            signature="s",
            previous_commit_hash=None)
    with pytest.raises(ValueError):
        CommitmentRecord(
            commit_index=0,
            artifact_hash="short",
            artifact_kind="x",
            committer_world_id="w",
            committer_public_key="aa" * 32,
            timestamp_claimed="t",
            signature="s",
            previous_commit_hash=None)


def test_record_signature_verifies():
    print("=== verify_commitment: signature valid ===")
    log, kp, records = _make_log(1)
    r = records[0]
    assert verify_commitment(r)


def test_record_wrong_key():
    print("=== verify_commitment: wrong key → False ===")
    log, kp, records = _make_log(1)
    r = records[0]
    tampered = CommitmentRecord(
        commit_index=r.commit_index,
        artifact_hash=r.artifact_hash,
        artifact_kind=r.artifact_kind,
        committer_world_id=r.committer_world_id,
        committer_public_key=KeyPair.generate().public_key_hex(),
        timestamp_claimed=r.timestamp_claimed,
        signature=r.signature,
        previous_commit_hash=r.previous_commit_hash)
    assert not verify_commitment(tampered)


def test_record_tampered_payload():
    print("=== verify_commitment: tampered artifact_hash → False ===")
    log, kp, records = _make_log(1)
    r = records[0]
    tampered = CommitmentRecord(
        commit_index=r.commit_index,
        artifact_hash="ff" * 32,
        artifact_kind=r.artifact_kind,
        committer_world_id=r.committer_world_id,
        committer_public_key=r.committer_public_key,
        timestamp_claimed=r.timestamp_claimed,
        signature=r.signature,
        previous_commit_hash=r.previous_commit_hash)
    assert not verify_commitment(tampered)


def test_record_json_roundtrip():
    print("=== CommitmentRecord: JSON roundtrip ===")
    log, kp, records = _make_log(1)
    wire = json.dumps(records[0].to_dict())
    revived = CommitmentRecord.from_dict(json.loads(wire))
    assert verify_commitment(revived)
    assert revived.ledger_commit_hash() == \
        records[0].ledger_commit_hash()


# =====================================================================
# CommitmentLog
# =====================================================================

def test_log_append_assigns_indices():
    print("=== Log: append assigns monotonic indices ===")
    log, kp, records = _make_log(3)
    for i, r in enumerate(records):
        assert r.commit_index == i
    assert log.size() == 3


def test_log_append_chains_previous_hash():
    print("=== Log: append chains previous_commit_hash ===")
    log, kp, records = _make_log(3)
    assert records[0].previous_commit_hash is None
    assert records[1].previous_commit_hash == \
        records[0].ledger_commit_hash()
    assert records[2].previous_commit_hash == \
        records[1].ledger_commit_hash()


def test_log_append_rejects_bad_hash():
    print("=== Log: append rejects bad artifact_hash ===")
    log = CommitmentLog()
    kp = KeyPair.generate()
    for bad in ("short", "", "gg" * 32, 123):
        with pytest.raises((ValueError, TypeError)):
            log.append(
                artifact_hash=bad,
                artifact_kind="x",
                committer_world_id="w",
                committer_kp=kp)


def test_log_get_commit():
    print("=== Log: get_commit returns all for a hash ===")
    log = CommitmentLog()
    kp = KeyPair.generate()
    h = "aa" * 32
    log.append(h, "kind-a", "world:1", kp)
    log.append("bb" * 32, "kind-b", "world:2", kp)
    log.append(h, "kind-a", "world:3", kp)
    matches = log.get_commit(h)
    assert len(matches) == 2
    assert matches[0].commit_index == 0
    assert matches[1].commit_index == 2


def test_log_get_commits_by_kind():
    print("=== Log: get_commits_by_kind ===")
    log = CommitmentLog()
    kp = KeyPair.generate()
    log.append("aa" * 32, "kind-x", "world:1", kp)
    log.append("bb" * 32, "kind-y", "world:2", kp)
    log.append("cc" * 32, "kind-x", "world:3", kp)
    matches = log.get_commits_by_kind("kind-x")
    assert len(matches) == 2
    # Since index
    matches_from_1 = log.get_commits_by_kind(
        "kind-x", since_index=1)
    assert len(matches_from_1) == 1


def test_log_get_commit_chain():
    print("=== Log: get_commit_chain clamps bounds ===")
    log, kp, records = _make_log(5)
    chain = log.get_commit_chain(1, 4)
    assert len(chain) == 3
    # Out of bounds
    assert log.get_commit_chain(10, 20) == []
    assert log.get_commit_chain(-5, 2) == \
        log.get_commit_chain(0, 2)


def test_log_first_commit_index():
    print("=== Log: first_commit_index ===")
    log = CommitmentLog()
    kp = KeyPair.generate()
    h = "aa" * 32
    log.append("bb" * 32, "k", "w", kp)
    log.append(h, "k", "w", kp)
    log.append(h, "k", "w", kp)
    assert log.first_commit_index(h) == 1
    assert log.first_commit_index("ff" * 32) is None


# =====================================================================
# Merkle tree
# =====================================================================

def test_level_sizes():
    print("=== _level_sizes ===")
    assert _level_sizes(1) == [1]
    assert _level_sizes(2) == [2, 1]
    assert _level_sizes(3) == [3, 2, 1]
    assert _level_sizes(5) == [5, 3, 2, 1]
    assert _level_sizes(8) == [8, 4, 2, 1]
    assert _level_sizes(0) == []


def test_merkle_root_empty():
    print("=== merkle_root: empty → empty string ===")
    assert merkle_root([]) == ""


def test_merkle_root_single():
    print("=== merkle_root: one leaf → leaf hash ===")
    h = "aa" * 32
    assert merkle_root([h]) == _leaf_hash(h)


def test_merkle_root_two():
    print("=== merkle_root: two leaves ===")
    a, b = "aa" * 32, "bb" * 32
    assert merkle_root([a, b]) == _internal_hash(
        _leaf_hash(a), _leaf_hash(b))


def test_merkle_root_three():
    print("=== merkle_root: three leaves (promotion) ===")
    a, b, c = "aa" * 32, "bb" * 32, "cc" * 32
    expected = _internal_hash(
        _internal_hash(_leaf_hash(a), _leaf_hash(b)),
        _leaf_hash(c))
    assert merkle_root([a, b, c]) == expected


def test_merkle_root_deterministic():
    print("=== merkle_root: deterministic ===")
    leaves = ["aa" * 32, "bb" * 32, "cc" * 32, "dd" * 32]
    assert merkle_root(leaves) == merkle_root(list(leaves))


# =====================================================================
# Inclusion proofs
# =====================================================================

def test_inclusion_proof_single():
    print("=== inclusion_proof: single leaf → empty proof ===")
    assert inclusion_proof(["aa" * 32], 0) == []


def test_inclusion_proof_two():
    print("=== inclusion_proof: two leaves ===")
    a, b = "aa" * 32, "bb" * 32
    proof_a = inclusion_proof([a, b], 0)
    proof_b = inclusion_proof([a, b], 1)
    assert proof_a == [_leaf_hash(b)]
    assert proof_b == [_leaf_hash(a)]


def test_inclusion_proof_three_promoted():
    print("=== inclusion_proof: three leaves, last promoted ===")
    a, b, c = "aa" * 32, "bb" * 32, "cc" * 32
    # Leaf 0: sibling b, then sibling c (at next level, index 0
    # of size-2 level whose sibling is c)
    proof_0 = inclusion_proof([a, b, c], 0)
    assert len(proof_0) == 2
    # Leaf 2 (c): promoted at level 0, so no sibling.
    # At level 1, sibling is H(a,b).
    proof_2 = inclusion_proof([a, b, c], 2)
    assert len(proof_2) == 1


def test_inclusion_proof_range():
    print("=== inclusion_proof: out-of-range → IndexError ===")
    with pytest.raises(IndexError):
        inclusion_proof(["aa" * 32], 1)
    with pytest.raises(IndexError):
        inclusion_proof(["aa" * 32], -1)
    with pytest.raises(ValueError):
        inclusion_proof([], 0)


def test_verify_inclusion_happy():
    print("=== verify_inclusion: happy path ===")
    leaves = ["aa" * 32, "bb" * 32, "cc" * 32, "dd" * 32]
    root = merkle_root(leaves)
    for i in range(4):
        proof = inclusion_proof(leaves, i)
        assert verify_inclusion(leaves[i], proof, i, 4, root)


def test_verify_inclusion_three():
    print("=== verify_inclusion: three leaves (odd) ===")
    leaves = ["aa" * 32, "bb" * 32, "cc" * 32]
    root = merkle_root(leaves)
    for i in range(3):
        proof = inclusion_proof(leaves, i)
        assert verify_inclusion(leaves[i], proof, i, 3, root)


def test_verify_inclusion_five():
    print("=== verify_inclusion: five leaves (odd twice) ===")
    leaves = [_hash_payload(f"x{i}".encode()) for i in range(5)]
    root = merkle_root(leaves)
    for i in range(5):
        proof = inclusion_proof(leaves, i)
        assert verify_inclusion(leaves[i], proof, i, 5, root)


def test_verify_inclusion_wrong_leaf():
    print("=== verify_inclusion: wrong leaf → False ===")
    leaves = ["aa" * 32, "bb" * 32]
    root = merkle_root(leaves)
    proof = inclusion_proof(leaves, 0)
    wrong_leaf = "ff" * 32
    assert not verify_inclusion(
        wrong_leaf, proof, 0, 2, root)


def test_verify_inclusion_wrong_root():
    print("=== verify_inclusion: wrong root → False ===")
    leaves = ["aa" * 32, "bb" * 32]
    proof = inclusion_proof(leaves, 0)
    assert not verify_inclusion(
        leaves[0], proof, 0, 2, "00" * 32)


def test_verify_inclusion_tampered_proof():
    print("=== verify_inclusion: tampered proof → False ===")
    leaves = ["aa" * 32, "bb" * 32, "cc" * 32]
    root = merkle_root(leaves)
    proof = inclusion_proof(leaves, 0)
    tampered = ["00" * 32] + proof[1:]
    assert not verify_inclusion(
        leaves[0], tampered, 0, 3, root)


def test_verify_inclusion_extra_hashes():
    print("=== verify_inclusion: extra hashes → False ===")
    leaves = ["aa" * 32, "bb" * 32]
    root = merkle_root(leaves)
    proof = inclusion_proof(leaves, 0)
    extra = proof + ["00" * 32]
    assert not verify_inclusion(
        leaves[0], extra, 0, 2, root)


def test_verify_inclusion_empty_proof():
    print("=== verify_inclusion: empty proof for n>1 → False ===")
    leaves = ["aa" * 32, "bb" * 32]
    root = merkle_root(leaves)
    assert not verify_inclusion(
        leaves[0], [], 0, 2, root)


# =====================================================================
# Chain verification
# =====================================================================

def test_chain_verify_happy():
    print("=== verify_commitment_chain: happy ===")
    log, kp, records = _make_log(5)
    v = verify_commitment_chain(log.entries())
    assert v.valid


def test_chain_verify_tampered_index():
    print("=== chain: tampered index → invalid ===")
    log, kp, records = _make_log(3)
    # Tamper record 1's index
    tampered = CommitmentRecord(
        commit_index=5,
        artifact_hash=records[1].artifact_hash,
        artifact_kind=records[1].artifact_kind,
        committer_world_id=records[1].committer_world_id,
        committer_public_key=records[1].committer_public_key,
        timestamp_claimed=records[1].timestamp_claimed,
        signature=records[1].signature,
        previous_commit_hash=records[1].previous_commit_hash)
    entries = [records[0], tampered, records[2]]
    v = verify_commitment_chain(entries)
    assert not v.valid
    assert v.bad_index == 1


def test_chain_verify_broken_link():
    print("=== chain: broken previous_commit_hash → invalid ===")
    log, kp, records = _make_log(3)
    # Tamper record 2's previous_commit_hash
    tampered = CommitmentRecord(
        commit_index=2,
        artifact_hash=records[2].artifact_hash,
        artifact_kind=records[2].artifact_kind,
        committer_world_id=records[2].committer_world_id,
        committer_public_key=records[2].committer_public_key,
        timestamp_claimed=records[2].timestamp_claimed,
        signature=records[2].signature,
        previous_commit_hash="ff" * 32)
    entries = [records[0], records[1], tampered]
    v = verify_commitment_chain(entries)
    assert not v.valid
    assert v.bad_index == 2


def test_chain_verify_tampered_sig():
    print("=== chain: tampered signature → invalid ===")
    log, kp, records = _make_log(3)
    # Tamper record 1's signature but keep everything else
    attacker = KeyPair.generate()
    tampered = CommitmentRecord(
        commit_index=1,
        artifact_hash=records[1].artifact_hash,
        artifact_kind=records[1].artifact_kind,
        committer_world_id=records[1].committer_world_id,
        committer_public_key=records[1].committer_public_key,
        timestamp_claimed=records[1].timestamp_claimed,
        signature=attacker.sign(
            records[1].commitment_payload()).hex(),
        previous_commit_hash=records[1].previous_commit_hash)
    entries = [records[0], tampered, records[2]]
    v = verify_commitment_chain(entries)
    assert not v.valid
    assert v.bad_index == 1


def test_chain_verify_empty():
    print("=== chain: empty log is trivially valid ===")
    v = verify_commitment_chain([])
    assert v.valid


# =====================================================================
# Tree head
# =====================================================================

def test_tree_head_sign_verify():
    print("=== SignedTreeHead: sign and verify ===")
    log, kp, _ = _make_log(3)
    fed_kp = KeyPair.generate()
    publisher = CheckpointPublisher(log, fed_kp)
    head = publisher.publish()
    assert head.tree_size == 3
    assert head.root_hash == log.merkle_root()
    assert verify_tree_head(head, fed_kp.public_key_hex())


def test_tree_head_wrong_key():
    print("=== SignedTreeHead: wrong key → False ===")
    log, _, _ = _make_log(3)
    fed_kp = KeyPair.generate()
    head = CheckpointPublisher(log, fed_kp).publish()
    wrong = KeyPair.generate()
    assert not verify_tree_head(head, wrong.public_key_hex())


def test_tree_head_json_roundtrip():
    print("=== SignedTreeHead: JSON roundtrip ===")
    log, _, _ = _make_log(3)
    fed_kp = KeyPair.generate()
    head = CheckpointPublisher(log, fed_kp).publish()
    wire = json.dumps(head.to_dict())
    revived = SignedTreeHead.from_dict(json.loads(wire))
    assert verify_tree_head(revived, fed_kp.public_key_hex())


def test_tree_head_empty_log():
    print("=== SignedTreeHead: empty log ===")
    log = CommitmentLog()
    fed_kp = KeyPair.generate()
    head = CheckpointPublisher(log, fed_kp).publish()
    assert head.tree_size == 0
    assert head.root_hash == ""
    assert verify_tree_head(head, fed_kp.public_key_hex())


# =====================================================================
# Integration: append, checkpoint, prove, verify
# =====================================================================

def test_full_flow():
    print("=== Full flow: append 4 commits, checkpoint, prove ===")
    log = CommitmentLog()
    kp = KeyPair.generate()
    hashes = [_hash_payload(f"h{i}".encode()) for i in range(4)]
    for h in hashes:
        log.append(
            artifact_hash=h,
            artifact_kind="test",
            committer_world_id="world:test",
            committer_kp=kp)
    fed_kp = KeyPair.generate()
    head = CheckpointPublisher(log, fed_kp).publish()
    assert verify_tree_head(head, fed_kp.public_key_hex())
    for i, h in enumerate(hashes):
        proof = log.inclusion_proof_for(i)
        assert verify_inclusion(
            log.entries()[i].ledger_commit_hash(),
            proof, i, log.size(), head.root_hash)

def test_demo(tmp_path):
    print("=== Demo: Appendix A scenario ===")
    audit = demo(artifact_dir=str(tmp_path))
    a = audit["case_a"]
    assert a["chain_valid"] is True
    assert a["head_signed"] is True
    assert a["tree_size"] == 3
    assert all(p["verified"] for p in a["proofs"])
    # Claimed order matches commit order in Case A
    assert a["first_seen"]["establishment"] == 0
    assert a["first_seen"]["citation"] == 1
    assert a["first_seen"]["revocation"] == 2

    b = audit["case_b"]
    assert b["chain_valid"] is True
    assert b["head_signed"] is True
    assert b["tree_size"] == 3
    assert all(p["verified"] for p in b["proofs"])
    # In Case B, commit order differs from claimed order:
    # revocation (claim 18:00) was committed at index 1,
    # citation (claim 17:00) at index 2
    assert b["first_seen"]["establishment"] == 0
    assert b["first_seen"]["revocation"] == 1
    assert b["first_seen"]["citation"] == 2
    # And the claimed timestamps confirm the intended inconsistency
    revocation_claim = next(
        p["claimed"] for p in b["proofs"]
        if p["kind"] == "contract_revocation")
    citation_claim = next(
        p["claimed"] for p in b["proofs"]
        if p["kind"] == "citation_act")
    assert citation_claim < revocation_claim
    assert (tmp_path / "lcs_demo.json").exists()
```

What This Establishes

Four properties, each one making the C61 spec a working artifact rather than a promise:

1. Inclusion proofs are checkable without trusting the log. test_verify_inclusion_happy, test_verify_inclusion_three, test_verify_inclusion_five — proofs verify against a Merkle root for tree sizes 4, 3, and 5. test_verify_inclusion_tampered_proof — a tampered proof fails. test_verify_inclusion_extra_hashes — extra hashes in the proof fail (rejected, not silently ignored). This is the property that turns "the log operator says this commit is in the log" into "I have mathematically checked that it is."
2. The tree head is federation-signed, and verifies independently. test_tree_head_sign_verify, test_tree_head_wrong_key, test_tree_head_empty_log — a signed tree head can be verified against a pinned federation key, without any log access. A client that pins the federation's key and receives a tree head has a root it can prove things against. This is the whole point of CT-style checkpointing: the log operator cannot rewind without producing a different signed head, which the client can detect.
3. The chain is what makes the log append-only. test_chain_verify_happy, test_chain_verify_tampered_index, test_chain_verify_broken_link, test_chain_verify_tampered_sig — the previous_commit_hash linkage means reordering, inserting, or removing an entry breaks the chain. This is different from the Merkle tree's property (which is about inclusion); it's about continuity. Both are necessary; C62 provides both.
4. The C61 Appendix A example is now executable. test_demo runs both cases:
   · Case A: commit order matches claimed order. Everyone agrees.
   · Case B: citation (claimed 17:00) is committed after revocation (claimed 18:00). The ledger order is establishment(0), revocation(1), citation(2). The claimed order is establishment, citation, revocation. These are two different facts, both checkable, both recorded.
   This is the honest answer to "what does a ledger give the arc?" — it gives the fact of ordering, not the resolution of disputes. A dispute between Case A and Case B is a policy question. The ledger makes both cases legible.

The Honest Limits

· No consistency proofs. A log operator could sign two different tree heads of the same size with different roots. verify_tree_head would verify both. Detecting this requires either a consistency proof (CT-style) or monitoring by a third party. This is what §12.C's federation-operated checkpointing exists to prevent — but C62 doesn't do the prevention, it only does the production and verification of individual heads.
· No fork detection. Same as above, seen from the operator side.
· No persistence. Everything is in-memory. Serialization is trivial (to_dict / from_dict on each record and head), but a caller who loses their log loses their ordering. C49's bundle pattern applies.
· No data availability. A commitment proves the artifact existed; it doesn't prove you can still find it. artifact_hash() returns the hash but doesn't help you re-fetch the artifact. A production deployment needs its own data-availability layer.
· Timestamp is a claim. The timestamp_claimed field is signed by the committer, so tampering is caught, but backdating is not. The ledger's order is what it provides; the time is what the committer claims.
· Single-writer. The reference implementation's append is one-at-a-time. A real ledger needs consensus to assign commit indices; the interface here is what that consensus would produce.

What Was Run

The tests in multiverse_c62_test.py have not been executed against a live Python environment in this session. The expected output derives from the test logic and the behavior of hashlib.sha256 and cryptography's Ed25519 primitives. Per the house rule, this is the honest status.

The arc is now complete in a specific sense: it can answer what the substrate is (C1–C21), what trust looks like (C24–C40), what architectures it supports (C41–C52), how worlds communicate (C55–C60), and how the federation's memory is shared (C61, C62). What remains is not architecture or protocol — it's deployment and application.
